projects.title: A HYBRID STATISTICAL AND DEEP LEARNING APPROACH FOR BITCOIN TRADING SIGNAL DETECTION
projects.title_slide: A HYBRID STATISTICAL AND DEEP LEARNING APPROACH FOR BITCOIN TRADING SIGNAL DETECTION
projects.student_description: This project turned Bitcoin price predictions into clear buy or sell signals using machine learning. It tested different methods such as K Means, XGBoost, and LSTM, and found that XGBoost worked best while LSTM needs more improvement. The results were shown in a Streamlit app, making the trading decisions easy to view and understand.

summary.plain: This project tried to turn past Bitcoin prices into simple 'buy' (long) or 'sell' (short) signals. The team built extra clues from the price history and gold prices, then trained two models; a tree-based model (XGBoost) got about 70% right while a deep-learning model (LSTM) did no better than a coin flip. They showed the whole pipeline in a Streamlit app.
summary.technical: Minute-level Bitcoin OHLCV data from Kaggle was combined with minute-level gold prices and transformed into technical indicators, lagged features and rolling support/resistance features. K-means clustering produced clustered support/resistance zones and a Monte Carlo simulation produced probabilistic (5th/95th percentile) support/resistance features; the Triple Barrier Method generated Long/Short labels (73% Long / 27% Short). An XGBoost classifier (300 boosting rounds, fixed hyperparameters, scale_pos_weight for imbalance) was trained with an 80/20 time-based split, and a PyTorch LSTM on 60-step sequences was trained on ~37k samples for comparison. XGBoost reported 70% accuracy, 74% Long precision and 80% Long recall (90% on the comparison slide), while the LSTM reported 50% accuracy, 80% precision and 41% recall. The pipeline was demonstrated in a Streamlit dashboard.
summary.question: How can historical Bitcoin price data be used to algorithmically identify reliable support and resistance levels and guide long or short trading decisions?
summary.problem: Trading decisions in a volatile crypto market often rely on subjective judgment; the project seeks consistent, data-driven long/short signals.
summary.beneficiary: Retail investors / traders
summary.inputs: Minute-level Bitcoin and gold OHLCV prices and derived technical, support/resistance, clustering and Monte Carlo features
summary.outputs: Binary Long/Short trading signal per timestep
summary.results: XGBoost: 70% accuracy, 74% precision (Long), 80% recall (Long; 90% on comparison slide), F1 81% (Long). LSTM: 50% accuracy, 80% precision, 41% recall, 54% F1. XGBoost chosen as the actionable model.

projects.title: AccessMap
projects.student_description: Its basically a ai powered map that helps disabled individuals navigate their way

summary.plain: AccessMap asks whether data can predict which sidewalks a wheelchair user can actually use. The team trained a random forest on Amsterdam sidewalk measurements and on crowd-labeled US addresses, found and removed a hidden geographic bias, and built a Streamlit app with a sidewalk checker and an address similarity search.
summary.technical: Two datasets were modeled separately with the same pipeline: the Amsterdam PMR sidewalk dataset (72,274 measured segments; width, curb height, crossing, length) and the CrowdFlower/Figure Eight Housing: Wheelchairs dataset (10,104 crowd-labeled US addresses). PMR labels were derived from a width + curb-height rule; data were cleaned, encoded, and a Random Forest was trained and scored on a 20% hold-out set, followed by feature-importance audits. The Housing model initially reached 67.4% accuracy vs an 85.3% majority baseline with 'state' driving 89% of decisions; after dropping state it reached 85.0% (recall on bad sidewalks 0.01), reported as a null result. For PMR, threshold tuning (0.5 to 0.65) failed because probabilities were pinned at 0/1; adding curb_height_max and a missing-value flag gave 100% accuracy, which the team notes only recovers their own label rule. ModernBERT embeddings (768-dim, 6,425 addresses) with FAISS similarity search power an address search in a Streamlit app deployed to the cloud.

projects.title: Adaptive Detection for Fraudulent Transactions
projects.student_description: Our project's goal is to determine if and how significantly an adaptive anomaly detection model improves fraud detection accuracy over time.

summary.plain: This project checks whether a fraud detector that keeps re-learning from recent transactions works better than one trained once. Using millions of simulated mobile-money transactions, the team compared a fixed Isolation Forest anomaly detector to one retrained every few days. The retrained model caught more fraud but also raised far more false alarms.
summary.technical: The PaySim synthetic mobile money dataset (6M+ transactions, ~0.13% fraud) was explored with distribution, time and correlation plots. Numeric transaction features (amount, balances, encoded transaction type, time index) were fed to an unsupervised Isolation Forest whose anomaly score is thresholded into a fraud prediction. A static model trained once was compared with an adaptive model trained on the first N days and then retrained on recent transactions with updated thresholds every 5-10 days (rolling window). Evaluation used precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC and confusion matrices on ~1.94M transactions: from the charts, the static model had precision ~0.42, recall ~0.31, F1 ~0.36 and ROC-AUC ~0.93, while the adaptive model had precision ~0.045, recall ~0.56, F1 ~0.08 and ROC-AUC ~0.93 (75,603 vs 2,801 false positives).
summary.question: Does an adaptive anomaly detection model improve fraud detection accuracy over time compared with a static model?
summary.problem: Fraud detection models become outdated as user behavior changes, yet many banks use static rules or static models.
summary.beneficiary: Banks / mobile money providers and their customers
summary.inputs: Transaction type, amount, old/new balances, time step
summary.outputs: Anomaly score thresholded into a fraud / normal prediction
summary.results: Read from charts (pdf p11-13): static precision ~0.42, recall ~0.31, F1 ~0.36, ROC-AUC ~0.93; adaptive precision ~0.045, recall ~0.56, F1 ~0.08, ROC-AUC ~0.93. Adaptive caught 3,554 vs 1,988 frauds but raised 75,603 vs 2,801 false positives.

projects.title: Advanced Phishing Detection
projects.student_description: We developed a general phishing detector and explored how modern day phishing tactics are evolving and becoming more advanced. After developing our strong performing MVP, we hope to further develop it to better adapt to more advanced phishing tactics.

summary.plain: This project built a detector that reads the text of an email and decides whether it is phishing. The team cleaned and combined several public email datasets, then trained and compared five standard machine-learning models; most reached about 97% accuracy, with LightGBM slightly ahead.
summary.technical: Several curated phishing email datasets from a figshare collection (including Assassin, CEAS, Ling and Nigerian) were combined and balanced by undersampling to 50k emails (25k per class). Email bodies were cleaned (duplicates/missing dropped, URLs, emails and punctuation removed, lowercased) and normalized with NLTK tokenization, stopword removal and lemmatization. LightGBM, SVM, logistic regression, random forest and naive Bayes were trained and evaluated on an 8,600-email test set with classification reports and confusion matrices; LightGBM also reported cross-validation accuracies around 0.97-0.98. Reported accuracies: LightGBM 97.7%, SVM 97.3%, logistic regression 97.2%, random forest 97.1%, naive Bayes 94.1%.

summary.plain: This project used a large language model to write fake spam messages and then tested whether adding them to training data helps spam filters. The team trained five standard spam classifiers on a public SMS dataset, generated example spam with the Qwen LLM, and compared results before and after adding the generated messages.
summary.technical: The UCI SMS Spam Collection (5,572 messages) was used to train logistic regression, naive Bayes, linear SVM, random forest and XGBoost classifiers evaluated on a ~1,115-message test split. Qwen-1.5-4B (instruction-tuned) was prompted with spam intents (e.g. crypto giveaways, lottery wins, fake job offers) to generate adversarial spam; the slides describe supervised fine-tuning on UCI spam, but this is not clearly demonstrated. Generated spam was added to the data (5,578 samples total) and classifiers re-evaluated. From pdf p12, accuracies before/after were: logistic regression 0.970/0.965, naive Bayes 0.978/0.974, linear SVM 0.990/0.985, random forest 0.981/0.973, XGBoost 0.978/0.974. The full iterative adversarial feedback loop is described as methodology and listed as next steps.
summary.question: How does adversarially generated spam impact the robustness and generalization performance of modern spam classifiers over multiple feedback cycles?
summary.problem: Spam filters struggle to keep up with evolving threats without exposure to adversarial examples.
summary.beneficiary: Security researchers and spam-filter developers
summary.subdomain: SMS/email spam detection with LLM-generated adversarial data
summary.inputs: SMS message text; prompts with spam intents for the LLM
summary.outputs: Spam/ham label; generated spam messages
summary.results: Before adding generated spam: LR 96.95%, NB 97.85%, Linear SVM 99.01%, RF 98.12%, XGBoost 97.85% accuracy. After (UCI + generated, 5,578 samples): LR 96.51%, NB 97.40%, Linear SVM 98.48%, RF 97.31%, XGBoost 97.40%. Qualitative examples of generated spam shown.

projects.title: Agent-EYE
projects.student_description: Security Risk Assessment for Agentic AI Models

summary.plain: Agent-EYE audits how risky actions by AI agents are scored. Using a simulated dataset of 2,200 AI-agent requests, the team predicted each request's risk score with XGBoost, explained what drives it with SHAP, and tested whether the risk score alone can decide if an action should be allowed or blocked.
summary.technical: The Kaggle Agentic AI Security Risk Dataset (2,200 simulated agent requests x 15 columns, 12 categorical) was explored for correlations, class imbalance and role-level bias, then categorical features were encoded. Q1: an XGBoost regressor predicted action risk score from agent role, action, tool, exfiltration risk, sensitivity, etc.; with user_role it reached RMSE 8.365, R^2 0.914, MAE 6.17 versus a baseline RMSE of 28.49 (pdf p12), and SHAP showed permission_match and data_exfiltration_risk as the main drivers. Removing hard-to-obtain predictors still gave R^2 0.844. Q2: multinomial logistic regression predicting access decision from risk score alone reached only 59% accuracy; after removing Needs_Human_Approval, the binary model achieved 93% recall on Blocked and 64% on Allowed, using a stratified train-test split.
summary.question: Can we predict the security risk score of an AI agent's action based on its autonomy level, permissions, requested tools, and resource access patterns, and decide whether an agent should be granted access based on that score?
summary.problem: AI agents acting with less human oversight create new security risks; risk scorers and access decisions need auditing for coherence and blind spots.
summary.beneficiary: Security teams and auditors overseeing agentic AI systems
summary.inputs: Agent request metadata: role, autonomy level, action, tool, resource sensitivity/type, permission match, prompt injection flag, exfiltration risk, failed attempts, user role
summary.outputs: Predicted action risk score (0-100); access decision (Blocked/Allowed)
summary.results: XGBoost risk regression: RMSE 8.365, R^2 0.914, MAE 6.17 vs baseline RMSE 28.49 (R^2 0.844 without exfiltration/permission features). Logistic regression access decision from risk alone: 59% accuracy for 3 classes; binary version 93% recall Blocked, 64% recall Allowed.

projects.title: AI + Misinformation Modeling Theme
projects.student_description: Our project uses machine learning to detect hallucinated AI-generated responses using the RAGTruth dataset. We compared Logistic Regression and Decision Tree models and deployed our best-performing model through an interactive Streamlit application.

summary.plain: This project tries to automatically spot when an AI chatbot's answer contains made-up information (a 'hallucination'). The team turned AI responses from the RAGTruth dataset into word-based features, trained two simple models, and put the better one (logistic regression, about 75% accurate) into a Streamlit web app.
summary.technical: The RAGTruth corpus (17,790 LLM responses with a binary has_hallucination label) was explored by response length, domain and source model (GPT-4, Llama-2-7B, Mistral-7B). Text features were built with TF-IDF (slides also list contextual similarity, response length and NER features), and data were split 80/20. Logistic regression and a decision tree were trained as binary classifiers; on 3,558 test responses logistic regression reached 74.5% accuracy (macro precision 0.76, recall 0.72, F1 0.72; hallucinated-class recall 0.55) and the decision tree 67.9% (F1 0.67). Coefficient and impurity-based feature importances were plotted, and the logistic regression model was deployed in a Streamlit app that scores user-pasted responses.

projects.student_description: Using Natural Language Processing (NLP) to perform sentiment analysis on restaurant reviews.

summary.plain: This project teaches a computer to tell whether a restaurant review is positive or negative. Reviews were cleaned and turned into word counts, then four standard models were trained; all reached roughly 87-89% accuracy, with Linear SVC the most consistent.
summary.technical: A Kaggle restaurant reviews dataset was preprocessed (lowercasing, punctuation and stopword removal, tokenization) with and without spaCy lemmatization, and vectorized with bag-of-words (CountVectorizer) and TF-IDF. Naive Bayes, logistic regression, Linear SVC and random forest were trained on an 80/20 split and evaluated with accuracy, precision, recall and F1 on 2,000 test reviews (515 negative, 1,485 positive). From pdf p6-7, accuracies were ~0.87-0.89 across configurations (e.g. BoW logistic regression 0.890, Naive Bayes 0.889; lemmatized TF-IDF Linear SVC 0.893), except lemmatized TF-IDF Naive Bayes at 0.800 with negative recall 0.23. Negative-class recall was consistently lower, attributed to class imbalance; lemmatization did not help.

projects.title: AI in healthcare dosage labelling
projects.student_description: Our project focused on numerical medical dosage labelling with a neural network.

summary.plain: This project is a first step toward a voice tool that helps healthcare workers record medication doses safely. The team trained neural networks to recognize spoken digits 0-9 from audio clips, compared several network designs, and added sound effects like pitch shifts and noise to make the training data more varied.
summary.technical: The AudioMNIST dataset (30,000 .wav files of spoken digits 0-9) was used with an 80/20 train/test split. Audio was summarized into hand-crafted features: MFCC, delta and delta-delta MFCC (mean + sd), spectral centroid/rolloff/bandwidth, zero-crossing rate, RMS energy and chroma. Dense neural networks were compared: a 3-layer base (56%), deeper (99.5%), wide (98%) and residual (99%) variants, and voice-adapted fine-tuned versions (10%, then 75%). The final model has 5 dense layers (256-128-64-32-10), batch normalization, dropout 0.4-0.1, Adam (lr 0.0005) with plateau reduction, early stopping and ~74k parameters, trained on an augmented set (pitch shift, time stretch, volume variation, background noise) including 100 additional recordings of a team member; training curves show ~100% validation accuracy. The team notes the model sometimes responds randomly when digits are not spoken 'perfectly'.
summary.question: Can we train a model to achieve >60% accuracy classifying spoken digits, using supervised learning and classification techniques, to assist healthcare workers in dosage labeling?
summary.problem: Nearly half of medication errors occur at prescribing/ordering, and clinicians spend much time on documentation; voice-based dosage entry could reduce errors and workload.
summary.beneficiary: Healthcare workers recording medication dosages
summary.subdomain: Spoken-digit recognition for medication dosage labeling

summary.results: Architecture comparison: base 56%, deeper 99.5%, wide 98%, residual 99%, voice-adapted 10% then 75%. Final augmented model: validation accuracy ~1.0 on training curves (no test number stated). Qualitatively unreliable on imperfectly spoken digits.

projects.title: AI Pathologist
projects.student_description: It detects breast cancer through histology images. It gives an answer that shows the probabilities of 4 different models and which one gave the best answer.

summary.plain: This project built a website where you upload a microscope image of breast tissue and an AI tells you whether it looks normal, benign, or one of two kinds of cancer. Four different image models vote on the answer, and colored heatmaps show which parts of the image the models looked at.
summary.technical: About 9,000 breast histology images in four classes (Benign, Carcinoma In Situ, Invasive Carcinoma, Normal) were deduplicated with MD5 hashing to 6,995 unique images, resized to 224x224 and ImageNet-normalized, with 30% held out for validation and testing. Four ImageNet-pretrained CNNs (ResNet50, DenseNet121, EfficientNet-B0, VGG16) were trained with a new classifier head (AdamW, lr 1e-4, batch 16, 20 epochs, class-weighted cross-entropy) and combined by soft voting. Grad-CAM++ heatmaps are produced per model. Reported accuracies are inconsistent across slides: ensemble 86.75% rising to 100% after fine-tuning (slide 3), 99.8% on a '400-image test set' chart (slide 7), and a perfect confusion matrix on a 1,128-image test set (slides 9-10). The system was deployed as a React + FastAPI web app with Supabase auth, hosted on Hugging Face, Railway and Vercel.
summary.question: Can breast tissue histology images be classified as normal, benign, or a type of malignant while highlighting the regions that influenced the decision?
summary.problem: Delayed breast cancer diagnosis and limited pathology access, especially in low and middle income countries.
summary.beneficiary: Pathologists and clinicians in resource-limited settings (prototype, not for clinical use)
summary.inputs: Breast histology image (resized to 224x224)
summary.outputs: Predicted class among 4, confidence, full probability distribution, and Grad-CAM++ heatmaps per model
summary.results: Ensemble accuracy reported as 86.75% initially and 100% / 99.8% after fine-tuning; individual models 84.00% (VGG16) to 99.75% (ResNet50) on the chart; perfect confusion matrix on 1,128 test images.

projects.student_description:
This project focuses on classifying bone conditions using deep learning models trained on X-ray images. The models used include ResNet50, modified ResNet18, Efficient Net-B3 The goal is to accurately classify images into three categories:
Osteopenia
Osteoporosis
Normal

summary.plain: This project trained computer models to look at knee X-rays and sort them into normal bone, low bone density (osteopenia) or osteoporosis. The team tried three well-known image networks and built a small web app where you upload an X-ray and get a diagnosis with a confidence score.
summary.technical: About 1,000 knee X-ray images from a public Kaggle dataset (3 classes) were quality-filtered (corrupt files, tiny images, brightness and variance checks) to ~950, enhanced with CLAHE, resized to 224x224, normalized and augmented (rotation, flip, brightness), then split 70/15/15. ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50, a modified ResNet18 and EfficientNet-B3 were fine-tuned via transfer learning. Reported test accuracies are 83% (EfficientNet), 83% (ResNet18; 83.33% with macro F1 82.9%) and 85.3% (ResNet50). A demo app averages ResNet18 and ResNet50 probabilities; the team reports the ensemble at only 40-70% for osteoporosis/osteopenia.
summary.question: Can transfer learning using pre-trained CNNs detect osteoporosis from X-ray images with an accuracy of at least 80%?
summary.problem: Osteoporosis usually goes undiagnosed until fractures occur; screening is rarely done in younger adults.
summary.beneficiary: Adults at risk of osteoporosis and clinicians doing screening
summary.inputs: Knee X-ray image
summary.outputs: Class (Normal / Osteopenia / Osteoporosis) with probabilities and confidence
summary.results: Test accuracy 83-85.3% across three CNNs; ResNet18 macro F1 82.9%; ensemble 40-70% accuracy on osteoporosis/osteopenia per the team.

projects.title: AI-Powered Accessibility Assistant for Diverse Learners
projects.title_slide: AI-POWERED ACCESSIBILITY ASSISTANT FOR DIVERSE LEARNERS
projects.student_description: The project is an AI-powered multimodal learning assistant that helps to simplify complex text based on users' reading level and learning style. The tool supports text-to-speech and vision diagrams for a diverse array of students.

summary.plain: This project built a web tool that rewrites hard school text so it is easier to read at a chosen grade level. It can also summarize, explain, give examples, break processes into steps, draw simple flowcharts and read text aloud, to help English learners and students with dyslexia or ADHD.
summary.technical: The tool uses the pretrained instruction-tuned google/flan-t5-base model without fine-tuning, prompted with a mode (simplify, summarize, explain, examples, steps) and a target grade level (3rd grade to college), with strict grade-level and sentence-length constraints. Extra components add text-to-speech audio and flowchart diagrams generated from extracted steps, all served in a Streamlit app. Evaluation used Flesch-Kincaid grade drop, sentence-length/compression ratio and a manual meaning-preservation check; most passages shrank to 60-80% of original length and 30-40 word sentences fell to ~15-25 words, but grade level did not drop much.
summary.question: How can AI simplify academic text for different reading levels while preserving meaning?
summary.problem: Manual text simplification for diverse learners is slow, inconsistent and inaccessible.
summary.beneficiary: ESL learners, students with dyslexia or ADHD, and visual learners
summary.inputs: Raw text, transformation mode, target grade level
summary.outputs: Simplified/summarized text, examples, step lists, flowchart diagrams, text-to-speech audio
summary.results: Sentences shortened (most passages compressed to 60-80% of length; long sentences cut to ~15-25 words) but Flesch-Kincaid grade level did not drop much; meaning checked manually.

projects.title: AI-Powered Recommendation System
projects.student_description: A system that uses K-Means clustering, sentiment analysis, vectorization, and cosine similarity to determine the top 3 movies a user would want to watch. A user would input the genre they would like to watch, a release date range, and a text description of what they want to see.

summary.plain: This project built a movie recommender: you type what kind of movie you are in the mood for, plus a genre, region and year range, and it suggests similar movies from a list of 5,000 popular films. It also measured the mood (positive, neutral or negative) of each movie's description.
summary.technical: Using the TMDB 5000 Movie Dataset, movie overviews and metadata (genres, cast, keywords, crew) were preprocessed (tokenization, stemming) and vectorized with TF-IDF. VADER sentiment classified each overview's tone, KMeans grouped movies into tone clusters visualized with 3D PCA, and cosine similarity between the user's free-text request and movie vectors produced recommendations, filtered by genre, region, release-year range and studio size to mitigate bias. Naive Bayes and KNN were listed as possible options. Evaluation was qualitative only, with no user ratings.

summary.problem: Streaming users face decision fatigue choosing what to watch.
summary.beneficiary: Movie viewers choosing what to watch

projects.title: AI-Powered Stock Market Predictor
projects.student_description: This project is a robust ML model that synthesizes multiple macroeconomic factors (such as volatility index, inflation, Fed rate, and unemployment rate), to predict the direction of the change in stock market prices (either up or down), as well as the magnitude of that change. We built the model using random forest classifiers and random forest regressors.

summary.plain: This project tried to predict whether the stock market would go up or down on a given day using economic signals like interest rates, unemployment, the yield curve and a market 'fear index'. Its best model was right about 54% of the time, only a little better than flipping a coin, which the team presents honestly as the difficulty of the problem.
summary.technical: Daily market data (roughly 2015-2025) were combined with macroeconomic and market indicators including the Fed funds rate, unemployment, the 10Y-3M yield curve and the VIX. projects.title: AI/ML/Data Science Salary Forecasting: 2020-2027
projects.student_description:
AI/ML professionals need salary expectations, companies need compensation planning. Market volatility creates uncertainty. Our Solution are analyzed 6 years of salary data and created predictive models by experience level
Provided evidence-based forecasts.

summary.plain: This project looked at about 29,000 salary records for AI, machine learning and data science jobs from 2020 to 2025 and used a statistics model to guess what salaries might be in 2026 and 2027. It found that salaries rose quickly until 2023 and then dipped slightly, and predicted slow growth afterwards for each experience level.
summary.technical: A salary dataset of 151,445 raw records was filtered to 29,326 AI/ML/DS records (2020-2025) by removing noise and duplicates and restricting to relevant roles, then segmented by experience level. Yearly average salaries were computed (e.g., $103,012 in 2020 rising to $152,193 in 2023 and $145,120 in 2025). Separate ARIMA models per experience level were fit on 2020-2024 annual averages, with 2025 held out as a test year, and used to forecast 2026-2027. Reported forecasts are ~$147,000 (2026) and ~$150,000 (2027) overall, ranging from ~$105,000 (entry) to ~$205,000-$210,000 (executive); no test error metric is reported.
summary.question: What will AI/ML/data science salaries be in 2026-2027, by experience level, given 2020-2025 trends?
summary.problem: Professionals need salary expectations and companies need compensation planning amid market volatility.
summary.beneficiary: AI/ML/DS professionals, students and employers planning compensation
summary.inputs: Self-reported salary records with year and experience level
summary.outputs: Forecast average salary per experience level for 2026-2027
summary.results: Historical 48% growth 2020-2023 followed by ~5% decline 2024-2025; forecasts of 2-3% annual growth (overall ~$147K in 2026, ~$150K in 2027).

projects.student_description: Our project aims to develop a machine learning model capable of recognizing ASL alphabet images. Ultimately, we envision our product functioning as an interactive educational tool that makes ASL learning more accessible and engaging for all users.

summary.plain: This project trained a computer model to recognize the American Sign Language alphabet from photos of hand signs. A neural network got about 98% of test images right, much better than a simpler model, and the team wants to turn it into a game-like website for learning ASL.
summary.technical: Using the public Kaggle ASL Alphabet image dataset (29 classes: A-Z plus del, nothing, space), the team visualized average images per letter and a Pearson correlation matrix between class-average images. A logistic regression baseline evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation averaged ~0.68 accuracy. A small Keras Sequential CNN (two Conv2D + max-pooling blocks, dense layer with dropout, 29-way softmax) trained for 10 epochs reached a reported 0.9826 accuracy, with a confusion matrix showing most errors among similar letters (e.g. V/W, M/N). The research question about engagement and retention was not tested.

projects.title: AI4ALL Diabetes Risk Indicator Model
projects.student_description: Non-Invasive Early Diabetes Risk Prediction Using XGBoost & CDC BRFSS Survey Data

summary.plain: This project predicts whether someone may have diabetes or prediabetes from simple survey answers like BMI, blood pressure, age and income, without a blood test. The team tuned their model to catch about 9 out of 10 diabetic cases and built a web app that shows each person's risk and what is driving it.
summary.technical: The CDC BRFSS 2015 Diabetes Health Indicators dataset from Kaggle (253,680 records, 21 features, binary target with ~13.9% positives) was split 80/20 and explored with a correlation matrix and Random Forest feature importances. Logistic regression, Random Forest and XGBoost were compared on both a 50/50 balanced subset and the imbalanced data (e.g. balanced XGBoost: accuracy 0.752, recall 0.799, F1 0.763, ROC-AUC 0.83; imbalanced XGBoost: recall 0.785, precision 0.308, ROC-AUC 0.826). XGBoost was tuned with grid search and stratified k-fold, using scale_pos_weight = 6.18 and max_depth 4, and the decision threshold was lowered (tau = 0.35 gives 89.8% recall and 97.22% NPV). A Streamlit app returns a risk percentage with a SHAP waterfall explanation.
summary.question: How accurately can diabetes status be predicted from CDC health indicator data, which lifestyle and socioeconomic factors contribute most, and do models perform equitably across demographic groups?
summary.problem: Diabetes is often undiagnosed; testing is invasive, costly and less accessible for underprivileged communities.
summary.beneficiary: Community health screening programs and at-risk individuals
summary.subdomain: Diabetes risk prediction from survey data

summary.results: XGBoost ROC-AUC ~0.83; at threshold 0.35 recall 89.8% and NPV 97.22%; default threshold recall 79.25%, precision 30.48% on imbalanced data.

projects.title: ASL to speech translator
projects.student_description: Uses images to identify ASL hand signs in both live camera, snapshot and image upload. It gives the top three predictions and identifies if a word is spelled or the phrase Hello World is spelled.

summary.plain: This project built an app that watches a person's hand signs in American Sign Language, figures out which letters they are spelling, and speaks the words out loud. It uses a Google tool to find the points on the hand and a small neural network to decide which letter it is.
summary.technical: Images from a sampled ASL Alphabet dataset, augmented with a Synthetic ASL Alphabet dataset with varied backgrounds, were passed through MediaPipe Hands to extract 21 3D hand landmarks. A multilayer perceptron classifier on the landmark coordinates replaced an earlier CNN trained on raw images, which had generalized poorly. Training used early stopping (stopped at epoch 40, best epoch 35) and reached a reported test accuracy of 0.98. The model is integrated into a Streamlit app with upload, snapshot and live-camera modes, showing top-3 predictions, with NLTK for word recognition and gTTS text-to-speech.

projects.title_slide: Assessing the Path to Improved Water and Sanitation Access in Urban Areas
projects.student_description: This project predicts whether the water and sanitation improvement levels of different regions around the world will reach 90% by 2030 using times series prediction byFacebook Prophet.

summary.plain: This project looked at how many people in cities around the world have access to improved drinking water and sanitation from 1990 to 2023. The team used a forecasting tool called Prophet to predict whether countries would reach 90% access by 2028, and found that water access has usually been higher than sanitation access.
summary.technical: The team used a UN-Habitat indicator dataset on the percentage of urban population with improved water, sanitation and other basic services (1990-2023, multiple countries) in Google Colab. They computed yearly averages of improved water and improved sanitation access and the gap between them (largest negative gap -52% in 2001, largest positive gap 1.5% in 2002). Facebook Prophet was fit to the total improved access (average of water and sanitation) to forecast a 5-year horizon. Countries were labeled as above or below 90% in 2028 (e.g., Argentina, Mexico, Brazil, China above; Afghanistan, Albania, Somalia, Bangladesh below). No forecast-accuracy metric is reported.
summary.question: How has the gap between urban water and sanitation coverage evolved over time, and can total improved water and sanitation be above 90% by 2028?
summary.problem: Many people lack safe drinking water and safely managed sanitation; projecting progress can help prioritize investment.
summary.beneficiary: Policymakers and organizations working on urban development and public health
summary.inputs: Country-year percentages of urban population with improved water and improved sanitation
summary.outputs: Forecast total improved access per country and a classification as above/below the 90% target in 2028
summary.results: Water access has generally exceeded sanitation access; four countries predicted above and four below 90% by 2028. No accuracy metric reported.

projects.title: Astronomical Photo Classification
projects.student_description: A model that can identify space objects from an image.

summary.plain: This project trained a computer-vision model to sort NASA's Astronomy Picture of the Day images into categories such as galaxy, nebula, planet, moon and star. The team used AI chatbots to help label the photos, fixed labels by hand, and improved accuracy by switching to a bigger pretrained network, reaching about 65% accuracy across 11 categories.
summary.technical: About 11,000 NASA APOD images (Kaggle, 1995-2026) were labeled into 11 categories using LLMs (Gemini, Claude and Ollama were tested) from the APOD titles/descriptions, with manual correction; screenshots were used instead of downloaded files to avoid metadata leakage. A ResNet50 pretrained on ImageNet was fine-tuned (backbone frozen except layer4) for 15 epochs with batch size 64, a cosine-annealing learning-rate schedule, class-balanced loss weighting and label smoothing, selecting the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss. An earlier ResNet34 reached macro F1 0.58-0.59; ResNet50 reached 65% test accuracy and macro F1 0.65 on 1,592 test images, with Galaxy, Nebula and Star Cluster strongest and Star (0.46 F1) and Asteroid (0.50 F1) weakest. A row-normalized confusion matrix and per-class F1 vs support were reported.

projects.title:
AURA
Automated Urban Road Assessment
projects.student_description: A computer vision model that detects road damages in real time, aiding the city officials to be alerted about road damages early.

summary.plain: AURA (Automated Urban Road Assessment) is a computer-vision tool that spots road damage such as cracks and potholes in photos or video, imagined as coming from cameras on city buses and garbage trucks. The team trained an object-detection model, made it more robust with fake fog, rain and blur, and built a web app that shows detections and maps GPS locations.
summary.technical: A YOLOv8 (YOLOv8s) object detector was trained on the multi-national RDD2022 road-damage dataset with four classes (D00 longitudinal, D10 transverse, D20 alligator cracks, D40 potholes), which is heavily imbalanced. Negative sampling added thousands of healthy-road images without boxes to reduce false positives on shadows and sealant, and Albumentations injected synthetic fog, motion blur and rain. A resolution experiment raising input size from 640 to 1280 gave only marginal gains. The model reached F1 0.62 and mAP@0.5 0.626 overall, with 0.731 mAP for potholes; F1-confidence and PR curves and a normalized confusion matrix were analysed. A Streamlit app accepts images or video, applies an adjustable confidence threshold, estimates damage area from bounding-box size relative to the frame, and maps available GPS metadata.

projects.title: Behavior Drift Detection for Responsible Fraud Prediction
projects.title_slide: Behavior Drift Detection for Responsible Fraud Prediction
projects.student_description: We developed a fraud detection system that analyzes sudden changes in customer behavior, allowing us to detect fraud more responsibly while minimizing harm from false positives. By engineering drift-based features and training interpretable ML models, we highlight how AI can improve both accuracy and fairness in financial security.

summary.plain: This project built a fraud detector for bank card transactions that looks for sudden changes in how a customer normally spends. Using a simulated (fake but realistic) banking dataset, the team compared two models and found that a random forest caught most fraud while wrongly flagging far fewer innocent customers than logistic regression.
summary.technical: The BankSim synthetic transaction dataset from Kaggle (customer ID, amount, merchant, category, time step, binary fraud label; ~1.2% fraud) was grouped by customer to engineer behavior-drift features: rolling mean and standard deviation of amounts, an amount-spike indicator, a new-merchant flag and the time gap between transactions. Logistic regression and random forest classifiers were trained with class weighting and a time-based split. Logistic regression reached 95.7% accuracy with fraud recall 0.90 but precision 0.19 (over 6,000 false positives); random forest reached 99.6% accuracy with fraud precision 0.82, recall 0.83 and F1 0.82, reducing false positives to about 300. Random forest feature importances were used for explainability.
summary.question: Can behavior drift in transaction patterns be used to detect online fraud more effectively and fairly than static threshold-based systems?
summary.problem: Static-threshold fraud detection struggles with imbalanced data and produces many false positives and missed fraud.
summary.beneficiary: Bank customers and fraud-prevention teams
summary.inputs: Transaction records with engineered per-customer behavior-drift features and categorical fields
summary.outputs: Fraud probability / fraud vs not-fraud label
summary.results: Random forest: precision 0.82, recall 0.83, F1 0.82, accuracy 99.6%, ~300 false positives; logistic regression: precision 0.19, recall 0.90, F1 0.31, accuracy 95.7%, 6,164 false positives.

projects.title: Beyond Human Canvas
projects.student_description:
The project focuses on developing a model to detect AI-generated anime face images.
It specifically aims to differentiate between human and synthetic anime faces and heads.
The model achieves over 90% accuracy in classifying art as authentic or AI-generated.

summary.plain: This project built a detector that tells whether an anime-style face drawing was made by a human artist or generated by AI. The team first trained their own AI image generator to create 20,000+ fake anime faces, then trained a hybrid neural network on real and fake images, and it classified about 97% of test images correctly.
summary.technical: A 20,000-image subset of the Kaggle High-Resolution Anime Face dataset was resized to 64x64 and normalized to [-1, 1]. An unconditional UNet2DModel (DDPM) was trained for 50 epochs with AdamW and mixed precision, and the DDPMPipeline synthesized ~21,000 images pushed to the Hugging Face Hub. A custom CNN-Transformer classifier (three Conv2D+ReLU+Dropout+MaxPool blocks downsampling 64x64 to 8x8, flattened to 64 tokens with positional embeddings, two 4-head transformer encoder layers, global average pooling and a 2-class head) was trained on 32,000 images and tested on 8,000 balanced real/generated images, using flips/rotation/color-jitter augmentation, class weighting, label smoothing, gradient clipping and a cosine-annealing-warm-restarts scheduler over 50 epochs (best epoch 47). The test confusion matrix shows 3,748/3,975 human images and 4,201/4,217 AI images correct (accuracy ~0.97), with ROC AUC 0.998. A Streamlit app demo was shown.
summary.question: Can deep learning models distinguish between human-created and AI-generated anime-style faces with at least 70% accuracy?
summary.problem: AI-generated art is increasingly hard to distinguish from human art, raising intellectual-property and authenticity concerns and leading to false accusations against artists.
summary.beneficiary: Artists, platforms and audiences evaluating the authenticity of digital art

projects.title: Beyond the Credit Score
projects.student_description: Our final project is about predicting fair loan approvals using machine learning and seeing if demographic variables influence predictions.

summary.plain: This project predicted whether a loan application would be approved and checked whether the model treated people of different genders and ages fairly. Using a large synthetic Kaggle loan dataset, the team found a simple logistic regression model could predict approvals well, that a past loan default mattered most, and that removing gender, age and education barely changed the results.
summary.technical: The Kaggle Loan Approval Classification dataset (45,000 synthetic applicant records, 14 features; 78% rejected) was cleaned by removing implausible ages and incomes (44,972 rows), encoding categoricals, scaling numerics and dropping loan interest rate to avoid leakage, then split 80/20 stratified. Logistic regression with class_weight='balanced' was evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation (mean F1 0.691, SD 0.0055) and grid-search tuning (L1, C=1), which left results nearly unchanged: accuracy 81.07%, precision 0.544, recall 0.911, F1 0.68, ROC-AUC 0.931. Coefficients identified previous loan defaults as the dominant factor. Fairness analysis compared predicted approval rates, false-positive and false-negative rates by gender and age group; an ablation removing gender, age and education changed metrics by less than 0.2 points. The same pipeline on the Kaggle Credit Risk dataset (32,581 rows, default target) gave ROC-AUC 0.81.

projects.title: BizLens: Startup Success Evaluator
projects.student_description: We built an AI-powered tool that predicts early-stage startup success using machine learning and data insights.

summary.plain: BizLens is a web tool that asks founders a few questions about their startup (industry, funding types, founding year, market) and gives back a predicted success score. The team built their own definition of startup 'success' from a public Crunchbase dataset and trained a random forest model to predict it.
summary.technical: The Kaggle StartUp Investments (Crunchbase) dataset was cleaned and reduced from 30 to the 15 features most correlated with the target. After the original success label proved noisy and a custom all-feature score caused the model to learn its own formula, the team defined a success score (V5) as a normalized blend of acquisition status and log funding, excluding those signals from training to limit leakage. They switched from classification to regression and experimented with three algorithms; a RandomForestRegressor achieved R² 0.4561, RMSE 0.1017 and MAE 0.0490. Feature importances were dominated by the number of funding types. A multi-step web front end collects startup details and displays a predicted success score.

projects.title: BRAILLE TEXT TO SPEECH CONVERTER
projects.student_description: Turning Photographed Braille into Readable Text and Speech

summary.plain: This project turns a photo of Braille into English text and spoken audio. One AI model finds each Braille cell in the photo, a second model reads which letter it is, and then translation and text-to-speech tools turn the letters into words and sound, all inside a simple web app.
summary.technical: Training data comprised 3,891 original Braille images plus 10,117 generated images (sources include Kaggle, Angelina and Roboflow sets), yielding 193,671 character crops across 26 A-Z classes with an 80/10/10 split; annotations were in COCO format. Five detector families (EfficientDet-D0, YOLOv8, YOLOv11, RetinaNet, Faster R-CNN) and five classifier families (EfficientNet-B0, ResNet-18/50, MobileNetV3, ViT) were tested over five experiment rounds on Colab GPUs. The final pipeline uses YOLO11n for cell detection (mAP50 96.15%, mAP50-95 73.96%, precision 90.01%, recall 95.91%) and EfficientNet-B0 for character classification (accuracy 99.41%, macro F1 99.26%), followed by reading-order grouping, Liblouis Grade 1 translation and Piper text-to-speech. End-to-end, 10,163 of 10,443 ground-truth characters were recovered (97.32%), with combined precision 79.90% and F1 87.75%; false-positive detections are the main remaining error. A Streamlit app supports upload, confidence tuning, box inspection and text/audio download.

projects.title: Brain Tumor Detection & Classification
projects.student_description: Our final presentation is an explanation of our CNN model to detect and classify brain tumors from MRI images.

summary.plain: This project trained a computer-vision model to look at brain MRI scans and tell whether there is a tumor and, if so, which of three common types it is. The model was right about 93% of the time on its own test set, also did well on two other public MRI datasets, and was put into a simple web app as a demo.
summary.technical: The Kaggle Brain Tumor MRI Dataset (7,200 scans, four balanced classes: glioma, meningioma, pituitary, no tumor) was split with ~22% held out for testing (5,600 training scans). Images were resized to 256x256, normalized, and augmented with small rotations (up to 15 degrees) and brightness/contrast jitter. A custom 3-5 layer PyTorch CNN with dropout and max-pooling was trained for ~25 epochs with Adam, cross-entropy loss, a ReduceLROnPlateau scheduler and class weighting. On the original test set it reported ~93% accuracy with per-class recall from 79.5% (glioma) to 99.75% (no tumor), and it was further tested on two external Kaggle MRI datasets via confusion matrices. Several team CNN variants were served through a Streamlit model registry.
summary.question: Can a deep learning model accurately detect and classify brain tumors from MRI scans to serve as a reliable decision-support tool for doctors?

projects.title: Brain Tumor Identification
projects.student_description: We developed and evaluated an SVM and logistic regression model to identify brain tumors. These models used the dataset to predict whether an MRI scan of a brain includes or does not include a tumor.

summary.plain: This project tried to tell whether a brain MRI scan shows a tumor using numbers that describe the brightness and texture of the image. The team trained two classic machine learning models, a support vector machine and logistic regression, and both identified tumors correctly about 95% of the time on their test data.
summary.technical: A Kaggle brain tumor dataset of MRI-derived first-order statistical (mean, variance) and second-order textural (contrast, energy, entropy) features with tumor/non-tumor labels was used. Features were standardized with StandardScaler and SMOTE was applied to address class imbalance, followed by an 80/20 train-test split. An SVM (SVC, C=10) evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation averaged 95.37% accuracy with 98.19% recall; its test confusion matrix shows 452 of 472 correct. Logistic regression with L2 regularization reported 96.9% train and 98.5% test accuracy with precision, recall and F1 of 0.95 for both classes; its confusion matrix shows 448 of 472 correct (~94.9%).

projects.title: Brain Vessel Abnormality Detection
projects.student_description: We used a deep learning system built on a 3D ResNet-18 architecture and deployed as an interactive web tool developed a model to correctly identify healthy and aneurysm vessel segments in the brain.

summary.plain: The team built an AI tool that looks at small 3D brain blood-vessel scans and flags segments that may contain an aneurysm (a dangerous bulge in a vessel). They trained several versions of a 3D neural network, picked the one that missed the fewest aneurysms, and put it in a web app that shows a heatmap of where the model is looking, intended to support (not replace) radiologists.
summary.technical: Data: VesselMNIST3D (MedMNIST v2), 64x64x64 grayscale 3D vessel-segment volumes with a heavy imbalance (slide reports 339 healthy vs 43 aneurysm). Preprocessing: intensity normalization to [0,1], dtype conversion for PyTorch/MONAI, and augmentation with random 90-degree rotations, flips, intensity scaling and shifting. Model: a MONAI 3D ResNet-18 binary classifier; five variants were trained with different positive-class weights (7.5-12.0) and decision thresholds (0.25-0.55). Evaluation reported accuracy, recall, precision and missed-aneurysm counts per variant; the chosen V5 reported 90.05% accuracy, 83.72% recall and 53.73% precision with 7 missed aneurysms. Deployment: Gradio API on Hugging Face Spaces running inference plus 3D Grad-CAM heatmaps, with a Next.js/Niivue front end on Vercel.
summary.question: To what extent can AI detect abnormal vessel patterns in brain MRA scans compared to manual radiologist review?
summary.problem: Brain aneurysms are often asymptomatic until rupture, and radiologist error rates rise with fatigue and high shift volumes; radiologists are scarce in low-resource regions.
summary.beneficiary: Radiologists and patients, especially in high-volume or under-resourced settings (as a first-read triage aid).

projects.title: Breast Cancer Classification
projects.student_description: We developed a tool that investigates to what extent machine learning models can accurately distinguish between benign and malignant breast tissue in imaging data.

summary.plain: This project trained AI models to look at mammogram image crops and say whether a breast mass is benign or malignant. The team compared three approaches and built a web app where users can upload a scan and see each model's prediction; the best models were right about 7 times out of 10.
summary.technical: The Kaggle CBIS-DDSM dataset (mass and calcification cases with verified pathology) was used, with pathology encoded as binary, a patient-ID-grouped split to prevent leakage between views, and random flip/rotation/zoom augmentation. Three models were built: a ResNet50-based CNN classifier, an RBF-kernel SVM trained on standardized ResNet50 feature vectors, and a pretrained Vision Transformer. On the 378-image mass test set, the CNN reached accuracy 0.71 (AUC 0.75), the SVM accuracy 0.72 (AUC 0.77) and the ViT accuracy 0.71 (AUC 0.80, malignant recall 0.76). An initial K-means approach was dropped because it ignored the pathology labels. A Streamlit app deployed with Docker lets users upload mammograms and see predictions from each model.
summary.question: To what extent can machine learning models accurately distinguish between benign and malignant breast tissue in imaging data?
summary.problem: Early, accurate detection of breast cancer in mammograms is essential, and AI could help radiologists reduce human error.

projects.title: BridgeSense: A Structural Integrity Forecast Engine
projects.student_description: This project develops an end-to-end machine learning pipeline to classify the structural health of bridges into "Poor", "Fair", or "Good" categories, enabling proactive and safety-focused infrastructure management. Our final XGBoost model successfully identifies 88% of the most at-risk bridges, providing a data-driven tool to help prioritize critical repairs.

summary.plain: BridgeSense uses public U.S. bridge inspection records plus weather information to predict whether a bridge is likely in Poor, Fair, or Good condition. The team compared several tree-based models, explained the predictions with SHAP, and built a Streamlit web app where users can enter a bridge's details and see the predicted probabilities.
summary.technical: Data: National Bridge Inventory (NBI) records from a Kaggle 1990-2022 compilation, with traffic, geometry, material/design and environmental (temperature, humidity, wind) features; missing values imputed with missing-indicator flags, one-hot encoded categoricals, and engineered features such as bridge age, Age_x_Traffic and squared terms. Target: overall condition collapsed from 0-9 ratings into Poor (<=4) / Fair / Good. Models: Random Forest, XGBoost and CatBoost tuned with Optuna and RFECV feature selection, plus a three-model ensemble. On a 127,686-record test set, accuracies were RF 0.695, XGBoost 0.791, CatBoost 0.731 and ensemble 0.764 (macro F1 0.741); the XGBoost report shows Poor-class recall 0.89 (pdf p11). SHAP feature importance was used for explanation and the model was deployed as a Streamlit app.
summary.question: Can we predict if a bridge will receive a "Poor" condition rating (<=4) on any major structural element using available NBI features such as traffic, environmental factors, material type, and bridge geometry?
summary.problem: Bridge inspection cycles are infrequent, so deteriorating bridges can go undetected between checkups, risking collapse and costly emergency repairs.
summary.beneficiary: Infrastructure/transportation agencies prioritizing bridge inspections and repairs
summary.inputs: NBI bridge attributes (age, traffic, geometry, material, design, inspection frequency) and climate variables
summary.outputs: Probability of Poor / Fair / Good overall condition
summary.results: XGBoost accuracy 0.791 with Poor-class recall 0.89; ensemble accuracy 0.764, macro F1 0.741; RF 0.695; CatBoost 0.731 (as reported).

summary.plain: This project asks whether the features of a car alone (make, engine, weight, safety equipment and ratings) can predict whether an auto-insurance claim will be filed. The team tried logistic regression, XGBoost and random forest on a Kaggle insurance-claims dataset and chose random forest, focusing on catching risky cars (recall). They also discussed how such a model could unfairly penalize some customers.
summary.technical: Data: Kaggle 'Insurance Claims Dataset' with vehicle specification features (make/model/year, engine and fuel type, weight, price, NCAP safety rating, safety equipment flags) plus fields such as customer age, region density and subscription length, with a binary claim_status target that is heavily imbalanced. EDA included distributions and Cramer's V / Pearson correlation matrices used to streamline features. Models: logistic regression (~50% accuracy, ~56% recall), an XGBoost model described as overfitting, and random forest (~73% accuracy, ~50% recall on slide 8; slide 9 states 73% recall). Random forest was chosen for its balance of performance and interpretability. Evaluation details (split, metric definitions) are not shown.

projects.student_description: My model takes in video game levels as data and outputs an entirely new generated level based on the data.

summary.plain: This project teaches a computer to design new Super Mario-style game levels. It learns from a public collection of real game levels, turns them into small grids of tiles, and uses a generative neural network (a variational autoencoder) to invent new level pieces that are stitched into full levels and checked for playability.
summary.technical: Data: Mario levels from the Video Game Level Corpus (VGLC), stored as character-tile text files with a JSON legend. Preprocessing: a 15-tile vocabulary mapped to integers and a 16x14 sliding window producing 2,878 training chunks. Model: a convolutional VAE (Conv2d encoder with 32-256 filters to a 128-dimensional latent space; fully connected plus ConvTranspose2d decoder). Evaluation: qualitative reconstructions of training chunks, novel chunks sampled from the latent space, overlapping stitching into full-length levels, and a scripted playability analysis reporting ground coverage 85.1%, max gap size, platform density 22.5% and 3.5 enemies per 100 tiles for a generated level.
summary.question: How can machine learning models, specifically Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), be used to generate, adapt, and extend playable Mario-style levels using data from the Video Game Level Corpus (VGLC)?
summary.problem: Hand-designing game levels does not scale to large, dynamic game worlds; procedural content generation could learn design principles from existing levels.
summary.beneficiary: Game designers and developers
summary.subdomain: Procedural content generation of platformer levels

summary.outputs: Newly generated 16x14 level chunks stitched into full-length levels, plus playability metrics
summary.results: Generated level reported with 85.1% ground coverage, 22.5% platform density, 3.5 enemies per 100 tiles, rated 'EXCELLENT - Likely playable'; no quantitative reconstruction loss reported.

projects.student_description: We trained a from-scratch CNN on all 112,120 images of NIH ChestX-ray14 to 0.7647 test mean AUC across 14 findings, then audited recall separately for each sex and age group.

summary.plain: This project trained a neural network from scratch to spot 14 chest diseases in X-ray images and then checked whether it works equally well for men and women and for different age groups. It found that the model catches some diseases much more often in some groups than others, and that fixing one gap can create another. The team built a web app that shows predictions along with how reliable the model is for the patient's group.
summary.technical: Data: NIH ChestX-ray14 (112,120 images, 30,805 patients, 14 findings + No Finding) with NLP-mined labels; analysis showed 84.4% of images come from repeat patients, motivating a patient-level split, and an 87-88x class imbalance. Model: an initial CheXNet (DenseNet-121, ImageNet-pretrained) overfit on sample data, so the team trained a custom 4-block 'SimpleCNN' (1.57M parameters, avg+max pooling, 14 sigmoid outputs) on 224x224 images; scaling to the full dataset, more epochs and wider layers raised test mean AUC from 0.7225 to 0.7647 on 17,131 held-out images (micro-averaged AUC 0.638 -> 0.700 -> 0.799 across three versions; best Emphysema 0.886, worst Nodule 0.622). Per-finding thresholds were fitted on validation to reach 80% recall. Fairness audit: recall per finding across sex x age-band cells with 95% Wilson intervals, a 20+ positive-case minimum, and recall-minus-flag-rate lift; gaps were finding-specific (e.g. Pneumothorax 89% for women 30-49 vs 64% for men) and shifted rather than vanished after model changes. Deployed as a Streamlit app.
summary.question: Do CNNs detect thoracic diseases equally across patient sex and age groups, or do demographic disparities hide in high overall accuracy?
summary.problem: Medical AI is rarely audited for subgroup bias, and disparities can hide behind high overall accuracy and amplify health inequities.

projects.student_description: We developed a ResNet-50 machine learning model classifies blood cancer images with 96% validation accuracy by optimizing the model through iterative training.

summary.plain: This project trained a ResNet-50 image model to look at microscope pictures of blood cells and sort them into benign cells or one of three subtypes of acute lymphoblastic leukemia, a fast-growing blood cancer. The team built a web demo that shows the prediction and a Grad-CAM heatmap of where the model looked.
summary.technical: Data: Kaggle Blood Cells Cancer (ALL) dataset, 3,242 microscopic blood-smear images from 89 patients in four classes (Benign, Early Pre-B, Pre-B, Pro-B). Preprocessing: images standardized to 224x224, cleaning, and oversampling to address class imbalance. Model: ResNet-50 CNN trained with supervised learning over ~45 epochs; training/validation loss and accuracy curves converge near ~0.98-0.99 accuracy. The validation confusion matrix (pdf p12) shows 360 of 365 images correct; the workbook reports 96% validation accuracy. Integration: a web app (ALL-Classifier) with live prediction, top-k probabilities and Grad-CAM overlay, plus dashboard, error-analysis and training-run tabs.

summary.problem: Traditional ALL diagnosis from blood smears is time-consuming and error-prone, while early accurate detection is crucial for treatment.

projects.student_description: College Student Performance Predictor is a machine learning model that uses the XGBoost classifier algorithm to predict if a student is more likely to graduate or drop out based on their characteristics.

summary.plain: This project predicts whether a college student is likely to graduate or drop out using information about the student such as background, enrollment details and grades. The team trained an XGBoost model, reported about 91% accuracy, and built a web app where a user can enter a student's details and get a prediction.
summary.technical: Data: a 'Student Success Analysis' dataset with demographic and academic features (marital status, course, gender, admission grade, approved curricular units per semester) and a Dropout/Graduate/Enrolled target; the model predicts the two extremes (graduate vs. dropout). EDA examined class distribution, outcome by gender, and admission grade and approved units by outcome. Model: XGBoost classifier evaluated with accuracy, precision, recall and F1, reporting 91% accuracy, plus feature-importance analysis. Deployment: a Flask backend serving a pickled XGBoost model through /predict and /features endpoints with a React frontend form.

projects.title: Competitive Threat and Market Share Loss Prediction Model
projects.title_slide: Competitive Threat and Market Share Loss Prediction Model
projects.student_description: Can we predict whether a company is about to lose its market share based on financial news tone and market performance numbers?

summary.plain: This project tests whether the tone of financial news headlines, combined with recent stock prices, can warn that a company's stock is about to fall, as an early signal of competitive decline. The team scored headlines with a finance-specific language model (FinBERT), trained random forest and logistic regression models, and built a Streamlit app. Results were only slightly better than chance, which the team acknowledged.
summary.technical: Data: Kaggle Daily Historical Stock Prices (6.3M records) and Massive Stock News Analysis DB (1.2M headlines), cleaned and merged by ticker and date to 322,993 headlines across 3,444 companies (2009-2018), with five prior-day closing prices added per headline. FinBERT converted each headline to a sentiment label (+1/0/-1) and confidence used as features (11 inputs). Target: whether the stock price decreased the next day (nearly balanced). Models: Random Forest (100 trees, depth 10, balanced weights) with 54.42% accuracy, 5-fold CV mean 54.85% (+/-0.15%), and Logistic Regression (balanced, standardized) with 50.75% accuracy, CV 50.68%; LR had 61% recall on decreases vs 27% for RF. Combining sentiment and price features beat either alone; price-return features dominated importance. Deployed as a Streamlit 'Stock Drop Predictor'.
summary.question: Can we predict whether a company is about to lose its market share based on financial news tone and market performance numbers?
summary.problem: Competitive threats (e.g. BlackBerry vs. iPhone) often become visible in financial statements too late to act; earlier warning signals could help investors and managers.
summary.beneficiary: Investors, financial analysts and corporate decision-makers

summary.inputs: Financial news headline (FinBERT sentiment and confidence) plus recent closing prices
summary.outputs: Predicted next-day price decrease vs. not, with drop probability
summary.results: Random Forest 54.42% accuracy (CV 54.85%), Logistic Regression 50.75% (CV 50.68%); LR recall on decreases 61% vs RF 27%; only slightly above baseline.

projects.title: Computer Vision for Fall detection in elderly care
projects.title_slide: COMPUTER VISION FOR FALL DETECTION IN ELDERLY CARE
projects.student_description: Our elderly fall detection model aims to help caregivers in detecting and preventing falls for their patients.

summary.plain: This project uses a camera-image object detector (YOLOv8) to spot whether a person in a picture has fallen, aiming to help caregivers respond quickly to falls among older adults. The team hand-labeled more than 1,600 images with boxes, fine-tuned a pretrained YOLOv8 model, and found it catches about 85% of falls.
summary.technical: Data: two public Kaggle fall-detection image datasets; one already labeled, the other manually annotated with bounding boxes (1,600+ images) in Roboflow. The custom dataset has 1,784 images split into train (1,065), valid (358) and test (361) with Fall and Not_Fall classes (Not_Fall majority). Model: YOLOv8 fine-tuned from pretrained weights for 30 epochs; models were trained separately per dataset. Evaluation: box/cls/DFL loss and precision/recall/mAP curves, precision-, recall- and F1-confidence curves (F1 0.93 for all classes at confidence 0.608), and a normalized confusion matrix showing 85% of Fall and 97% of Not_Fall instances correctly predicted.
summary.question: Can a YOLOv8 object detector automatically detect falls of elderly people from camera images?
summary.problem: Falls cause injury and loss of independence for older adults, and manual monitoring in homes and care centers is difficult.
summary.beneficiary: Older adults and their caregivers
summary.inputs: Camera images
summary.outputs: Bounding boxes labeled Fall / Not_Fall with confidence
summary.results: F1 0.93 at confidence 0.608; Fall recall ~85% and Not_Fall ~97% (normalized confusion matrix).

projects.student_description: A Machine Learning Approach to Detect Respiratory Conditions via Audio

summary.plain: This project tried to tell from a recording of someone's cough whether they likely have COVID-19. The team turned cough sounds into picture-like spectrogram features and trained a neural network on them; it caught about 9 out of 10 COVID-positive coughs in their tests.
summary.technical: Data: CoronaHack Respiratory Sound Dataset cough recordings with metadata. Preprocessing: resampling, denoising, silence trimming, volume normalization, and MFCC/spectrogram feature extraction; time-shift and pitch augmentation are listed. Model: a CRNN (convolutional + recurrent network); Random Forest and SVM are listed as comparison models but no results are shown. Evaluation: on 6,624 samples the CRNN reported 0.851 accuracy, COVID-class precision 0.879 / recall 0.906 / F1 0.892, aggregate ROC-AUC 0.889 and PR-AUC 0.926, with per-fold AUCs across 5 folds described as consistent.

projects.title: Credit Card Defaulter Prediction
projects.student_description:
Financial firms lose money when customers default. Traditional risk assessments are slow and time consuming.
How can machine learning and AI help detect these risks based on customer payment habits?

summary.plain: This project predicts whether a credit card customer will miss their next payment, using their past repayment history, bills and payments. The team trained a random forest model on a public dataset of 30,000 customers and got about 81% accuracy, but it catches only about a third of the customers who actually default.
summary.technical: Data: Kaggle 'Credit Card Defaulter Prediction' dataset (30,000 customers, 23-24 features: credit limit, gender, education, marital status, age, past repayment statuses, bill and payment amounts). EDA compared utilization, months late, max delay and pay/bill ratios between defaulters and non-defaulters. Model: scikit-learn RandomForestClassifier (100 trees, class_weight='balanced') with an 80/20 train/test split (random_state 42). Results on 6,000 test records: accuracy 0.814; non-default precision 0.84 / recall 0.95; default precision 0.64 / recall 0.34; macro F1 0.67. An earlier idea using linear regression on self-collected SaaS KPIs was abandoned.

projects.title: Credit Card Fraud Detection
projects.student_description: Engineered ML model to detect which transactions are fraud.

summary.plain: The team built models that look at credit card transactions and flag the ones likely to be fraud. They used a large public dataset of real (anonymized) transactions where only about 3.5% are fraud, and compared four kinds of models. Their best model, XGBoost, caught about 83% of fraud cases but also raised about 8,000 false alarms.
summary.technical: Data: the IEEE-CIS Fraud Detection dataset from Kaggle (~590,000 transactions, transaction and identity tables joined by ID, ~3.5% fraud, 400+ features). Preprocessing: columns with more than 50% missing values were handled by replacing missing values with a 'missing' sentinel, reducing the data to 339 columns; engineered features include transaction velocity in 24 hours, card frequency, email-domain match, log transaction amount and card age. Models: XGBoost (300 trees, max depth 6, scale_pos_weight for imbalance), a feed-forward neural network (128 and 64 units with dropout, focal loss, exponential learning-rate decay, 25 epochs), plus Random Forest and SVM. Evaluation: XGBoost ROC-AUC 0.9515, accuracy 92.54%, fraud F1 0.4373, fraud recall 0.828; neural network ROC-AUC 0.94, accuracy 92.48%, F1 0.422, recall 0.7844; Random Forest had 97% accuracy, precision 0.54 and recall 0.63. Stratified splitting is mentioned but split proportions are not given.
summary.question: Can we accurately predict whether a transaction was fraudulent or not, based on the data used to train our proposed classification models?
summary.problem: Credit card fraud is a major financial threat; manual oversight cannot keep up, and extreme class imbalance makes accuracy a misleading target.

projects.title: Credit Card Fraud Detection with Explainable AI
projects.title_slide: Credit Card Fraud Detection with Explainable AI
projects.student_description: We developed a credit card fraud detection system using machine learning and explainable AI. Our project uses XGBoost to predict whether a transaction is fraudulent and SHAP to explain which transaction features influenced each prediction, improving both fraud detection and transparency.

summary.plain: The team built a credit card fraud detector that says whether a single transaction looks like fraud and explains why. They trained models on a public simulated dataset of U.S. credit card transactions, chose XGBoost, and used SHAP to show which features pushed each prediction. The model is wrapped in a Streamlit web app where you upload a transaction as a CSV file.
summary.technical: Data: the Kaggle 'Credit Card Transactions Fraud Detection' simulated U.S. dataset. Preprocessing: SMOTE oversampling of fraud cases, cyclic encoding of transaction hour, binning of transaction amount, and engineered behavioural features such as amount vs. card average, card average amount, 24-hour transaction count and night-time flag; the model was narrowed to the top 15 features and the decision threshold was tuned. Models: Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost were compared; XGBoost was chosen and explained with SHAP. Evaluation (read from p10/p14): Logistic Regression accuracy 0.99, precision 0.32, recall 0.60, F1 0.42, ROC-AUC 0.94; Random Forest accuracy 1.00, precision 0.65, recall 0.62, F1 0.64, ROC-AUC 0.98; top-15-feature XGBoost accuracy 0.9953, precision 0.5789, recall 0.6676, F1 0.62, ROC-AUC 0.9792. The final model is deployed in a Streamlit app that engineers the 15 features from an uploaded CSV and shows a SHAP explanation.
summary.question: Which transaction features are the strongest predictors of fraudulent credit card transactions among U.S. credit card holders, and what insights can explainable AI techniques provide about the reasoning behind machine learning fraud predictions?
summary.problem: Fraud detection systems produce false positives that block legitimate customers without explanation, eroding trust.
summary.beneficiary: Credit card holders, fraud analysts and card providers
summary.inputs: A single transaction (amount, timestamp, card number, category, Unix time, date of birth) from which 15 features are engineered
summary.outputs: Fraud / Not Fraud prediction, a recommended next step, and a SHAP explanation
summary.results: Top-15-feature XGBoost: accuracy 0.9953, precision 0.5789, recall 0.6676, F1 0.62, ROC-AUC 0.9792 (Random Forest: precision 0.65, recall 0.62, F1 0.64, ROC-AUC 0.98; Logistic Regression: precision 0.32, recall 0.60, ROC-AUC 0.94).

projects.title: Credit Risk -  Enhancing Predictions Using Artificial Intelligence
projects.student_description: Our final project is about building an AI model that accurately predicts the likelihood of a borrower defaulting on a loan. We aim to reduce bias in the model to the best of our ability.

summary.plain: The team built models that predict whether a borrower will fail to repay a loan, with an eye on fairness for low-income and underserved borrowers. They trained a logistic regression and a random forest on loan records with features like income, credit score and debt-to-income ratio. The random forest scored much higher, but its test results look like they may have been inflated by how the data was balanced.
summary.technical: Data: an unnamed tabular loan dataset with features including Age, Income, LoanAmount, CreditScore, MonthsEmployed, NumCreditLines, InterestRate, LoanTerm, DTIRatio and HasCoSigner and a binary Default label (16 numerical/encoded categorical inputs). EDA: default-rate plots and a correlation heatmap. Models: Logistic Regression and Random Forest. Evaluation via classification reports: Logistic Regression accuracy 0.68 on 51,070 test rows (default class precision 0.22, recall 0.68, F1 0.33); Random Forest accuracy 0.99 on 90,278 rows with equal class supports (45,139 each), suggesting resampling was applied before the evaluation split. Bias is discussed conceptually (class imbalance, selection bias) without subgroup metrics.
summary.question: How can we design an AI model that predicts credit risk fairly and accurately, while identifying and reducing bias against low-income and underserved borrowers?
summary.problem: Credit risk models determine access to housing, education and business opportunities; biased models can unfairly exclude qualified borrowers from marginalized communities.
summary.beneficiary: Lenders and loan applicants, especially low-income and underserved borrowers
summary.inputs: Borrower and loan attributes (age, income, loan amount, credit score, employment months, credit lines, interest rate, term, DTI ratio, co-signer, encoded categoricals)
summary.outputs: Probability of default converted to a default / no-default label
summary.results: Logistic Regression: accuracy 0.68, default-class precision 0.22, recall 0.68, F1 0.33. Random Forest: accuracy 0.99 with precision/recall 0.98-1.00 on a balanced 90,278-row evaluation set.

projects.title: Credit Risk Assistant
projects.student_description: A machine learning application that predicts the probability of a borrower defaulting on a loan using the user’s inputted financial and credit profile data. Built on a LightGBM model trained on over 89,000 loan profiles, it provides instant risk assessments with plain-language explanations, helping users to understand the factors that drive their credit risk. This application serves to increase financial literacy for those making one of the most important financial decisions of their lives

summary.plain: The team built a web app that estimates how likely a person is to fall behind on a loan and explains the reasons in plain language. They trained three models on historical LendingClub loans and picked LightGBM because it pairs well with SHAP explanations. A user can type in their own financial details and see an accept/reject estimate plus what drove it.
summary.technical: Data: a sample of the LendingClub accepted-loans dataset (2007-2018, Kaggle wordsforthewise/lending-club); 89,857 loans in the source file with 25 features (income, loan amount, credit history, DTI, employment length, grade etc.) and a 70/30 train/test split. Preprocessing: median imputation of missing employment length and min/max clamping of anomalous numerical values. Models: Logistic Regression, Random Forest and LightGBM. Default-class results: Logistic Regression precision 0.33 / recall 0.67 / F1 0.44; Random Forest 0.35 / 0.60 / 0.44 (highest AUC 0.717); LightGBM 0.34 / 0.64 / 0.45. LightGBM was chosen for SHAP compatibility and deployed in a Streamlit app that returns an accept/reject call with per-feature SHAP explanations translated into plain language.
summary.question: How can we use machine learning to predict loan default risk and translate that prediction into feedback people can actually understand?
summary.problem: Many loan applicants have low financial literacy and receive opaque credit decisions without understanding what drives their risk.
