projects.title: Credit Scoring for Everyday Borrowers
projects.student_description: This study predicts the likelihood of credit default for regular borrowers using machine learning.  It finds important characteristics associated with default and assesses how equitable predictions are for various demographic groups by training models on actual banking data.  The objective is to create a credit rating system that is accountable, accurate, and comprehensible in order to facilitate more equitable lending decisions.

summary.plain: The team tried to predict which bank customers would default on a loan and checked whether predictions were unfair to some groups. They trained logistic regression, a decision tree and gradient boosting on a public bank dataset and compared predicted 'default' rates for married, single and divorced customers. The features and numbers suggest the target they predicted is actually whether a customer accepted a marketing offer, not loan default.
summary.technical: Data: Kaggle 'bank-credit-scoring' dataset (~4,521 rows judging from the decision tree's 3,616 training samples and the 905-row confusion matrix), with features such as call duration, previous campaign outcome, age, account balance and contact month. Models: logistic regression (used to bucket borrowers into low/medium/high risk), a depth-2-visualized decision tree using Gini splits, and gradient boosting with feature importances. Evaluation of gradient boosting on a hold-out set: accuracy 89.8%, precision 55%, recall 32%, F1 ~40% (confusion matrix 781/26/66/32). Fairness check: predicted default rate 16% for married, 31% single, 25% divorced, i.e. single borrowers ~2x as likely to be flagged. Call duration is identified as a leaky post-interaction feature.
summary.question: How effectively can machine learning models predict loan default risk, and what fairness challenges arise in their use?
summary.problem: Default prediction affects borrowers' access to credit and interest rates, and models can encode sampling, label and demographic bias.
summary.beneficiary: Lenders and everyday borrowers, particularly those with thin credit files
summary.subdomain: Credit scoring / default prediction with fairness auditing
summary.inputs: Bank customer attributes (age, marital status, balance) and campaign-contact features (call duration, previous campaign outcome, contact month)
summary.outputs: Default / no-default label and low/medium/high risk category
summary.results: Gradient boosting: accuracy 89.8%, precision 55%, recall 32%, F1 ~40%. Predicted default rates: married 16%, single 31%, divorced 25%.

projects.title: CreditPilot
projects.student_description: Simplified complex financial decisions by helping users identify the most cost-effective credit card based on their personal credit profile and spending habits.

summary.plain: CreditPilot recommends which credit card gives a person the most value based on how much they spend on travel, dining, groceries, online shopping and other things. The team gathered credit card reward terms from a government survey, created simulated users, worked out which card would pay each user the most, and trained a model to predict that best card. Users can enter their monthly spending into a web app to get a recommendation.
summary.technical: Data: card reward terms (base rate, category rates, quarterly caps, post-cap rates) from the CFPB Terms of Credit Card Plans (TCCP) survey, combined with synthetically generated users' monthly spending by category. Labels: a reward calculation determines the best card for each synthetic user. Model: multinomial logistic regression predicting the optimal card among four classes (Capital One Savor Rewards, Amex Blue Cash Preferred, Citi Double Cash, BoA Customized Cash). Evaluation: a confusion matrix on 200 test users (119/11/8, 4, 6/1/51 by row), which implies about 87% accuracy though no metric is stated; Amex Blue Cash Preferred never appears as a true label in the test set. Deployment: a web-based card recommendation tool where users enter monthly spending.
summary.question: How do we determine which credit card provides the most optimal value for an individual user in the USA?
summary.problem: Choosing a credit card is a complex financial decision; users lack transparent tools to match card terms to their own spending, and banks waste money on untargeted marketing.

summary.plain: The team tried to predict what type of crime is most likely to happen at a given time and place in Connecticut cities, using crime records from the FBI. They trained a random forest and a dense neural network (and tried LightGBM and XGBoost) and built a web app where you enter a city, location type and date to see predicted crime types. They did not report an accuracy number, and the confusion matrix shows the model mostly predicts a few common crime types.
summary.technical: Data: labeled incident data for Connecticut from the FBI website (offense categories consistent with NIBRS), with city, location type, year, month, day of week, population and other temporal/spatial/environmental features; data cleaning described but not detailed. Models: Random Forest classifier (deployed in a Streamlit app running locally), a dense neural network with softmax output, cross-entropy loss, early stopping and learning-rate tuning, and LightGBM (and XGBoost) as alternatives. Evaluation: only a multi-class confusion matrix over ~25 offense types (p9), in which predictions concentrate in Larceny/Theft, Assault, Fraud and Destruction/Vandalism columns while many classes are never predicted; no accuracy or per-class metrics are reported. The team notes class imbalance makes underrepresented crime types poorly predicted.

projects.title: Dark Pattern Recognition
projects.student_description: This project uses machine learning to detect dark-pattern language in e-commerce websites. A two-stage model identifies suspicious text and predicts its likely category, such as urgency, scarcity, or social proof, while highlighting the limitations and ethical challenges of automated detection.

summary.plain: The team built a tool that reads text from shopping websites and flags manipulative 'dark pattern' wording, like fake urgency or pressure to buy. A first model decides whether a snippet is a dark pattern, and a second model guesses which kind it is (urgency, scarcity, social proof and so on). They put it in a Streamlit app and a webpage scanner, and were clear that text alone cannot catch visual tricks.
summary.technical: Data: three Kaggle dark-pattern text datasets normalized into a shared schema (text, label, category, source) and deduplicated to 4,151 unique rows; the primary dataset is balanced (1,178 dark / 1,178 not dark). Features: TF-IDF. Stage 1 (dark vs not dark): Logistic Regression, Linear SVM, Naive Bayes, Random Forest and Decision Tree compared; Logistic Regression chosen for its confidence scores (accuracy 93.9%, precision 0.973, recall 0.903, F1 0.936; 6 false positives and 23 false negatives on 472 test snippets). Stage 2 (7-way type classification on 1,861 category rows): the same five models compared using macro metrics; Linear SVM best with macro F1 0.894 (macro recall 0.870), per-class F1 from 0.80 (Obstruction) to 0.96 (Scarcity). Stratified splits, per-class F1 review and confusion matrices are used. Deployed as a Streamlit text app and a Playwright webpage scanner.
summary.question: How effectively can supervised text-classification models detect dark-pattern language in e-commerce website text - and what are the limits of using a text-first model for consumer-protection review?
summary.problem: Dark patterns nudge online shoppers into unintended purchases, subscriptions or data sharing; detecting them supports consumer protection and platform accountability.
summary.beneficiary: Online consumers, UX designers and consumer-protection / legal reviewers
summary.inputs: Website text snippets (typed in the app or extracted from a webpage scan)
summary.outputs: Dark / not-dark label with confidence, plus likely dark-pattern type (Urgency, Scarcity, Social Proof, Misdirection, Obstruction, Sneaking, Forced Action)
summary.results: Stage 1 Logistic Regression: accuracy 93.9%, F1 0.936 (precision 0.973, recall 0.903). Stage 2 Linear SVM: macro F1 0.894; per-type F1 0.80-0.96.

projects.student_description: ML CNN model that detects deepfake videos.

summary.plain: This project tried to build a tool that tells whether a video is a deepfake (AI-faked) or real. The team fine-tuned an image neural network on a small set of real and fake videos and wrapped it in a simple web app, but it was only right about 60% of the time and they concluded it was overfitting.
summary.technical: Data: SDFVD2.0 (461 real and 461 fake short videos, pre-augmented with flips, rotation, shear, brightness/contrast, noise and scaling). Model: a transfer-learning EfficientNet-B0 for binary real/fake classification with all 4.0M parameters trainable, optimizer listed as AdamW. A face-detect-and-crop step is described as a plan. Evaluation on a validation set: accuracy 0.5986, precision 0.5975, recall 0.5986, F1 0.5970, AUC-ROC 0.6215 (real 372/700 correct, fake 514/780). A Gradio video-upload demo was run from Colab. The team judged the model to be overfitting.

projects.title: Demand Prediction for EV Charging Stations
projects.title_slide: Demand Prediction for EV Charging Stations
projects.student_description: Built an AI model that predicts when and where EV charging stations in California will be busiest, helping make charging more convenient for drivers

summary.plain: This project predicts how busy electric-vehicle charging stations in Palo Alto, California will be at different hours and days. The team cleaned years of charging-session records, added weather information, built many time-based features, and trained a LightGBM model that was on average about 12.6 percentage points off the real station utilization.
summary.technical: Data: 200k+ EV charging-session records (33 columns) from California city stations, merged with Open-Meteo hourly weather codes. Preprocessing: removal of sessions longer than one day, imputing missing end dates, timezone localization to US/Pacific then UTC, date-part extraction, simplified weather codes. Target: an engineered hourly 'Utilization' = ports in use / total ports. Features: season, holiday flags, lag features (1h-168h) with seasonal fill, rolling mean/std/min/max windows, and sine/cosine cyclical encoding of hour (5 to 40 features). Model: LightGBM regression with a time-aware split. Test RMSE 0.126 and R² 0.712; feature importance shows 1-hour lag and 168-hour rolling mean as top features.
summary.question: Can historical charging data predict station-level usage at different times of day and days of the week, helping providers optimize deployment and operations?
summary.problem: Overcrowded or underused EV stations reduce reliability for drivers and waste infrastructure.

summary.inputs: Historical charging sessions, calendar features and hourly weather

projects.title: Dementia Detection Utilizing Speech Samples
projects.student_description: Our project uses artificial intelligence to detect potential signs of dementia through speech analysis. We developed text, audio, and fusion machine learning models that analyze linguistic and acoustic features from speech samples to classify cognitive health patterns.

summary.plain: This project tries to spot early signs of dementia from how people speak while describing a picture. The team built one model that looks at the words people use, one that listens to the sound of their voice, and one that combines both, and found the word-based model did most of the work (about 77% accuracy).
summary.technical: Data: Pitt Corpus (DementiaBank) picture-description recordings and transcripts, aligned by speaker ID to 352 recordings (189 Alzheimer's vs 163 control; 43 ambiguous MCI/vascular cases excluded); interviewer speech removed using transcript timestamps. Features: spaCy-derived linguistic features (vocabulary variety, sentence length, clause density, repetitions, information units) and 88 openSMILE eGeMAPS acoustic features. Models: logistic regression on text features and on audio features (class-weighted), plus a leakage-safe out-of-fold stacking meta-model fusing both. Evaluation: speaker-independent cross-validation; accuracy majority baseline 53.7%, audio 63.6%, text 77.0%, fusion 77.6%, with a fusion confusion matrix. Coefficient-based feature importance and a check of feature correlation with education and age were performed. Delivered as a Streamlit app comparing the three models.
summary.question: Can linguistic patterns (transcripts) or acoustic markers (raw audio) detect characteristics of dementia?
summary.problem: Dementia screening is costly; speech may carry early, non-invasive markers.
summary.beneficiary: Clinicians and older adults seeking early dementia screening
summary.inputs: Picture-description transcripts (CHAT format) and audio recordings
summary.outputs: Dementia vs control label with confidence score
summary.results: Speaker-independent accuracy: text 77.0%, audio 63.6%, fusion 77.6% vs 53.7% majority baseline.

projects.title: Depressive Text Detection Trained On English Reddit Posts
projects.title_slide: Depressive Text Detection Trained On English Reddit Posts
projects.student_description: Analyzes Reddit posts from a kaggle dataset with Logistic Regression, Linear SVC, and BERT. Outputs either "Depressive-Associated text" or "Non-Depressive-Associated text".

summary.plain: This project built tools that read a Reddit post and flag whether its language sounds depression-related, to help researchers sort through large numbers of posts (not to diagnose anyone). The team compared two simple text models with a BERT language model, and BERT was right about 98% of the time on their test posts.
summary.technical: Data: 'Depression: Reddit Dataset (Cleaned)' (7,731 posts; 81 duplicates removed to 7,650; labels 0 non-depressive / 1 depression-associated), split 80/20 (6,120 / 1,530). Logistic Regression and Linear SVC were trained on TF-IDF features; BERT was fine-tuned on tokenized posts for binary classification. Evaluation with accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and confusion matrices: Logistic Regression 94.51% accuracy, Linear SVC 95.16%, BERT 98.43% (F1 98.5%). An earlier Twitter/X dataset was abandoned because labels were per-user rather than per-post. Models were saved and served in a Streamlit app that returns each model's label.

projects.title: Detecting AI-Generated​ Tweets​
projects.student_description: We built and evaluated models to detect whether tweets were written by humans or generated by AI.

summary.plain: This project built classifiers that guess whether a tweet was written by a person or generated by AI. The team combined two public research datasets of human and AI tweets and compared three models; a fine-tuned BERT language model did best at about 92% accuracy, and they built a small web tool to try it.
summary.technical: Data: TweepFake (25,553 tweets after cleaning; human vs Markov/RNN/LSTM/GPT-2 generated) and ElectAI (9,890 election tweets; human vs Falcon/LLaMA/Mistral), downloaded from their public GitHub repositories, mapped to a binary label, cleaned (whitespace, empties, case-insensitive duplicates) and merged into 35,443 tweets (44.2% human / 55.8% AI). EDA of tweet length and class balance. Models on the same stratified 80/20 split: TF-IDF + Logistic Regression baseline (accuracy 82.35%, F1 0.8441, AUC 0.9189), TF-IDF + Random Forest with 100 trees (82.37%, recall 89.77%, F1 0.8504), and BERT with a classification layer (92.09%, F1 0.9227). Error analysis found ~98% accuracy on ElectAI vs ~76% on TweepFake and reliance on election-topic words. A web demo lets users enter a tweet and pick a model.
summary.question: Can we classify between human vs. AI-generated tweets?
summary.problem: Bots and AI-generated text make it hard to know whether social-media content was written by a real person.
summary.beneficiary: Researchers, journalists and social-media platforms
summary.inputs: Tweet text
summary.outputs: Human vs AI-generated label

projects.student_description: A comparison of Logistic Regression, SVM, and Random Forest models for detecting fraudulent credit card transactions in a severely imbalanced dataset, evaluating each on precision, recall, and F1-score rather than accuracy alone.

summary.plain: This project tries to catch fraudulent credit card transactions, which are very rare (about 1 in 1,000). The team compared three models and found that the random forest balanced catching fraud and avoiding false alarms best, though all models struggled because fraud is so rare.
summary.technical: Data: Kaggle 'transactions-fraud-datasets' with 13M+ labeled transactions (fraud ~0.10%); features include amount, time, merchant category code, payment method and transaction errors. EDA found errors (~2.5x) and online transactions associated with fraud. Imbalance handling: undersampling for SVM (only ~5% of data used), SMOTE for Logistic Regression. Models: RBF-kernel SVM, Logistic Regression, Random Forest. Reported results (comparison slide): Logistic Regression accuracy 88%, precision 1%, recall 75%, F1 0.02, ROC-AUC 0.893; SVM 86%, 0.75%, 70.2%, 0.01, 0.898; Random Forest 99.87% accuracy, ROC-AUC 0.919, precision 68% / recall 28.3% at default threshold, and recall 45% / F1 0.474 after lowering the decision threshold.

projects.student_description: a CNN trained on multispectral Sentinel-2 satellite imagery that classifies cyanobacteria harmful algal bloom severity (Low, Moderate, High) in inland water bodies to support early public health warning systems

summary.plain: This project uses satellite pictures of lakes to judge how severe a harmful algae bloom is (low, moderate or high), which could help warn people about unsafe water. Instead of the planned image neural network, the team computed color and spectral statistics for each water tile and compared several models; a random forest was best at 75% accuracy.
summary.technical: Data: Amfitrite Inland Waters HAB Sentinel-2 dataset of 4,698 12-band Sentinel-2 tiles (2017-2021) labeled Low/Moderate/High from ground-truth sampling and the CyFi tool (High 1,958 / Low 1,401 / Moderate 1,339). Features: water-masked reflectance mean/std/median for 10 bands plus spectral indices (NDCI, 3-band phycocyanin proxy, FAI, NDVI, NDWI, blue:green and green:red ratios). Models: majority-class baseline, Logistic Regression, Gradient Boosting and Random Forest on a held-out test set (80/20 split, water-body separation described). Results: Random Forest accuracy 0.750, balanced accuracy 0.739, macro F1 0.741 vs Gradient Boosting 0.745 / 0.732, Logistic Regression 0.675 / 0.679, baseline 0.406 / 0.192. Moderate severity was hardest. A CNN on 256x256 crops and a Vision Transformer remain proposals.

projects.title: Detecting Parkinson’s Disease
projects.student_description: Parkinson’s disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disease that impacts neurons in the motor cortex, specifically causing them to weaken its physiological purpose over time. On a global scale, more than 10 million people are impacted by the disease. For patients and clinical staff, diagnosing the disease and monitoring the symptoms are inconvenient logistically and financially. To combat this, speech tests are a noninvasive form of evaluation to determine a patient’s prognosis for Parkinson’s and assess the severity of the disease via voice biomarkers.

summary.plain: This project explored whether machine learning can detect Parkinson's disease from voice recordings, measure how severe it is, and spot moments when a patient's walking 'freezes' using motion sensors. Voice features separated patients from healthy people well (about 92-94% accuracy), voice could not predict severity better than simply guessing the average, and sensor data detected freezing episodes in new patients fairly well.
summary.technical: (1) Classification on the UCI Parkinsons voice dataset (195 recordings): Random Forest, XGBoost and LightGBM with patient-level GroupShuffleSplit/GroupKFold, RandomizedSearchCV tuning, feature importance and SHAP; ~92% accuracy (RF 93.3% with patient-level validation), ROC-AUC XGBoost 0.979, LightGBM 0.976, RF 0.962; patient-level majority vote 23/24 correct. (2) Regression of total_UPDRS on UCI Parkinsons Telemonitoring (5,875 recordings, 42 patients): XGBoost/LightGBM under patient-level splits gave RMSE ~10-14 and negative R², not beating a mean baseline; a next-visit formulation scored R² 0.98 but was shown to be an interpolation artifact matched by a persistence baseline, and a gap-enforced change-prediction setup still lost to persistence. (3) Freezing-of-gait on Daphnet accelerometer data (10 patients, 4-second windows, 9,100 windows, ~9:1 imbalance): balanced Random Forest (max_depth 10) with GroupKFold gave accuracy 89.1%, balanced accuracy 0.78, ROC-AUC 0.884, freeze F1 0.53 after threshold tuning to 0.387; patient-specific models reached mean ROC-AUC 0.950; a freeze-fraction regressor was also built (calibrated R² ~0.65, unseen ~0.16).
summary.question: How can MLs detect Parkinson and its gravity from the tremor of one's voice?
summary.problem: Diagnosing and monitoring Parkinson's disease is logistically and financially burdensome; non-invasive voice and wearable data may help.
summary.beneficiary: Parkinson's patients and clinical staff
summary.subdomain: Parkinson's disease detection, severity estimation and freezing-of-gait detection
summary.inputs: Biomedical voice measurements; wearable tri-axial accelerometer signals
summary.outputs: PD vs healthy label; UPDRS severity score; freeze vs normal window; freeze fraction
summary.results: Voice classification ~92-94% accuracy (ROC-AUC up to 0.979); UPDRS regression failed to beat baselines (negative R²); FoG detection ROC-AUC 0.884 on unseen patients.

projects.student_description: Leverage machine learning to analyze and classify histology images for breast cancer detection

summary.plain: This project trained computer vision models to look at microscope images of breast tissue and decide whether a tumor is benign or malignant. A deeper network called ResNet-18 reached about 96% test accuracy, compared to 81% for a simpler CNN, and the team built a web demo where you can upload an image to get a prediction.
summary.technical: Data: the BreakHis histopathology dataset, 400x magnification subset (777 malignant and 371 benign images as reported). Preprocessing: resizing to 224x224, random horizontal flips, random rotation, color jitter and ImageNet normalization. Models: a 3-layer baseline CNN and a ResNet-18; class imbalance handled with BCEWithLogitsLoss pos_weight; epochs, batch size and learning rate were tuned. Evaluation: confusion matrix, ROC curve (AUC = 0.9835) and a classification report. Results: ResNet-18 reached 96% test accuracy versus 81% for the baseline CNN. A Streamlit-style upload demo was shown.
summary.question: How can CNNs and data augmentation improve classification of breast tumors as benign or malignant using histopathology images?
summary.problem: Early and accurate breast cancer diagnosis from histopathology images is challenging; an ML diagnostic aid could help.
summary.beneficiary: Pathologists and clinicians diagnosing breast cancer; patients

summary.plain: This project built a tool that estimates a person's risk of diabetes from basic health measurements like glucose, blood pressure and BMI. The team trained three simple machine learning models, picked the most accurate one, and turned the output into four risk levels from low to high.

projects.title: Digestive Autoimmune Disease Detection
projects.student_description: This AI model aims to detect the presence of an autoimmune disease in the digestive tract sooner, leading to the identification of the potential GI disease to allow patients to receive earlier treatment.

summary.plain: This project tried to help spot autoimmune diseases of the digestive tract earlier using two public patient datasets. A first model tried to predict individual symptoms from clinical and lifestyle data, and a second model used blood and antibody measurements (plus the first model's predictions) to guess which of about seven GI autoimmune diseases a patient has, reaching about 88.5% accuracy.
summary.technical: Data: two Kaggle datasets: a Gastrointestinal Disease Dataset (30,560 patients, 37 clinical/lifestyle features) and an All Autoimmune Disorders dataset (12,500 patients, 79 columns, filtered to 8-9 GI diseases). Model 1: a random forest predicting a synthetic autoimmune label reached only ~50% accuracy, so the task was redefined as per-symptom random forest classifiers (accuracy 0.56-0.76, AUC 0.486-0.505); k-means clustering visualized with PCA showed three patient profiles. Model 2: a random forest multi-class disease classifier with feature importances (autoantibody markers dominate) and an 80-20 split, evaluated with a confusion matrix. Adding Model 1 insights raised accuracy from 0.8673 to 0.8850 (+0.0177).
summary.question: How can autoimmune diseases affecting the digestive tract be better identified to receive required medical attention sooner?
summary.problem: Digestive autoimmune diseases are often diagnosed late; earlier identification could allow earlier treatment.
summary.beneficiary: Patients with suspected GI autoimmune disease and their clinicians
summary.inputs: Clinical markers, lifestyle factors, blood counts and autoantibody markers
summary.outputs: Predicted symptoms (Model 1) and predicted GI autoimmune disease (Model 2)
summary.results: Model 2 accuracy 0.8673 without and 0.8850 with Model 1 insights; Model 1 per-symptom AUCs around 0.49-0.51.

projects.title: Disaster Prediction Using Pre-Disaster Images
projects.student_description: Our project uses satellite-based flood data to classify disaster severity and support emergency response. We applied supervised machine learning to analyze key environmental features and demonstrate how AI can improve community preparedness and humanitarian impact.

summary.plain: This project wants to predict which areas are likely to flood before a disaster happens by looking at satellite images taken beforehand. The team explored radar and optical satellite images and designed a neural network pipeline that would label each pixel as safe, at risk or flooded, but the model was still being built when they presented.
summary.technical: Data: Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 optical imagery from the SEN12FLOOD and STURMFlood datasets. EDA with rasterio and matplotlib showed heavy-tailed (gamma-like) SAR pixel distributions and multimodal optical reflectance, motivating separate normalization (e.g. log-scaling SAR) before fusing channels. Planned model: a CNN performing semantic segmentation of stacked SAR+optical channels into safe/at-risk/flooded, producing a probabilistic flood risk map. Planned evaluation: precision, recall (priority) and leave-one-region-out generalization testing. No training or results are reported.
summary.question: Can a deep learning model trained on pre-disaster satellite images detect early indicators of flooding, and how accurately can it predict high-risk zones before the disaster occurs?
summary.problem: Flood management is largely reactive; early detection of high-risk zones could enable proactive evacuation and resource staging.
summary.beneficiary: Emergency responders, NGOs and communities in flood-prone regions
summary.subdomain: Flood risk prediction from satellite imagery
summary.inputs: Pre-disaster Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 optical image stacks
summary.outputs: Planned probabilistic flood risk map (per-pixel safe / at risk / flooded)

projects.title: Does AI Usage Improve Student Academic Performance?
projects.title_slide: Does AI Usage Improve Student Academic Performance?
projects.student_description: Using a dataset of over 50 thousand student records, our model can determine whether a student’s AI usage is positively or negatively affecting their academic performance. We have implemented a number of techniques to increase the accuracy of our model over time. This helped tackle one of our challenges, the inaccuracy of our model during its initial testing phases.

summary.plain: This project used a large public dataset of student records to ask whether using generative AI helps students' grades. Charts showed that traditional study hours were linked much more strongly to GPA gains than AI use, and heavy AI users reported more burnout and exam anxiety. The team also trained simple models to predict whether a student's AI use helps or hurts their performance and shared a Streamlit app.
summary.technical: Data: a Kaggle 'AI Impact on Students' dataset of roughly 50,000 student records. Analysis: correlation of features with GPA change (study hours +0.38 vs AI usage -0.05), scatter of weekly GenAI hours vs GPA change colored by burnout risk, and exam anxiety by usage tier. Models: logistic regression (max_iter=1000) and a random forest (200 trees, max depth 8), both with class_weight='balanced', trained on a train/test split. No accuracy or other metrics are reported; the team notes initial inaccuracy as a challenge.

projects.title: Don’t Turn a Blind Eye
projects.student_description: Our project utilizes a 2D Convolutional Neural Network on various preprocessed retinal scans labeled for diabetic retinopahty to predict onset of blindness caused by DR. The model is deployed via a streamlit application to serve as a triaging/screening assistant, rather than replacing eye care providers, helping expand access to early eye care.

summary.plain: This project trained a neural network to look at photos of the back of the eye and grade how severe diabetic retinopathy is, a disease that can cause blindness. It combined two public eye-scan collections, cleaned up lighting differences, and put the model in a Streamlit app meant as a screening helper for eye doctors, not a replacement.
summary.technical: Data: merged 2015 Kaggle EyePACS (n=88,702) and 2019 APTOS (n=3,662) fundus images (~92k), resized to 1024px max and labeled 0-4 (No DR to Proliferative); 73% are No DR. Preprocessing: Ben Graham enhancement, rotations/flips/cropping, a weighted random sampler oversampling rare classes, and patient-grouped splitting with GroupShuffleSplit to avoid left/right eye leakage. Model: a custom 2D CNN with 5 conv blocks (Conv2d, BatchNorm2d, ReLU, max pooling), adaptive average pooling and a fully connected layer (~4.86M parameters), trained with a soft ordinal (SORD) loss. Evaluation at best epoch 25: recall 0.80, precision 0.82, F1 0.80 with a validation confusion matrix showing weak performance on Mild and Severe classes. Deployed as a Streamlit app that applies the same preprocessing to uploaded scans.
summary.question: How can we use a retinal scan as a predictor for the onset of blindness while using multiple datasets for diversity?
summary.problem: Diabetic retinopathy can cause blindness; screening access is limited where specialists are scarce.
summary.beneficiary: Primary care clinics and low-resource settings triaging patients for ophthalmologists

summary.results: Recall 0.80, precision 0.82, F1 0.80 on validation; Mild class largely misclassified as No DR or Moderate.

projects.title: Drivers of Emergency Department Wait Times and Admission Risk
projects.title_slide: Drivers of Emergency Department Wait Times and Admission Risk
projects.student_description: Our project uses machine learning on two datasets to study disparities in emergency department wait times and estimate hospital admission risk from information available at triage.

summary.plain: This project studied why some people wait longer in hospital emergency rooms and whether race, ethnicity or insurance still matter once you account for how sick the patient is. Using national ER visit data, the team found that these differences in wait time stayed about the same after adding medical urgency. They also built a model that predicts from triage information whether a patient will be admitted to the hospital, and deployed an app.
summary.technical: Data: NHAMCS national ED visit survey data for wait times and the Yale ED triage dataset (EMMLC) for admission outcomes. Wait-time models: OLS linear regression on log-transformed minutes-to-provider with demographics only (Model 1) versus demographics plus triage urgency/clinical controls (Model 2), a multinomial logistic model for short/medium/long wait categories, and a random forest as a comparison benchmark. Admission model: logistic regression on triage vitals, age, acuity and chief complaint. Results: race, ethnicity and insurance coefficients stayed similar after adding clinical controls; the admission model reached ROC-AUC of about 0.875. A deployed app and repository are referenced.
summary.question: To what extent are emergency department wait times explained by patient symptoms and clinical urgency, and do demographic factors remain associated with wait times after accounting for medical need?
summary.problem: ED wait times may differ by race, insurance and language beyond what medical need explains, affecting outcomes, trust and fairness.
summary.beneficiary: Hospital administrators, ED staff and health-equity researchers

summary.outputs: Predicted (log) wait time, wait category, admission probability, and equity coefficients
summary.results: Demographic/insurance wait-time differences persist after clinical controls; admission logistic regression ROC-AUC ≈ 0.875.

projects.title: Drug Interaction Severity Predictor
projects.student_description:
Here's a clean 1-2 sentence version:

---
We built a machine learning model that predicts the severity of drug-drug interactions — Minor, Moderate, or Major — using pharmacological features like drug class and metabolizing enzymes, trained on real clinical interaction data. The project also includes a bias evaluation across drug categories and a deployed web app that lets users check any two medications for potential interaction risk.

summary.plain: This project built a tool that predicts how dangerous it is to take two medications together: minor, moderate or major. It learns from drug features like which liver enzymes break the drugs down, reached 79% accuracy, and checks whether it works equally well across different kinds of drugs. Users can type two drug names into a web app to get a severity estimate.
summary.technical: Data: DDInter drug-pair interaction records (~240K, labeled Minor/Moderate/Major across 8 categories) merged with DrugBank drug features (ATC class, CYP enzymes, approval status, mechanism/target text). A 4,800-row balanced training set was built with two-tier sampling (200 per severity per category). Features: ATC classes, CYP enzyme indicators, a shared-enzyme flag, approval status and TF-IDF of mechanism text (100 features per drug). Models: random forest (primary), XGBoost (comparison) and KNN (baseline), with a stratified 70/15/15 split and cross-validation during model selection. Results: random forest 79% accuracy, 82% Major recall, 87% Minor recall, 2% catastrophic miss rate (5/240 Major predicted Minor); XGBoost 77%; KNN 59%. Bias evaluation by drug category showed Major recall from 92% (blood) to 69% (digestive). Deployed as a Streamlit app using a DrugBank lookup table.
summary.question: Can a machine learning model accurately predict the severity of a drug-drug interaction (Minor, Moderate, or Major) using pharmacological features, and does performance vary across drug categories?
summary.problem: Existing interaction checkers give binary flags, cause alert fatigue and lag behind real-world evidence, leaving providers without severity context.
summary.beneficiary: Prescribers and pharmacists
summary.inputs: Two drugs' ATC class, CYP metabolizing enzymes, shared-enzyme flag, approval status and TF-IDF mechanism/target text
summary.outputs: Interaction severity (Minor/Moderate/Major) with a confidence score
summary.results: Random forest 79% accuracy, 82% Major recall, 87% Minor recall; XGBoost 77%; KNN 59%; Major recall 92% for blood drugs vs 69% for digestive drugs.

projects.title: E-Commerce AI Model
projects.student_description: This AI Model utilizes Linear Regression to determine whether or not a customer will churn from a business. Provides insight to company stakeholders to better prioritize customer loyalty.

summary.plain: This project tried to predict which online-shop customers are likely to stop buying (churn), so businesses can focus on keeping them. The team trained a logistic regression model on a public Kaggle customer dataset and showed which customer traits mattered most. The model separated churners from non-churners fairly well (AUC 0.89) but missed about half of the churners in the test set.
summary.technical: A public Kaggle e-commerce churn dataset with demographic, purchasing, engagement and satisfaction/complaint features was used with pandas and matplotlib. Categorical features were one-hot encoded (visible as dummy columns such as PreferedOrderCat_Others) and a scikit-learn logistic regression was trained on an 80/20 split. The top 10 features by absolute coefficient were reported (e.g. preferred order category, tenure, complaints). projects.student_description: Energy consumption often comes with hidden costs and inefficient use. Our project aims to use AI to conserve energy by identifying opportunities based on demand.

summary.plain: This project tried to forecast how much electricity a household will use, and how 'dirty' (carbon-heavy) the grid's power will be, hour by hour. The team trained an XGBoost model and an LSTM neural network on household energy data and built a demo app that also uses a reinforcement-learning agent to recommend a lower-carbon time to use electricity. The goal was to cut peak-hour CO2 emissions without raising bills for low-income families.
summary.technical: Household appliance-level energy data from Pecan Street was explored (feature counts, appliance correlation heatmap, grid import/export over time, average consumption by day-of-week and hour). Planned additional sources were CityLearn (battery/EV simulation), U.S. Census ACS income data and ERCOT/CAISO carbon intensity. An XGBoost regressor was used as a benchmark and an LSTM forecaster as the main model; reported RMSE was $0.293 / 0.0923 kWh for XGBoost versus $0.127 / 0.006 kWh for the LSTM, with a separate unexplained 'accuracy > 85%' label. A 'Monte Carlo RL Policy' agent recommends an hour to use electricity, shown in a demo app that predicts power demand, price and carbon intensity for the next 24 hours. Validation procedure and RL details are not described.

projects.student_description: Used logistic regression to detect risk factors for dropping out of college in STEM Majors.

summary.plain: This project tried to predict whether a college student will drop out, stay enrolled, or graduate, using early grades and background information. The team compared two simple models, improved them with smarter features and class balancing, and found first- and second-semester course results matter most. They packaged the result as an interactive dashboard that runs in a Docker container.
summary.technical: The UCI 'Predict Students' Dropout and Academic Success' dataset (academic, demographic and financial features) was used for three-class prediction (Dropout / Enrolled / Graduate). Logistic regression served as the benchmark against a decision tree; LR won on accuracy (76.84% vs 75.59%) and Dropout recall (0.77 vs 0.69), while both had ~0.41 F1 on Enrolled. Feature engineering (passed/enrolled approval ratio) raised the decision tree from 69.5% to 71.6%, and low-cardinality one-hot encoding raised LR cross-validated accuracy from 72.9% to 74.7-75.2%. Class-weight tuning improved Enrolled recall from 33% to 64% in the normalized confusion matrix, and SHAP showed semester curricular-unit approvals as top predictors. The models are served in a Streamlit dashboard packaged with Docker/docker-compose.

projects.title: Electric Vehicle Charging Station Demand Predictor
projects.title_slide: Electric Vehicle Charging Station Demand Predictor
projects.student_description: Uses Random Forest model to forecast EV charging station utilization in Austin, TX 30 minutes in advance, using historical charging patterns and time-based features to predict periods of high and low demand.

summary.plain: This project tried to predict how busy electric-vehicle charging stations in Austin, Texas will be 30 minutes ahead. Using a public Kaggle dataset, the team trained a random forest model that beat both a simple linear model and a naive guess, and built a Streamlit app where users pick options and see predictions.
summary.technical: A Kaggle EV charging station availability dataset recorded at 30-minute intervals in Austin was cleaned in Jupyter, explored with Seaborn, checked for leakage, encoded, and reduced via correlation-based feature selection to ~20 inputs (traffic, amenities, hour of day, location type, etc.). A 200-tree random forest regressor predicted station utilization rate, compared with linear regression and a naive baseline using a chronological time-series split. Random forest reported MAE 0.0582, RMSE 0.0844, R2 0.9399 (train R2 0.9670) versus linear regression (MAE 0.0782, RMSE 0.1078, R2 0.9020) and naive baseline (MAE 0.2025, RMSE 0.2576, R2 0.4401). Actual-vs-predicted, residual and bias-by-utilization-range plots showed over-prediction at low and under-prediction at high utilization. The model was deployed in a Streamlit app with compressed joblib files.

projects.title: Electronic Schematic Symbol Classifier
projects.student_description: We trained a YOLOv8 model to detect and classify 17 foundational electronic component classes when given handwritten drawings of a schematic.

summary.plain: This project teaches a computer to find and name electronic parts (like resistors and capacitors) in hand-drawn circuit sketches. The team trained a YOLOv8 object-detection model on a public dataset of hand-drawn circuits and built a Streamlit web app where users upload a sketch and see the detected parts. It found parts very accurately on the test data.
summary.technical: The Digitize-HCD dataset of hand-drawn circuit diagrams with bounding-box labels was converted to YOLO format and used to train a YOLOv8 Nano detector on 17 component classes, with images resized and normalized to 640x640. Evaluation reported 98.8% mAP50 across 17 classes, 97.5% precision and recall, 76.1% mAP50-95, ~99% on foundational components and ~2.9 ms per-image GPU inference. A Streamlit UI lets users upload schematics or choose samples and adjust the confidence (sensitivity) threshold. Bias discussion covers class imbalance and annotation subjectivity.

projects.title: Emotion Recognition in Gaming Using EEG Signals
projects.title_slide: EMOTION RECOGNITION IN GAMING USING EEG SIGNALS
projects.student_description: Our project explores how EEG brainwave data can be used to recognize players’ emotions during video gameplay. By training a machine learning model on EEG signals from 28 participants, we aim to predict emotional states like calmness or frustration in real time.

summary.plain: This project tried to tell whether a video-game player is feeling positive or negative emotions from their brainwave (EEG) recordings. The team combined recordings from 28 players, summarized the signals by brain region, and trained a random forest that was right about 63% of the time, beating logistic regression and SVM.
summary.technical: EEG recordings from 28 subjects in the Kaggle 'Emotion Recognition using EEG and Computer Games' data were merged across raw and preprocessed CSVs, corrupted recordings were removed, and signals were aggregated by brain region with per-region mean and variance features. Five emotion classes from SAM ratings (Calm, Satisfaction, Funny vs Boredom, Horrible) were collapsed into a binary positive/negative label. A random forest was compared with SVM and logistic regression; reported accuracy was 62.9% for random forest versus 58.0% (LR) and 56.1% (SVM). Per-class results: negative precision 0.71 / recall 0.61 / F1 0.65, positive precision 0.55 / recall 0.66 / F1 0.60. Feature importance was spread across many brain regions.

summary.problem: Games and affective-computing systems cannot adapt to players' emotions without a way to recognize emotional state from physiological signals.

projects.title: Stock News Sentiment Analysis
projects.student_description: Our project uses AI and financial news headlines to predict whether the stock price of a FAANG company or Microsoft will go up or down the next day. By combining sentiment analysis from FinBERT with historical trading data, we aim to support faster and more informed decision-making in the stock market.

summary.plain: This project asked whether the emotions in news headlines (like fear, anger or disgust) are linked to how the stock market moves over the next few days. The team used ready-made AI language models to label millions of headlines with emotions and sentiment, combined them with S&P 500 prices, and trained a random forest to predict 3-day market returns.
summary.technical: A headline corpus from 47 outlets (over 23 million headlines) was labeled with Hugging Face pretrained transformers: emotion-english-distilroberta-base (7 emotions) and distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english (positive/negative), then filtered to 4 major outlets for 2015-2019. S&P 500 data from the Yahoo Finance Python library was merged by date and daily sentiment trends, emotion distributions and 3-day market returns were engineered. A random forest regressor, chosen as best among unnamed models tested, was tuned with GridSearchCV using a 70/30 split and 5-fold cross-validation. Reported results: R2 0.879, MAE 0.00385, RMSE 0.00544, mean bias error 0.00004; feature importance ranked sentiment and headline count highest, with disgust and anger the top emotions. A Streamlit demo is referenced.
summary.question: To what extent do varying levels and types of emotions evoked by news headlines influence day-to-day fluctuations in stock market prices?
summary.problem: Increasingly emotional news headlines may drive outsized investor reactions; the project tests whether headline emotion predicts short-term market returns.

projects.title: Environmental Epidemiologist
projects.student_description: here's a short description of the project: This project uses machine learning models (Linear Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost) to analyze the relationship between agricultural pesticide use and respiratory health outcomes across California counties. By examining pesticide exposure patterns with lag features and cumulative exposure metrics, the research aims to provide evidence-based insights that can inform public health policies and protect communities disproportionately affected by pesticide exposure.

summary.plain: This project asked whether counties in California that use more farm pesticides also have more people hospitalized for lung disease (COPD). The team combined state pesticide records with hospital, income, population and air-quality data for 51 counties over about 20 years and tested three models. They found income and poverty explain most of the differences, while long-term pesticide exposure adds a smaller but noticeable signal, and built a Streamlit app to explore predictions.
summary.technical: County-year panel data (51 California counties, 2000-2022, 1,139 observations) were assembled from CDPR pesticide use reports, Tracking California COPD hospitalization rates, census demographics, poverty/income estimates and AQI, with engineered pesticide intensity, 1-20 year lags and 5-20 year cumulative exposure features. OLS linear regression with confounder controls reached R2 ~0.38 (poverty coefficient +0.73, p < 0.001) and revealed a sulfur-driven 'protective' artifact. XGBoost (25 features, max depth 3, learning rate 0.05, 80/20 random split stratified by year) reached test R2 0.5895, RMSE 6.51 (train R2 0.7242), 36% better than a mean baseline. Random forest with GroupKFold spatial cross-validation by county gave mean R2 0.3151 (+/-0.0964), RMSE 7.06, MAE 5.14; sequential models (socioeconomic only 0.38, pesticides only -0.39, combined 0.40), residual analysis and income-stratified correlations (significant in low- and high-income counties, not middle) were reported. A Streamlit app lets users adjust inputs and generate predictions.
summary.question: Is there a connection between the amount of pesticides used in California agriculture and the prevalence of respiratory conditions (asthma, COPD) in California citizens at the county level?
summary.problem: Links between agricultural pesticide use and community respiratory health are under-examined, especially for farmworker and low-income communities.

projects.title: EquiBirth AI
projects.student_description: Our final project grapples with the question can we predict preterm birth from U.S. birth certificates, and is the model fair? We think so, with results revealing that while certain groups are more-or-less likely to experience preterm birth, we do not yet have a pinned 'why'. We hypothesize that disparity in healthcare treatment and access is responsible for this gap.

summary.plain: The team asked whether a computer model could predict which babies will be born too early using U.S. birth certificate records, and whether that model treats different groups of mothers fairly. They found that the most impressive scores came from information only known after birth, so they removed it and reported a much more modest, honest result. They also showed that the model flags Black mothers far more often and that measured factors like education explain less than half of the racial gap in preterm birth.
summary.technical: About 24.9 million U.S. singleton birth records (CDC/NCHS natality files, 2018-2024) were used to predict preterm birth (<37 weeks; base rate 8.57%). The team quantified leakage: all features gave AUC-ROC 0.939 and post-delivery variables alone 0.917, versus 0.659 for pre-delivery features only; removing eclampsia/gestational hypertension/diabetes as reverse-causal features lowered AUC from 0.684 to 0.654. XGBoost tuned with Optuna was selected (held-out AUC-PR 0.1720 with 95% bootstrap interval; headline AUC 0.656) and compared with LightGBM (0.1699), a stacked ensemble (0.1713), TabNet (0.1299) and FT-Transformer (0.1201), the neural models being compute-capped at 30K rows. Fairness analysis reported equal-opportunity differences (e.g. +0.393 for NH Black vs NH White) and a 2.74x flag rate for NH Black mothers at a shared threshold; a learning-curve check (100K-500K rows) and single-feature AUCs showed a data ceiling. A pathway decomposition attributed 22% (SES), 19% (clinical) and 43% (both) of the Black-White gap to measured factors.
summary.question: Can we predict preterm birth from U.S. birth certificates, and is the model fair?
summary.problem: Preterm birth is common and unequally distributed across racial groups; the team wanted to know whether birth-record data can predict it without leakage and whether such a model is equitable.
summary.beneficiary: Public health researchers and policymakers studying maternal health disparities
summary.subdomain: Maternal health / preterm birth risk and health equity
summary.inputs: Pre-delivery fields from U.S. birth certificates (e.g. medical risk flags, previous preterm birth, pre-pregnancy BMI, insurance, race/ethnicity, education)
summary.outputs: Preterm-birth risk score / flag; fairness and disparity analyses by group
summary.results: Selected XGBoost: AUC-ROC reported as 0.656 (0.659 and 0.654 on other slides), AUC-PR 0.1720 vs 8.57% base rate. Leaky feature sets reached 0.917-0.939 AUC. NH Black mothers flagged 2.74x as often as NH White mothers. Measured pathways explain at most 43% of the Black-White gap.

projects.title: F1 Pit Stop Optimizer
projects.student_description: Our model takes in race data, and outputs whether the driver should pit next lap, or stay out the next lap.

summary.plain: This project tried to predict, lap by lap, whether a Formula 1 driver should make a pit stop on the next lap. The team trained a Random Forest on lap data such as tire age, lap time and race position, and tried to deal with the fact that pit laps are rare. The model did better than random guessing on pit laps but still missed most of them, and the team concluded their features were not yet good enough.
summary.technical: Lap-level F1 data for 2022-2025 (about 101,146 laps, ~3.2% pit laps) from a Formula One historical data API was used with features such as lap number, tyre life, position, stint number, lap time and engineered stint/tyre-life endpoint and stint_comp features. An initial decision tree was visualized, then a Random Forest classifier (100 estimators, max depth 5, class weights {0:1, 1:8}, 35% decision threshold) was evaluated with 5-fold GroupKFold cross-validation. Mean accuracy was 86.55% (+/- 3.97%), mean pit recall 31.50%, per-fold pit precision 6.5-10.4%, and out-of-fold PR-AUC 0.0719 versus 0.0321 by chance (2.24x lift), while a 'never pit' baseline reached 96.79% accuracy. Feature importance was plotted and a race demonstration on the 2024 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix caught 10 of 28 actual pit stops.
summary.question: Can a decision tree model accurately predict when an F1 driver should pit based on lap time, tire life, position, and stint length?
summary.problem: Pit stop timing is a high-stakes strategic decision in Formula 1; the team wanted a simple data-driven decision tool.
summary.beneficiary: F1 race strategists / pit crews
summary.inputs: Per-lap features: lap number, tyre life, position, stint number, lap time, engineered stint features
summary.outputs: Binary decision: 0 = stay out, 1 = pit next lap
summary.results: 5-fold group CV: mean accuracy 86.55%, mean pit recall 31.50%, pit precision ~6.5-10.4%, PR-AUC 0.0719 vs 0.0321 chance (2.24x); 'never pit' baseline accuracy 96.79%; 10/28 pit stops caught in 2024 Abu Dhabi GP demo. Team states the model is feature-limited.

projects.title: Flight Departure Delay Prediction Analysis
projects.student_description: We made an AI model that can predict if your flight will get delayed based on weather and historical flight data.

summary.plain: The team tried to predict how many minutes a United Airlines domestic flight would be delayed using weather and past flight information from January 2025. A simple linear model barely worked, while tree-based models looked much better. However, the strongest inputs were fields describing the recorded causes of each delay, which are only known after a delay happens.
summary.technical: 60,000+ United Airlines domestic flights from January 2025 were combined with weather variables (wind speed, cloud cover, weather code, temperature, precipitation; Open-Meteo ERA5 archive cited) and features such as departure time bins, route distance and scheduled duration; an 80/20 train/test split was used. A Lasso regression gave RMSE 76.49, MAE 49.06, R^2 0.007 (CV R^2 0.008) after the team removed a leaking departure-time variable. Random Forest and Gradient Boosting regressors reached R^2 of roughly 0.74 and 0.72 (read from chart), with Random Forest feature importances dominated by CarrierDelay_present, NASDelay_ratio and LateAircraftDelay features. An MLPRegressor is discussed but no results are shown.
summary.question: To what extent can AI predict flight departure delay time for United Airlines Domestic Flights, using weather data, and historical flight data?
summary.problem: Flight delays cost airlines money and frustrate passengers; better delay prediction could support scheduling and resource planning.
summary.beneficiary: Airlines, airport planners and travelers
summary.inputs: Flight schedule features (departure/arrival time, scheduled duration, distance), delay-cause fields, and weather variables
summary.outputs: Predicted departure delay in minutes
summary.results: Lasso: RMSE 76.49, MAE 49.06, R^2 0.007. Random Forest R^2 ~0.74 and Gradient Boosting R^2 ~0.72 (chart). Top RF features are delay-cause fields.

projects.title: Food Image Calorie Estimator
projects.student_description: Our project uses computer vision to classify food images into Low, Medium, or High calorie ranges using the Nutrition5k dataset. We trained and evaluated CNN-based models and deployed the final model through a Streamlit app where users can upload food images and receive predictions.

summary.plain: This project trained a computer vision model to look at a photo of a meal and guess whether it is low, medium or high in calories. Using about 3,200 overhead photos of cafeteria dishes with known nutrition, the team improved their model from about 66% to about 73% validation accuracy and built a web app where you can upload a food photo. Medium-calorie meals were the hardest to tell apart.
summary.technical: 3,244 overhead RGB images from Nutrition5k were matched to dish nutrition labels, dishes with missing values/images removed, and calories binned into Low (<150 kcal), Medium (150-400) and High (>=400); data were split 70/15/15 by dish with no dish overlap. Images were resized to 224x224 and augmented with flips, small rotations and color jitter. The final model is an ordinal multi-task CNN: a CNN feature extractor shared between an ordinal Low/Medium/High classifier and a regression head for calories, mass, fat, carbohydrates and protein, trained with a combined classification plus weighted regression loss over ~25 epochs. Validation accuracy improved from ~66% (basic CNN) to ~73%; one-vs-rest ROC AUCs were 0.892 (Low), 0.889 (Medium) and 0.884 (High), and a confusion matrix shows Medium as the most confused class. The model was deployed as a Streamlit upload-and-predict prototype.

projects.title: Forecasting Fiscal-Year Revenue Growth Relative to Industry & Varied Macroeconomic Conditions
projects.title_slide: Forecasting Fiscal-Year Revenue Growth Relative to Industry & Varied Macroeconomic Conditions
projects.student_description: RQ: How are company-level financial characteristics and macroeconomic conditions associated with next fiscal-year revenue growth relative to industry peers?

summary.plain: This project asked whether a company's public financial reports and the state of the economy can predict whether the company's revenue will grow faster than similar companies in its industry next year. The team built a large dataset from SEC filings and Federal Reserve economic data and trained a gradient boosting model that was tested year by year on future data. The model was right about two-thirds of the time overall, and about 90% of the time for the companies it was most confident about, but struggled in unusual years like 2020-2021.
summary.technical: Quarterly SEC financial-statement ZIP files (2010q1-2026q1, 5.6 GB; 86,409 U.S. 10-K filings) were processed into an annual track (53 metrics plus same-filing comparatives) and a quarterly track (227,272 quarter observations), combined with FRED macroeconomic variables, giving 37,279 company-years for 6,455 firms with 164 features. The target is peer-relative revenue growth: whether next-year growth exceeds the median of at least 20 same-SIC2 peers with fiscal year-ends within +/-92 days, with all inputs from the prior fiscal year and a 300-430 day gap guard. A scikit-learn HistGradientBoostingClassifier (lr 0.05, 300 iterations, 31 leaves, L2 0.1, early stopping, 5-seed rank ensemble) with train-fold median imputation and 1/99 winsorization was evaluated by expanding-window walk-forward validation over nine test years (2016-2024). Results on 25,221 out-of-time predictions: pooled accuracy 67.69%, mean annual AUC 74.67%, precision at P>0.5 68.72% and mean top-decile precision 89.74%, varying by industry (~68% to 97%). A Monte Carlo Dirichlet search over 70 lag weightings found only the most recent year carries signal, and PCA of macro conditions showed 2020-2022 as outlier regimes (concept drift).
summary.question: How are company-level financial characteristics and macroeconomic conditions associated with next fiscal-year revenue growth relative to industry peers?
summary.problem: Revenue growth is economically important but hard to compare across firms and industries; public filings are rich but heterogeneous and backward-looking.

projects.title: Forecasting Technology and Energy Stocks Through Macroeconomic Disruption
projects.title_slide: Forecasting Technology and Energy Stocks Through Macroeconomic Disruption
projects.student_description: Our final project is using different macroeconomic features and stock price features in order to predict future stock prices within the energy and technology sectors.

summary.plain: The team tested whether adding economic and policy information, like inflation, interest rates, consumer sentiment and tariff announcements, helps predict the stock prices of big tech and energy companies better than past prices alone. They tried three kinds of models: a classic time-series model (ARIMA), a simple linear regression and a deep learning model (CNN-LSTM). The classic ARIMA model had the smallest errors, mostly because daily prices behave a lot like a random walk.
summary.technical: Daily OHLCV data for 14 large-cap tickers (7 tech, 7 energy) over 1,254 trading days (July 2021-July 2026) were merged with FRED CPI, consumer sentiment, Treasury yields, oil data and a manually curated USTR tariff-event calendar into 42 features, including log returns, 20/50-day SMAs, 10-day momentum, 14-day RSI, a volatility-based regime label and a binary tariff flag; sparse macro series were forward/back-filled. Three models were built: a univariate rolling ARIMA (test RMSE 3.87, MAE/MAPE by ticker, compared against a naive baseline), multiple linear regression comparing price/volume-only vs macro-augmented features (test RMSE 95.4; META example RMSE 111.84, R^2 -2.259), and a CNN-LSTM on all 42 features with a 126-day lookback forecasting 30 days ahead (test RMSE 44.47, MAE 38.78). Error analysis found the largest ARIMA errors around tariff-shock volatility spikes. The team notes metrics are not yet standardized across models, and the primary macro-vs-price-only result is not reported numerically.
summary.question: Can macroeconomic and policy signals (inflation, yields, tariffs, sentiment) improve stock price prediction beyond price history alone?
summary.problem: U.S. policy shifts ripple through markets and retail investors lack tools to anticipate these shocks, especially across sectors with different sensitivity.
summary.beneficiary: Retail investors

summary.results: Test RMSE: ARIMA 3.87, linear regression 95.4, CNN-LSTM 44.47 (MAE 38.78). Linear regression R^2 negative for META (-2.259).

projects.title: Forecasting the EFFR
projects.student_description: This project focuses on forecasting the EFFR using machine learning models and macroeconomic indicators. It aims to provide insights for policymakers, investors, and businesses regarding short-term interest rate predictions.

summary.plain: The team tried to predict the U.S. effective federal funds rate, a key interest rate set through Federal Reserve policy, using economic numbers like inflation, unemployment and GDP growth. They created extra clues from past months and averages and tested several tree-based models. The models followed the general trend well but had trouble with sudden big rate changes.
summary.technical: Monthly EFFR and macroeconomic indicators (CPI, inflation, unemployment rate, GDP growth) from July 1954 to February 2017 (FRED; Kaggle 'Federal Reserve Interest Rates, 1954-Present') were used. Features included 1/3/6-month lags, 3- and 6-month rolling means and rolling standard deviations, and interaction terms (e.g. CPI x inflation). Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost regressors and a linear baseline were evaluated with a time-series split and 5-fold cross-validation, and Random Forest was tuned (depth, number of trees, min samples per leaf). projects.title: Fraud Classification Overview
projects.student_description: Our final project used Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost that was trained off of data from Amazon product descriptions, customer reviews, and ratings to categorize whether an item would be fraudulent or not.

summary.plain: The team tried to spot suspicious or counterfeit product listings on Amazon by looking at review text and ratings. They built several machine learning models that read features like sentiment and keywords in reviews and flag a review as suspicious or not, and found Random Forest worked best.
summary.technical: About 34,000 Amazon product review records (product descriptions, review text, ratings) were cleaned, merged and turned into engineered features such as sentiment score/magnitude, text length, unique-word ratio and an 'authentic' keyword flag; SMOTE was used to balance the rare negative/suspicious class. Naive Bayes was used as a baseline, followed by Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost. Models were compared on suspicious-class recall, precision, F1 and overall ROC AUC (bar charts only); Random Forest was reported as best and more stable than XGBoost, with suspicious-class F1 around 0.9 and ROC AUC near 0.99 read from charts. Feature importances were shown for LR, XGBoost and RF, and a small input form demonstrated predicting 'Suspicious' with a confidence score.

projects.title: Geomagnetic Storm Predictor
projects.student_description: Forecasting 3-hour-ahead geomagnetic storm risk from public space-weather data

summary.plain: Geomagnetic storms happen when activity on the Sun disturbs Earth's magnetic field, and they can disrupt satellites, GPS and power grids. This team combined public space-weather data into 3-hour time windows and trained three models to predict whether a storm will start in the next 3 hours, then built a Streamlit dashboard so people can compare the models and adjust the alarm threshold.
summary.technical: Four public space-weather datasets (solar flare events, DONKI space weather events, OMNI solar wind parameters, space weather indices) were aggregated into 3-hour bins with a future label storm_3h = 1 when Ap >= 56 three hours later, using backward-looking features and train-only preprocessing to avoid leakage. The team first tried a CME-anchored framing, then pivoted; logistic regression and XGBoost improved from ROC-AUC 0.55/0.43 (non-time-binned) to 0.97/0.97 (time-binned). Final models XGBoost (engineered current-bin features), LSTM (48-hour solar-wind + Ap history) and a temporal convolutional network (48-hour solar-wind sequence without current Ap) were trained on 2010-2021 and tested on 2022-2024, where only about 2% of bins were storms. Reported test PR-AUC was 0.575 (XGBoost), 0.610 (LSTM) and 0.602 (TCN), with F1 from 0.485 to 0.580; LSTM had the highest precision, TCN the best F1 and XGBoost the highest recall. Models were served in a Streamlit dashboard with adjustable thresholds and a forecast explorer.
summary.question: Can solar-wind, flare, and CME data predict whether a geomagnetic storm will occur in the next 3 hours?
summary.problem: Strong geomagnetic storms affect satellites, GPS/radio, aviation and power systems; earlier warning improves situational awareness, but storms are rare.
summary.beneficiary: Space-weather forecasters and operators of satellites, communications and power grids (decision support)
summary.inputs: Solar wind, interplanetary magnetic field, flare, CME and Ap-index signals aggregated into 3-hour bins (and 48-hour sequences)
summary.outputs: Probability of a geomagnetic storm (Ap >= 56) in the next 3 hours
summary.results: Test (2022-2024) PR-AUC 0.575-0.610 and F1 0.485-0.580 across XGBoost, LSTM and TCN, versus a ~2% storm base rate; no single best model.

Page 4 explains how the project changed from CME-anchored data to time-binned forecasting. It names a challenge (sparse CMEs, noisy labels) and the fix (rebuilding the data into 3-hour windows). projects.title: Hallucination Detection in RAG Systems
projects.student_description: The project investigates hallucination detection in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems using ML and NLP techniques. By analyzing the relationship between generated answers and their underlying evidence, this project aims to improve the evaluation and reliability of RAG-based AI systems.

summary.plain: AI chatbots that look up documents before answering (RAG systems) sometimes make claims the documents don't support, called hallucinations. This team built a model that compares a claim with its source document and predicts whether the claim is supported or hallucinated, and put it in a Streamlit demo.
summary.technical: The LLM-AggreFact benchmark (document-claim pairs from 11 sources labeled supported/hallucinated) was split on a combined label+source key with the original test split held out. Features were lexical overlap measures (word coverage, bigram overlap, TF-IDF cosine similarity) plus semantic similarity from all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings; collinear and source-confounded features (novel_ratio, jaccard, document length) were removed after controlled comparisons. An L2-regularized logistic regression was compared with a random forest; logistic regression had higher hallucinated-class validation recall (72.03% vs 66.77%) but lower accuracy (64.80% vs 69.35%) and a small train/validation error gap (32.42% vs 32.71%). The final model reports AUC-ROC 0.847 and detects 57% of hallucinated claims. An earlier HaluBench random forest reached 0.814 accuracy but hid 0.573 recall on the hallucinated class.
summary.question: How effectively can NLP and machine learning models classify AI-generated responses as grounded or hallucinated in a RAG system?
summary.problem: Hallucinated claims from RAG systems can influence critical decisions; automatic grounding checks could act as an additional guardrail.
summary.beneficiary: Users and developers of RAG-based AI systems
summary.inputs: Document-claim pairs (source document text and generated claim)
summary.outputs: Probability that the claim is supported (1) or hallucinated (0)
summary.results: Logistic regression AUC-ROC 0.847, 57% of hallucinated claims detected; validation hallucinated recall 72.03% vs 66.77% for random forest.

projects.title: Hard Drive Failure Detection
projects.student_description: Our project is about predicting hard drive failures using SMART metrics which is beneficial for data center engineers so they can project the data before it fails. We compared Logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost and used metrics such as  PR-AUC, Event Recall, Alerts per Day, and Events Caught per 1,000 Alerts to evaluate our models.

summary.plain: Hard drives in data centers sometimes fail without warning, risking lost data. This team used daily health readings from hundreds of thousands of drives to predict whether a drive will fail in the next 7 days, comparing three machine learning models against a simple rule.
summary.technical: Backblaze's Q1 2026 Drive Stats data (30,597,484 daily SMART records from 351,095 drives) was streamed from ZIP archives and processed incrementally into 30-day rolling SMART features with a fail_next_7d label over 53 eligible prediction dates. Healthy examples were downsampled for training only, with balanced class weighting and threshold tuning, and models were evaluated on chronological train/validation/test periods. Logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost were compared with a rule baseline using PR-AUC, event recall, alerts per day and events caught per 1,000 alerts. On test, XGBoost had the best PR-AUC (0.0558, ~270x no-skill lift) and 125 alerts/day with 28.1 events per 1,000 alerts; random forest had the highest model recall (25.4%); the rule baseline caught 76.1% of events but with 10,231 alerts/day. Test PR-AUC dropped 25-48% from validation.
summary.question: Can a hard drive's SMART measurements from the previous 30 days predict whether it will fail within the following seven days, and which measurements give the clearest warning?
summary.problem: Unexpected drive failures interrupt services and put data at risk in data centers.
summary.beneficiary: Data-center engineers and operators
summary.inputs: 30-day rolling SMART health metrics per drive
summary.outputs: Binary prediction: healthy vs will fail in the next 7 days
summary.results: Test PR-AUC 0.0185 (LR), 0.0469 (RF), 0.0558 (XGBoost); event recall 21-25% for models vs 76.1% for the rule baseline at far higher alert volume; model selection inconclusive.

projects.title: Health Facility Resilience to Power Outages in the United States
projects.title_slide: HEALTH FACILITY RESILIENCE TO POWER OUTAGES IN THE UNITED STATES
projects.student_description: This project aims to address the critical challenge of natural disasters disrupting both energy supply and health services. It proposes developing an emergency power allocation model, especially drawing from renewable energy sources, for mobile health units and backup systems in the U.S.

summary.plain: Hospitals and clinics need electricity, especially during storms and disasters. This team built two simple models: one predicts how much electricity will be used from the weather, and another predicts what kind of power fault (like an outage or overload) might happen, and they put both into a Streamlit app.
summary.technical: Two Kaggle datasets were used: Smart Grid Asset Monitoring (voltage, current, power, frequency, energy consumed, load type, fault event) and Weather and Renewable Energy Analysis (temperature, humidity, wind speed, average past consumption, electricity consumed). A random forest classified Fault_Event (UnderVoltage, Overload, Outage, No Fault) with one-hot encoded load type, reporting weighted precision 0.7632, recall 0.8611 and F1 0.8054 (accuracy 86.11%). A linear regression predicted electricity consumption from weather variables (R^2 0.372, RMSE 0.157). A TVAESynthesizer generated synthetic tabular data (overall quality score 0.8746) to fill data gaps. A Streamlit 'Grid Fault and Energy Predictor' takes a facility location and average past consumption.
summary.question: How accurately can we predict the type of fault event U.S. health facilities have during hazardous weather conditions?
summary.problem: Natural disasters disrupt both power and health services, and there is no unified dataset linking U.S. health facilities with energy and infrastructure data.
summary.beneficiary: Emergency managers and healthcare facilities planning backup power
summary.subdomain: Power fault and energy-consumption prediction for health facilities

summary.outputs: Fault event category and predicted electricity consumption
summary.results: Random forest accuracy 86.11%, weighted F1 0.8054, weighted precision 0.7632; linear regression R^2 0.372; synthetic data quality 0.8746.

projects.title: Hospital Readmission Prediction
projects.student_description: We have been developing a machine learning model using MIMIC-IV and MIMIC-IV-ED data to predict ER patient outcomes. Specifically, whether a patient will be safely discharged, require close monitoring, or deteriorate and transition to the ICU.

summary.plain: Hospitals want to know which emergency room patients can safely go home, which will get worse and need intensive care, and which are likely to come back within a month. Using a large research database of real (de-identified) hospital records, this team built separate models for each of these three questions.
summary.technical: MIMIC-IV and MIMIC-IV-ED tables (edstays, triage, vitals, diagnosis, admissions, icustays) were merged and restricted to ICD-10 era stays (2015-2019, 456,035 rows). Features included vitals, acuity, normalized 0-10 pain scores and pain bins, a 0-4 chief-complaint severity mapping, length of stay, Charlson comorbidity index and encoded race/gender/transport. Task 1 (safe discharge = disposition HOME) used a balanced random forest (200 trees, max_depth 10) with a stratified 80/20 split: accuracy 0.72, macro F1 0.72. Task 2 (ICU transfer) used a randomized-search-tuned XGBoost pipeline with SMOTETomek and scale_pos_weight: accuracy 91%, minority-class F1 0.71, ROC-AUC 0.9469. Task 3 (30-day readmission, 15.3% positive) compared tuned logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost with 5-fold CV and an ensemble; test AUC was only 0.57-0.65 despite CV AUC up to 0.84, and a chi-square test showed pain level is associated with readmission.
summary.question: Can we predict whether an ER patient will be safely discharged, deteriorate and transition to the ICU, or require close monitoring post-discharge to prevent readmission?
summary.problem: About 20% of Medicare patients are readmitted within 30 days at an estimated $17 billion annual cost; readmissions indicate gaps in care.
summary.beneficiary: Hospital care teams and discharge planners
summary.subdomain: ER disposition, ICU transfer and 30-day readmission prediction
summary.inputs: ED triage vitals, acuity, pain, chief complaint severity, diagnoses (ICD-10), demographics, transport, length of stay
summary.outputs: Binary predictions: safe discharge, ICU transfer, 30-day readmission
summary.results: Safe discharge RF accuracy 0.72; ICU XGBoost ROC-AUC 0.9469, accuracy 91%; readmission test AUC 0.57-0.65 (CV AUC 0.68-0.84).

projects.title: Improving Market Prediction through N-BEATS Enhanced with Topological Data Analysis
projects.title_slide: Improving Market Prediction through N-BEATS Enhanced with Topological Data Analysis
projects.student_description: This project investigates the impact of integrating features derived from Topological Data Analysis (TDA) with a baseline deep learning architecture, like N-BEATS, to quantitatively determine if topological features provide a measurable improvement in time series forecasting accuracy.

summary.plain: This project tried to predict Microsoft's stock price with a deep learning forecasting model called N-BEATS, and tested whether adding 'shape' features from topological data analysis made the predictions better. The version with topological features had somewhat smaller errors.
summary.technical: Raw stock price data (S&P 500 universe; results shown for MSFT) was z-score normalized, converted into sliding windows (input length 5x the forecast horizon) and split by time into train and validation sets. The team implemented N-BEATS from blocks and stacks with doubly residual stacking, trend (polynomial), seasonality (Fourier) and generic bases. Topological features were computed via persistent homology (point cloud, filtration, persistence diagrams) and incorporated into N-BEATS. On MSFT, baseline N-BEATS reported MAE $17.09, RMSE $21.31, MAPE 5.48%, while TDA + N-BEATS reported MAE $15.77, RMSE $19.72, MAPE 5.1%.
