projects.title: Instruction Complexity Analyzer
projects.student_description: Our project is an AI-powered Instruction Complexity Analyzer that predicts how cognitively demanding a set of instructions will be, helping people with executive-function challenges (like ADHD) plan and start tasks. We’re training a regression model on instructional text and validating it with human-labeled data, broader datasets, and user testing so the score reflects real-world effort.

summary.plain: People with ADHD and other executive-function challenges can feel overwhelmed by long multi-step instructions. This team trained a model on 10,000 wikiHow articles to give any set of instructions a complexity score from 0 to 1, and built a web app where you paste instructions and get the score.
summary.technical: A 10,000-article subset of the Kaggle wikiHow dataset was converted into engineered linguistic and structural features (avg steps per method, sentence/word counts, average word and sentence length, unique words, Flesch reading ease and Flesch-Kincaid grade, number of tips and warnings). A complexity_score target (0-1) was derived from engineered features such as step count and readability. Linear, Lasso and Ridge regression, a tuned random forest and a tuned gradient boosting regressor were compared by RMSE (0.0454, 0.0469, 0.0454, 0.0387, 0.0354 respectively), with gradient boosting selected. Feature importances showed avg_steps_per_method and sentence_count dominate; an actual-vs-predicted plot shows underestimation of high-complexity tasks. A Streamlit-style demo predicts the score for pasted instructions.
summary.question: Can a supervised regression model trained on engineered linguistic and structural features from instructional texts accurately predict a complexity score to help users with executive function challenges assess task difficulty?
summary.problem: Multi-step instructions create high cognitive load and hinder task initiation for people with executive-function challenges.
summary.beneficiary: People with executive-function challenges such as ADHD
summary.inputs: Instructional text (e.g. recipes, DIY guides)
summary.outputs: Predicted complexity score from 0 to 1
summary.results: Tuned gradient boosting regressor RMSE 0.0354 vs 0.0387 random forest and ~0.045 linear models; underestimates highly complex tasks.

projects.title: Investigating Artificial Light at Night (ALAN) and Bird Migration Patterns
projects.title_slide: Investigating Artificial Light at Night (ALAN) and Bird Migration Patterns
projects.student_description: We investigated how exposure to Artificial Light at Night (ALAN) affect the intensity, altitude, speed, and direction of nocturnal bird migration and if weather conditions affected bird migration more.

summary.plain: This project asked whether artificial light at night (light pollution) changes how many birds migrate at night and how high, fast and in what direction they fly. The team combined bird radar estimates, satellite night-light measurements and weather data for New Jersey (urban) and Vermont (rural) and trained tree-based models. They found weather, especially wind speed, mattered more than light pollution.
summary.technical: Nightly BirdCast migration estimates (web-scraped) were combined with gap-filled VIIRS night-time light data and Open-Meteo weather data for New Jersey and Vermont. Skewed features were log- or Yeo-Johnson-transformed, and engineered features included a weather-condition category, ALAN x cloud-cover and ALAN x lunar-irradiance interactions, and a binary 'disoriented' target (1 on low-activity nights). Random forest and XGBoost regressors predicted peak birds, total passed, peak speed and peak altitude (R2 mostly 0.06-0.42), while peak-direction classification reached 0.53-0.67 accuracy. For the disorientation target, a stacking ensemble, XGBoost and random forest reached 0.82/0.81/0.84 accuracy and 0.85/0.83/0.83 AUC-ROC, with the team noting the models favour the majority 'Normal' class. A two-proportion z-test found no significant difference in disorientation rate between NJ and VT (p about 0.85), and SHAP analysis showed weather features (wind speed at 10 m) and lunar irradiance outranked ALAN.
summary.question: How does exposure to Artificial Light at Night (ALAN) affect the intensity, altitude, speed, and direction of nocturnal bird migration?
summary.problem: Artificial light at night is a fast-growing pollutant that may disorient nocturnally migrating birds; the project tests how strongly it relates to migration behaviour compared with weather.
summary.beneficiary: Conservation researchers and city lights-out programs
summary.subdomain: Light pollution and nocturnal bird migration
summary.inputs: Nightly radar-based migration estimates, satellite night-time light radiance, lunar irradiance and weather variables for two states
summary.outputs: Predicted migration intensity/altitude/speed, peak direction class, and a disoriented/normal night classification; feature importances
summary.results: Regression R2 roughly 0.06-0.42 (RF/XGB); peak-direction accuracy 0.53-0.67; disorientation classifier accuracy 0.81-0.84 and AUC 0.83-0.85; weather (wind speed) most predictive per SHAP; no significant NJ vs VT disorientation difference (p about 0.85).

projects.title: IoT Network Intrusion Detection
projects.student_description: Use supervised machine learning models classify IoT network traffic as benign or malicious - and further identify the specific type of attack using the TON_IoT Network Dataset.

summary.plain: This project trained computer models to spot cyberattacks in the network traffic of smart home and industrial 'Internet of Things' devices. Using a public simulated dataset, a random forest model could tell normal traffic from attacks about 99% of the time and name the exact attack type about 98% of the time. A separate text model linked vulnerability descriptions to attack families.
summary.technical: The TON_IoT network dataset (211,043 flows) was cleaned by removing targets, identifiers and conflicting records, then split 80/20 with stratification. Binary logistic regression on numeric features reached 85.19% accuracy (F1 90.52%), rising to 92% with categorical features such as conn_state; a binary random forest reached 99.02% accuracy (F1 99.37%), and a 10-class random forest reached 97.73% accuracy (macro F1 94.66%), with attack types further mapped to CWE-style families (97.76% accuracy, macro F1 92.28%). A separate NLP component used TF-IDF features of CVE/CWE text with logistic regression to classify attack families, serving as a baseline for a fine-tuned BERT model that reached only ~0.70 accuracy after ~5 hours of training. XGBoost gave ~0.94 accuracy with no gain over random forest. The weakest class was man-in-the-middle (F1 0.67, 261 samples).
summary.question: How accurately can supervised machine learning models classify IoT network traffic as benign or malicious, identify the specific attack type using the TON_IoT Network Dataset, and which features contribute most?
summary.problem: IoT devices have limited built-in security and are vulnerable to attacks; automatic traffic classification can provide early warning.
summary.beneficiary: Network security teams protecting IoT/IIoT networks
summary.inputs: Network-flow and protocol features (bytes, connection state, etc.); CVE/CWE vulnerability text for the NLP component
summary.outputs: Benign/malicious label, one of 10 traffic/attack types with confidence, mapped attack family
summary.results: Binary LR 85.19% (numeric) / 92% (with categorical); binary RF 99.02% (F1 99.37%); multiclass RF 97.73% (macro F1 94.66%); XGBoost ~0.94; fine-tuned BERT ~0.70; mitm class F1 0.67.

projects.title: Layoff Prediction Using Financial Sentiment Analysis
projects.title_slide: Layoff Prediction Using Financial Sentiment Analysis
projects.student_description: An analysis by predicting the likelihood or timing of layoffs in a company or sector by analyzing financial sentiment signals and historical layoff data

summary.plain: This project tried to predict whether U.S. tech companies would have layoffs in the next quarter after ChatGPT's release. The team combined a public layoffs tracker with a dataset about companies adopting generative AI tools, turned employee reviews into a positive/negative mood score, and trained a small neural network. The model caught most layoff quarters (88%) but also raised some false alarms.
summary.technical: Layoffs.fyi tech-layoff records (from Nov 30, 2022) were merged with a Kaggle Enterprise GenAI Adoption & Workforce Impact dataset and aggregated quarterly. Five features were built: a GenAI-adoption flag, a 4-quarter rolling sum of layoffs, TextBlob polarity of employee reviews (0 when missing or pre-adoption), and sine/cosine quarter encodings; sparse or misaligned columns were excluded with stated reasons. A Keras feed-forward binary classifier (Dense 128-64-32 with ReLU, BatchNorm, dropout, L2 1e-4, sigmoid output, Adam LR 1e-4 with learning-rate reduction) predicted layoffs in the next quarter. On 1,463 evaluation samples it reported 0.82 accuracy, Layoff precision 0.69 / recall 0.88 / F1 0.78, macro F1 0.81, and validation AUC around 0.89 in the training curves. The team prioritised recall over false positives.

projects.title: London Energy Predictor
projects.student_description: Machine learning project that predicts electricity consumption during heatwaves using London weather and energy data. Achieves up to 86% accuracy with Random Forest regression, supporting better planning for extreme weather events.

summary.plain: This project looked at how hot weather and heatwaves change electricity use in London. The team gathered weather and electricity datasets for the UK and London, flagged heatwaves with a simple rule, and trained regression models (linear regression, decision tree and random forest) to predict electricity consumption from temperature, humidity and sunshine.
summary.technical: Four candidate datasets were compared: UK Met Office weather and National Grid ESO electricity (2009-2024; 4,745 entries after preprocessing) and London weather (European Climate Assessment & Dataset) with UK Power Networks smart-meter consumption for 5,576 households (2011-2014; 829 entries). Data were cleaned and imputed, and a rule flagged heatwaves as 3+ consecutive days with max temperature >= 28 C. Linear regression (baseline), decision tree and random forest regressors were trained; on the UK data R2 was 0.25-0.43 and on the London data R2 was 0.74-0.77 (London RMSE ~0.93-0.98). After adding five features (TX, TN, TG, humidity, sunshine) the team reports a final model with R2 0.989 (RMSE 2148.76, MAE 1360.51). Residual and prediction-vs-temperature plots were examined.
summary.question: How do temperature and heat waves impact electricity consumption in London?
summary.problem: Rising heatwaves put pressure on energy grids; accurate demand forecasting helps prevent blackouts and supports utility planning.
summary.beneficiary: Energy utilities and grid operators
summary.inputs: Daily max/min/mean temperature, humidity, sunshine and a heatwave flag
summary.outputs: Predicted electricity consumption (kWh)
summary.results: UK data R2 0.25-0.43; London data R2 0.74-0.77; final five-feature model reported R2 0.989, RMSE 2148.76, MAE 1360.51. Workbook description claims up to 86% accuracy with random forest.

projects.title: Lung Cancer Risk Prediction- Leveraging Machine Learning to identify high-risk individuals beyond traditional screening criteria.
projects.student_description: We work to create a model to identify who benefits from Low-Dose CT screening before cancer develops.

summary.plain: This project tried to predict which people are at high risk of lung cancer so doctors could recommend CT screening to people current guidelines miss. The team used a large public Kaggle dataset about smoking, family history and environmental exposures, focusing on U.S. records, and trained logistic regression and random forest models. Logistic regression caught about 69% of cancer cases, while the random forest missed most of them.
summary.technical: The U.S. subset of the Kaggle 'Lung Cancer Risk in 25 Countries' dataset (220,000 anonymized records overall) with demographics, smoking history, environmental exposures and medical history was used to predict a binary lung-cancer diagnosis. Planned/described preprocessing includes pack-year calculation, one-hot encoding, smoking x pollution interaction terms, standardization, SMOTE and train/validation/test splits with 5-fold CV and grid/random search. Logistic regression (baseline) and random forest were trained; normalized confusion matrices show logistic regression with 0.69 true-positive rate and 0.61 true-negative rate, and random forest with 0.91 true-negative but only 0.12 true-positive rate. A 1.2% risk threshold for a screening recommendation and a Streamlit clinical dashboard are proposed.
summary.question: Can a machine learning model incorporating demographic information, smoking history, family history, and environmental exposures predict 5-year lung cancer risk with superior discrimination and clinical utility compared to USPSTF 2021 screening criteria?
summary.problem: Lung cancer screening is underused and USPSTF criteria rely on simple age and pack-year cutoffs that miss at-risk people.
summary.beneficiary: Primary care clinicians and patients eligible for low-dose CT screening
summary.inputs: Age, sex, smoking status/years/intensity, pack-years, passive smoke, family history, air pollution, occupational exposure, prior lung disease
summary.outputs: Lung cancer risk probability and binary screening recommendation
summary.results: Normalized confusion matrices: logistic regression TPR 0.69, TNR 0.61; random forest TPR 0.12, TNR 0.91. No accuracy/AUC figures reported.

projects.title: Malaria Cell Detection
projects.student_description: This project explores how CNN's can distinguish between infected/uninfected blood smears. We further tested our custom CNN by augmenting the data as a way of testing our model on real world situations.

summary.plain: This project trained a computer vision model to tell whether a blood cell image is infected with malaria. The team then tested how well it still worked when the images were changed to mimic real-world problems such as different brightness, blur, low resolution or covered patches. Accuracy stayed around 93-96% across these changes.
summary.technical: The Kaggle cell-images-for-detecting-malaria dataset (27,558 thin-smear cell images from the NIH, classes Parasitized and Uninfected) was split 80/20. A custom convolutional neural network was built and trained in PyTorch. Robustness was tested by applying image augmentations (brightness shift, Gaussian blur, rotation, affine shift, perspective, cutout, low resolution and a combination) and measuring accuracy under each condition. Reported accuracy was 95.50% with no augmentation, 93.45% with brightness, 95.56% blur, 95.59% rotation, 94.92% affine, 95.36% perspective, 93.81% combo, 94.05% cutout and 94.27% low resolution.
summary.question: How effectively can AI models generalize malaria detection across diverse image conditions (e.g., lighting, staining, resolution)?
summary.problem: Microscopy-based malaria diagnosis is slow and needs trained staff; automated models must remain reliable under variable image quality in under-resourced clinics.
summary.beneficiary: Clinics in under-resourced malaria-endemic regions
summary.inputs: Thin blood smear single-cell images
summary.outputs: Parasitized or Uninfected label
summary.results: 95.50% accuracy without augmentation; 93.45-95.59% across augmentation test conditions (lowest: brightness 93.45%, combo 93.81%).

projects.title: Malicious Network Traffic Detection Model
projects.student_description: Use metadata from network packets to detect whether a packet is malicious or normal.

summary.plain: This project built models that flag network connections as normal or malicious using only summary information about the traffic (like bytes and packet timing), not the private contents. Using a public benchmark dataset, the best models were right about 92% of the time, and the team built a small web app to try example connections.
summary.technical: The UNSW-NB15 dataset (~2.5 million records, 49 flow-level features, normal vs attack with nine attack categories) was cleaned, feature-selected and split 70/30. Random forest, XGBoost, an MLP neural network, a decision tree and logistic regression were trained and compared on accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and ROC-AUC. The headline model reports ~92% accuracy, ~90% precision, ~91% recall and AUC ~0.98; ROC-AUC was 0.9869 (XGBoost), 0.9864 (RF), 0.9800 (MLP), 0.9782 (decision tree) and 0.9290 (logistic regression). Feature importances highlighted sttl, smean, sbytes, sload, rate and dbytes. A Streamlit web app lets users load benign or attack examples and see per-model predictions and probabilities.
summary.question: Can machine-learning models detect malicious network activity using only flow-level metadata?
summary.problem: Encrypted traffic makes signature-based firewalls ineffective, and attacks can hide in normal-looking flows.
summary.beneficiary: Network defenders and security researchers

projects.title: Malware Detection & Classification
projects.student_description: Our project trained a model on LightGBM to detect and classify malware samples.

summary.plain: This project trained a model to decide whether a Windows program file is malware or safe, using features such as which system libraries it imports, its text strings and how random (entropy) its contents are. Working with a 20% sample of the EMBER2024 dataset, the model was right about 88% of the time and caught about 84% of the malware. Results were shown in a Streamlit app.
summary.technical: A deterministic 20% sample of Win32 files from EMBER2024 was used. Three raw JSON columns (imports, strings, general) were flattened by custom extraction functions into numeric features: number of DLLs/functions, average functions per DLL, flags for six common system DLLs, string count/average length/printable characters/entropy, file size, file entropy and an is-PE flag. A LightGBM classifier (n_estimators=100, learning_rate=0.1) predicted malicious vs benign. On 359,994 test samples it reported 87.92% accuracy, ROC-AUC 0.957 and 83.8% malware recall (150,870 of 180,000 detected; 14,356 false positives, 29,130 false negatives), with feature importances plotted. A behaviour-identification model for malicious files reached only 56% accuracy, and the challenge set was not yet evaluated.
summary.question: Using a portion of the EMBER2024 dataset, can we classify whether a file is malicious or benign, determine malicious behaviour, and generalize to emerging malware that evaded commercial antivirus?
summary.problem: Signature-based antivirus cannot keep up with thousands of new malware variants daily; ML can generalize from known malware.
summary.beneficiary: Security analysts triaging suspicious files
summary.subdomain: Static malware detection for Windows PE files
summary.inputs: Engineered static features from file imports, strings and general metadata
summary.outputs: Malicious vs benign label (and, experimentally, behaviour tags)
summary.results: Accuracy 87.92%, ROC-AUC 0.957, recall 83.8%; 14,356 FP and 29,130 FN; behaviour identification ~56% accuracy.

projects.student_description: Detecting AI generated vs human generated text in news article.

summary.plain: The team wanted to tell whether a news article was written by a person or by AI, and also whether it showed political bias. They trained a model that guessed human vs. AI writing correctly about 83% of the time; the bias detector was not finished in time to test.
summary.technical: Using a Kaggle human-vs-LLM text corpus, the team trained text classifiers (likely on TF-IDF/token features) to separate human-written from AI-generated text. Logistic Regression achieved 83% accuracy with precision/recall/F1 around 0.82-0.84 for both classes and ROC AUC 0.92, while Random Forest and Naive Bayes reportedly scored below 50% accuracy. A second model to detect political bias using a Kaggle media-bias dataset was planned/built by a teammate but could not be tested or visualised. Slides also discuss sources of bias and responsible-use guidelines.

projects.title_slide: Mind and Melody: Predicting Student Burnout
projects.student_description:
Academic burnout is especially prevalent in higher education institutions. 

Since Covid-19, burnout among college students has increased from 30% to 60%

The “silent help-keeping” phenomenon explains why students don’t seek help.

Research question: How accurately can machine learning predict burnout risk among college students and how can personalized music recommendations be used to support student well-being?

summary.plain: This project built a free web app that estimates whether a college student is at low, medium or high risk of burnout from a short check-in. It then suggests music and next steps based on a survey about how music relates to mental health.
summary.technical: A 1M-record student mental health and burnout dataset (target: low/medium/high risk) was cleaned, misleading variables removed, categories encoded, and stratified sampling and a train-test split applied before training a Random Forest in a preprocessing pipeline. The model reached 80.4% accuracy, 75.5% macro F1 and 79.5% high-risk recall; feature importance showed stress, anxiety, depression and sleep as top predictors. A second dataset, a 736-response music and mental health survey, was used to build genre/listening recommendations. The saved model was integrated into a Streamlit app with confidence scores, disclaimers and an optional Spotify player.

projects.title_slide: Mobile Payment Fraud Detection Using Machine Learning
projects.student_description: A machine learning project for detecting fraudulent mobile payments using the PaySim dataset, comparing Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost with reproducible evaluation and an interactive Streamlit demo.

summary.plain: The team built models to catch fraudulent mobile-money transactions in a large simulated dataset. Because fraud is very rare, they focused on catching fraud without raising too many false alarms, and their Random Forest caught all 19 fraud cases in the test set, which they caution may not hold up in the real world.
summary.technical: From the 6.3M-row PaySim simulated mobile-money dataset, a 100,000-row stratified development sample was drawn. Leakage-safe features were engineered (log amount, origin/destination balance errors, account-emptied flag, hour-of-day and day from the step field), avoiding account identifiers and frequency features. Data were split into stratified train/validation/test sets; decision thresholds were tuned on validation only and the 15,000-transaction test set (19 fraud cases) used once. Compared to the original PaySim rule (0/19 detected), Logistic Regression achieved precision 0.917, recall 0.579, F1 0.710, and Random Forest (threshold 0.30) achieved precision, recall and F1 of 1.000 with 0 false positives. XGBoost was excluded because its notebook did not run reproducibly.
summary.question: Which supervised model best detects PaySim fraud while maintaining high recall and minimizing false positives?
summary.problem: Fraudulent mobile-money transactions are rare and hard to detect without blocking legitimate users.

summary.results: Random Forest: precision/recall/F1 1.000 (19/19 fraud, 0 false positives); Logistic Regression: precision 0.917, recall 0.579, F1 0.710; PaySim rule detected 0/19.

projects.title: Multi-Factor Predictive Model for Stock Price Direction
projects.title_slide: Multi-Factor Predictive Model for Stock Price Direction
projects.student_description: By using news sentiment, earnings data and stock price data, our model predicts stock price movements based on market sentiment, providing users with data-driven insights for portfolio optimization.

summary.plain: The team tried to predict where stock prices are heading using past prices plus the mood of news articles and company earnings calls. They first trained a deep learning model to predict next-day prices, then built a classifier that says whether a stock will go down, stay flat or go up.
summary.technical: Daily stock closing prices, news articles with sentiment variables, and quarterly earnings-call transcripts were collected through Alpha Vantage and Polygon.io APIs, compiled into CSVs and aligned by date. A FinBERT model extracted sentiment scores (-1 to 1) from text. A PyTorch Transformer was trained on past prices to predict next-day closing prices (1D output for MSFT, 5D output for five stocks), with training loss falling from about 0.247 to 0.0085 over 30 epochs and actual-vs-predicted plots shown. A Random Forest classifier then predicted stock movement (-1, 0, 1) from sentiment and price-difference features, reporting an average weighted F1 of 0.6963 across folds with a 3-class confusion matrix.

projects.title: Music and Mental Health
projects.student_description: A machine learning approach to predicting the effects of music genres on mental health conditions.

summary.plain: Using a public survey about music listening and mental health, the team trained a model to guess whether a person's favorite music genre improves, worsens or has no effect on their mental health. They found genre is only a weak predictor and noted the survey mostly reflects young, self-selected people.
summary.technical: The MxMH survey from Kaggle (music genres, listening habits, self-reported anxiety, depression, insomnia, OCD and music effect) was encoded with ordinal vs one-hot encoding and used to train a Random Forest classifier predicting music effect (Improve / No Effect / Worsen). n_estimators was tuned over [10, 50, 100, 500], with 100 best. Performance was measured as mean absolute error on label-encoded classes: ordinal encoding validation MAE 0.306 vs one-hot 0.319, and final test MAE 0.236.

summary.problem: Understanding genre-specific effects could support personalized music therapy for people lacking access to traditional treatment.
summary.beneficiary: People using music for mental wellness; music therapy researchers
summary.inputs: Survey answers on genres, listening habits and self-reported mental health
summary.outputs: Music effect: Improve / No Effect / Worsen
summary.results: Test MAE 0.236 (label-encoded classes); ordinal encoding slightly better than one-hot (0.306 vs 0.319 validation).

projects.title: Music Popularity on Spotify
projects.student_description: We trained an SVM classifier model to understand the relationship between musical attributes and the popularity of a song on Spotify.

summary.plain: The team asked whether a song's danceability, energy and acousticness can predict how popular it is on Spotify. They sorted songs into low, medium and high popularity groups and trained a model, which was right only 38% of the time.

projects.title: Navigating Vocational Student Well-being
projects.student_description: We created a model that can predict the mental status of vocational students.  We trained three supervised models, attempted to fix some bias in the data set, and chose the best performing model.

summary.plain: The team tried to predict whether vocational college students are healthy, at risk or struggling with their mental health, using things like sleep, steps, GPA and emotions found in the students' daily written reflections. Their best model was right 68% of the time but mostly just identified struggling students because there were very few healthy or at-risk examples.
summary.technical: A cleaned Kaggle dataset of vocational students (ages 17-24) with demographic, academic, behavioral features and daily reflection text was used. NRCLex extracted emotion counts from reflections, converted to proportions and appended as features; numeric features were standardized and categoricals label-encoded. After inspecting feature importances, depression, anxiety and stress scores were dropped as likely target proxies, along with IDs and raw text. XGBoost, Logistic Regression and Random Forest were tuned with nested cross-validation and evaluated on an 80-20 split: XGBoost 61% accuracy (F1 0.33), Logistic Regression 67% (F1 0.27), Random Forest 68% (F1 0.33, recall 1.00 for 'Struggling'). All models failed on the minority 'Healthy' (22) and 'At Risk' (137) classes versus 341 'Struggling'.
summary.question: Can we predict vocational students' mental health status based on demographic, academic, behavioral, and self-reported textual data?
summary.problem: Vocational students are overlooked in mental health research and institutions lack capacity for individual screening.
summary.beneficiary: Vocational college students and their institutions
summary.inputs: Age, gender, GPA, sleep hours, steps per day, NRC emotion proportions from daily reflections
summary.outputs: Mental health status: Healthy / At risk / Struggling
summary.results: Random Forest best: 68% accuracy, macro F1 0.33, perfect recall for 'Struggling' but 0 recall for Healthy and At Risk.

projects.title: Oil Spill Detection
projects.student_description: This project uses machine learning techniques to detect and monitor oil spills in marine environments, enabling faster response to environmental hazards.

summary.plain: The team trained a computer vision model to look at photos of water and say whether there is an oil spill. Starting from a model already trained on millions of images, they improved accuracy from about 50% to about 87% and built a demo where you upload a photo and get a prediction.
summary.technical: A Kaggle marine oil spill image dataset (300 images: 150 oil spill, 150 no oil spill) was augmented with simple rotations and magnifications. An ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 was used via transfer learning with early layers frozen and later layers fine-tuned, ImageNet normalization and early stopping on validation accuracy; ResNet-50 was tried earlier but replaced for speed. Before transfer learning the model predicted every image as oil spill (~50% accuracy, oil-spill precision 0.489, recall 1.000); after fine-tuning it reached ~86.7% accuracy. An upload interface displays the prediction with a confidence score.

projects.title: OptiFund AI Presentation
projects.student_description: This allows individuals to understand different ways that Machine Learning can be utilized to perform optimization of investment portfolios for users as well as the pros and cons that are associated with it

summary.plain: OptiFund is a web app that suggests how to split money across stocks based on how much risk you are comfortable with and how much you care about environmental and social values. It uses a classic finance formula to find good mixes of stocks and a machine learning model that learns to copy those mixes quickly.
summary.technical: Five years of daily stock data (open/high/low/close/volume/dividends per company) were converted into return matrices. Modern Portfolio Theory (mean-variance optimization using expected returns, covariance matrix and a 0-2 risk-aversion level) produced optimal weights; a Random Forest Regressor was then trained on 30-day return windows plus risk level to predict MPT-like weights for top stocks for faster real-time use. A user ESG preference filters companies. Evaluation shows histograms of total return, Sharpe ratio and maximum drawdown for about ten backtested portfolios (mean total return ~0.07, Sharpe ~9.7 read from charts). A web interface lets users set risk tolerance and ESG preference and view allocations.

projects.title: Optimized Music Listening Design
projects.student_description: In order to investigate the issue of bias in music apps, I created a Python-fueled machine-learning algorithm that takes in a dataset of songs, sorts them based on user input, and outputs the songs that best fit the user's choice.

summary.plain: This project builds a simple Python program that recommends songs from a Spotify top-songs dataset based on the kind of music the user asks for, like 'high danceability' or 'low energy'. Because it filters on song features rather than popularity, the team argues it can reduce bias toward famous artists.
summary.technical: Data come from two Kaggle Spotify datasets (Most Streamed Songs; Top 50 Spotify Songs 2019) with audio features such as danceability, valence, energy and acousticness. The core recommender is a rule-based filter: for each user-chosen category it keeps songs above or below the dataset mean of that feature and prints matching artist/track names. The slides also describe a 'clustering model technique' and show scatter plots of songs coloured into three segments by danceability/acousticness and danceability/energy, but the clustering algorithm and how it feeds recommendations are not stated. No quantitative evaluation is reported; the team discusses sources of bias in the data qualitatively.

projects.title: PatentLens
projects.student_description: In this project, we evaluate four different models to see how they perform to retrieve similar text.

summary.plain: PatentLens is a search tool that helps inventors find existing patents similar to their idea. The team compared four ways of measuring text similarity on 100,000 neural-network patents and found a small transformer model (MiniLM) and the classic BM25 search method worked best.
summary.technical: About 100,000 US patents in CPC class G06N3 (neural networks) were pulled from Google Patents BigQuery, using metadata and abstracts. Four retrieval approaches were compared: TF-IDF with cosine similarity (baseline), BM25, Latent Semantic Analysis, and MiniLM sentence-transformer embeddings. Evaluation used recall@k, AUC for citation-pair detection, precision-recall curves, confusion matrices, retrieval time, and paired bootstrap significance tests against MiniLM. MiniLM had the highest recall (10.3%) and 0.70 AUC on low-overlap citation pairs vs 0.52 for BM25; it was significantly better than TF-IDF (p < 0.001) and LSA (p = 0.023) but not BM25 (p = 0.21). BM25 was fastest (26 ms) with MiniLM at 29 ms. An interactive interface lets users type an idea, choose a model and number of results, and see ranked patents with similarity strength.

projects.title: Pawspect
projects.student_description: An AI-powered cat and dog breed identification app that provides standard breed health information, completely free with a saved history to revisit results.

summary.plain: Pawspect is a free app where you upload a photo of a cat or dog and it guesses the breed, then shows common health problems and screenings for that breed. It also estimates whether the pet is purebred or mixed, and reminds users it is not veterinary advice.
summary.technical: Images from the Stanford Dogs, Oxford-IIIT Pet, Mixed Breed Dog and FeliBreed cat datasets were merged, breed names normalized, duplicates/invalid images removed, breeds capped for balance, and split into train/validation/test. Separate EfficientNetV2-S CNNs were trained with transfer learning and a fine-tuning phase for 14 cat breeds and 120 dog breeds. A scikit-learn logistic regression on the CNN's confidence scores classifies purebred vs mixed breed. The cat model reports 78.71% top-1 / 95.96% top-3 accuracy and the dog model 87.53% top-1 / 97.40% top-3; the purebred/mixed classifiers report 99%+ accuracy with confusion matrices and classification reports. projects.title: Phishing Email Classification: Final Presentation
projects.student_description: Our model uses Naive Bayes algorithm to successfully classify emails as phishing or legitimate. We deployed the app using Streamlit. We hope to reduce cybercrime.

summary.plain: This project built a web app that reads the text of an email and predicts whether it is a phishing scam or a legitimate message. The team tried a few models and chose Naive Bayes because it is simple and fast, reaching about 96% accuracy.
summary.technical: Several public phishing corpora (Ling, CEAS-08, Nazario, and a Zenodo phishing validation set, via a Kaggle phishing email dataset) were combined and balanced between phishing and legitimate classes. Email bodies were cleaned (junk characters, HTML, extra spaces removed), long bodies trimmed, and sender and body combined into one field. Naive Bayes, Linear SVC and Logistic Regression were tested; Naive Bayes was chosen for simplicity and speed. Classification reports show about 0.96 accuracy with precision/recall/F1 around 0.93-0.99 per class on test sets of 4,490 and 7,831 emails, with confusion matrices. The model is deployed in a Streamlit app that labels pasted email text as phishing or legitimate.

projects.title: Phishing Email Prediction Models
projects.student_description: My project analyzes the porformance of three models: Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, and BERT to learn which is the most effective at detecting phishing emails.

summary.plain: This project compares three machine learning models for spotting phishing emails using a large public collection of about 108,000 labeled emails. Logistic regression did best (about 99% accuracy), and the team built a Streamlit app where you can pick a model and test an email.
summary.technical: The MeAJOR Email Corpus from Hugging Face (108,685 emails merged from TREC 2005-2007, Nazario, Nigerian Fraud and other corpora; ~60K legitimate vs ~48K phishing) was condensed to key features: email text, lengths, punctuation percentage, typo count, sender domain length, URL count, attachments and content type. Text was represented with TF-IDF. Logistic Regression, Multinomial Naive Bayes and DistilBERT were trained and compared on accuracy, precision, recall and F1. Logistic Regression reported 99.28% accuracy / 99.38% F1, DistilBERT 98% accuracy / 99% F1, and Multinomial NB 96.03% accuracy / 95.38% F1. A Streamlit dashboard lets users select a model, view extracted features and classify an email.
summary.question: Which machine learning model provides the best balance of accuracy, precision, and recall for phishing email detection?
summary.problem: Phishing is one of the most common cybersecurity threats and attacks are becoming harder to recognize.
summary.beneficiary: Email users and organizations' email security teams
summary.inputs: Email subject, body, sender information, URLs, attachments and engineered text features
summary.outputs: Phishing vs legitimate label
summary.results: Logistic Regression 99.28% accuracy (P 99.44%, R 99.31%, F1 99.38%); DistilBERT 98% accuracy (P/R/F1 99%); Multinomial NB 96.03% accuracy (P 98.11%, R 92.80%, F1 95.38%).

projects.title: PhishyMail AI
projects.student_description: PhishyMail AI is a machine learning–powered system for detecting phishing emails. It analyzes the content and metadata of incoming emails using natural language processing.

summary.plain: PhishyMail AI is a tool that checks whether an email is a phishing scam. The team trained three different machine learning models on a public email dataset and built an app where users choose which model to use, since each has strengths and weaknesses.
summary.technical: From a curated collection of seven phishing email datasets (203,176 emails), the team used only TREC-05 (53,954 emails, 41.6% phishing) due to compute limits. Sender, subject, body and URL fields were encoded with a TF-IDF vectorizer, and Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost were trained using 80/20 or 60/20/20 splits. Reported accuracies are about 0.974 for the 'LexiGuard' model, 0.98 for Random Forest and 0.9663 for the 'PhishBoost' (XGBoost) model, with per-class precision/recall/F1 of 0.95-0.98, plus an XGBoost confusion matrix and ROC curve (AUC = 1.00). A locally run app lets the user select a model and enter sender, subject and body to classify an email.

projects.student_description: Online poker is growing fast, but many training tools only show charts and expect players to memorize answers. We wanted to build something more helpful: a tool that explains poker decisions and also watches for early signs of risky gambling behavior.

summary.plain: This project builds a poker practice app that gives feedback on your choices, and studies betting data to spot signs of risky gambling such as 'chasing losses'. The team found players raised their bets more often after losing, and trained a model that sorts players into low, moderate or high risk using a home-made rule-based label.
summary.technical: Using the Kaggle Bustabit gambling dataset, a chi-square test showed bets increased after 40.17% of losses vs 35.47% of wins (chi-square 105.63, p = 8.88e-25). Per-player features (4,149 players) were built, and a proxy risk tier was constructed from three warning signs (loss-chase rate >50%, top-25% bet swings, top-25% days played). A classifier trained only on average bet, max bet, win rate and total profit (label features banned), with SMOTE applied after the split and inside each CV fold, reached 78% accuracy on 830 held-out players and 0.776 +/- 0.017 in 5-fold CV; High-tier precision was only 0.22 (recall 0.81), with all errors off by one tier. A poker coach prototype (Streamlit frontend, FastAPI backend, SQLite scenarios grounded in the PHH hand-history dataset) deals scenarios and compares the user's action to GTO-style action frequencies.

projects.student_description: We achieved 98% accuracy in predicting unsafe drug combinations by utilizing a stacking ensemble model with Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and CatBoost on the 2014-2024 U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) dataset, all while demonstrating the model in a Gradio web application for more convenient usage.

summary.plain: This project trains a model to predict whether a combination of drugs is likely to cause harmful side effects, and puts it in a simple web app where you pick drug names and get a prediction with a confidence score. It uses a large FDA-derived dataset of drug interactions.
summary.technical: The High-Order Drug-Drug Interaction (HODDI) dataset, built from FDA Adverse Event Reporting System records 2014Q3-2024Q3 (100k+ records, ~2k drugs), provides drug combinations labeled as causing adverse effects or not, balanced between classes. Inputs are DrugBank IDs only. A stacking ensemble with Logistic Regression, Random Forest and CatBoost base learners and a logistic regression meta-model was trained with 5-fold cross-validation, after simple random and stratified sampling attempts. Reported results are training accuracy 0.9610, test accuracy 0.9598 and test ROC AUC 0.9937, with train/test gaps of 0.0012 across metrics. A Gradio web app lets users select drugs and returns a prediction and confidence score.

projects.title: Predicting Company Financial Performance
projects.student_description: This project implements 14-day ahead forecasting for tech stocks using SARIMAX models with truly exogenous variables.

summary.plain: This project tries to forecast an index of 24 AI and tech company stocks using a classic statistical time-series model (SARIMAX) plus outside economic signals like market volatility and interest rates. It worked well for predicting the next day but failed for long-range forecasts because the AI boom changed how the market behaved.
summary.technical: Daily prices (2019-2025, weekends removed) for 24 AI/tech stocks were combined into an equal-weighted AI Tech Index, with 60+ candidate exogenous variables (VIX/VVIX, Treasury yields, sector ETFs, currencies, commodities, SEC sector fundamentals). Exogenous variables were screened for economic relevance, leakage (excluding series built from the same companies), collinearity (correlation heatmaps, VIF) and the target was tested for stationarity with ADF and first-differenced. SARIMAX(1,1,1) and SARIMAX(2,1,2) were fit on a 90/10 time-ordered split. Long-horizon forecasting gave R^2 = -1.95 due to a 2025 regime shift, while rolling 1-step-ahead forecasting gave R^2 = 0.9726, which the team notes is inflated by autocorrelation and comparable to a naive persistence model.
summary.question: How reliable is SARIMAX for forecasting the AI Tech sector index based on historical performance and exogenous macro-financial indicators?

projects.title: Predicting County-Level PMOS Underdiagnosis Risk in the US
projects.title_slide: Predicting County-Level PMOS Underdiagnosis Risk in the US
projects.student_description: We developed a county-level machine learning model to predict PMOS underdiagnosis risk across the United States using social vulnerability, healthcare access, and rurality data from three public datasets. We engineered a composite underdiagnosis-risk target and compared Random Forest, Logistic Regression, and XGBoost models, with XGBoost achieving the best overall performance (80% F1 score).

summary.plain: PMOS (formerly PCOS) is a common hormonal condition that often goes undiagnosed. Because there is no public data on who is undiagnosed, this team built a rule-based risk label from public CDC county data on social vulnerability, rurality and preventive care, then trained models to predict which US counties are most at risk and shared the results in a web app with a county map.
summary.technical: County-level data from CDC/ATSDR SVI 2022, CDC PLACES 2025 and the 2023 NCHS urban-rural classification were merged (25 literature-based features; missingness analysed, e.g. 187 counties missing PLACES measures). A binary composite target was engineered: high SVI (RPL_THEMES >= 75th percentile) AND (low preventive care engagement via CHECKUP/MAMMOUSE <= 25th percentile OR rural NCHS code >= 4); the label-defining variables were excluded from features. With an 80/20 split (2,515 train / 629 test), a regularized Random Forest (100 trees, also used to select the top 10 features), a Logistic Regression baseline on those features and an XGBoost benchmark were compared. Reported results: RF precision 81% / recall 72% / F1 76% / accuracy 90%; LR 65% / 86% / 74% / 87%; XGBoost 79% / 81% / 80% / 91%. A fairness audit compared false-negative rates across minority, Black population and poverty groups, and a deployed web app shows a county lookup and risk map.
summary.question: Which county-level social vulnerability and healthcare access factors best predict PMOS underdiagnosis risk across the United States, and which counties are most at risk?
summary.problem: Up to 70% of women with PMOS go undiagnosed, driven by healthcare access, socioeconomic and geographic barriers.
summary.beneficiary: Public health researchers and planners targeting outreach for women's health
summary.inputs: County-level social vulnerability, health measures and rurality features
summary.outputs: Binary county underdiagnosis-risk prediction and ranked risk map
summary.results: XGBoost best: 91% accuracy, 80% F1 (precision 79%, recall 81%); unequal false-negative rates across groups.

projects.title: Predicting Dengue Fever Outbreak Using Climate Variables
projects.title_slide: Predicting Dengue Fever Outbreak Using Climate Variables
projects.student_description: This project explores two machine learning approaches for predicting dengue fever cases and outbreak risk using climate and public health data. We compare an initial climate-based model with a near-real-time API model to improve outbreak detection and support more proactive public health responses

summary.plain: This project predicts weekly dengue fever cases and the chance of an outbreak using weather and health data. A first model for San Juan and Iquitos used older data and missed about half of outbreaks, so the team built a second Puerto Rico model that pulls near real-time health department and weather data and caught about 91% of outbreak weeks in their test.
summary.technical: Initial model: DrivenData climate and weekly case data (San Juan, Puerto Rico and Iquitos, Peru, 1990-2010) with weather lags, case lags/changes and sine/cosine seasonality; outbreaks defined as above the seasonal 75th-percentile threshold. A two-stage HistGradientBoosting system estimated outbreak probability (calibrated with logistic regression) and routed to specialist normal-week or outbreak-week regressors; it reported MAE 11.09 cases/week vs 11.68 for a single-stage baseline, with outbreak recall 51.6%, precision 31.6%, F1 39.2%. API model: Puerto Rico Department of Health arbovirus API and Open-Meteo weather (6 island points) with weather lags 0/2/4/8 and rolling 4/8-week features, seasonal q75 thresholds from prior years only, a bundle of three quantile HistGB regressors (P50/P80/P90) and a balanced-weight HistGB outbreak classifier with logistic calibration and a recall-tuned alert gate. It reported MAE 23.99 cases/week, recall 90.7%, precision 80.0% and F1 85.0%. Both versions were deployed as Streamlit apps.
summary.question: How can we use climate variables and public health records for weekly, near real-time prediction of dengue case counts and estimate the probability of an outbreak in Puerto Rico?
summary.problem: Dengue puts half the world's population at risk and public health responses remain largely reactive rather than proactive.
summary.beneficiary: Public health agencies and residents in dengue-endemic areas (Puerto Rico)
summary.inputs: Weekly dengue case reports, hospitalizations and weather variables (temperature, rainfall, humidity, etc.)
summary.outputs: Next-week case count forecast (P50/P80/P90) and calibrated outbreak probability with alert
summary.results: Initial model MAE 11.09, outbreak F1 39.2%; API model MAE 23.99, recall 90.7%, precision 80.0%, F1 85.0%.

projects.title: Predicting Failure, Auditing Fairness
projects.student_description: A machine-learning audit of Chicago restaurant inspections

summary.plain: The team trained a model to predict which Chicago restaurants will fail a health inspection, then checked who the model's mistakes fall on. They found the model's false alarms are spread very unevenly across ZIP codes, and argue this reflects where inspectors have historically focused rather than worse food safety, so the tool could reinforce unfair enforcement if used blindly.
summary.technical: Data: City of Chicago Food Inspections (312,415 raw records, 267,477 after cleaning, 43,356 establishments, 22.4% fail rate). Features: four one-hot encoded pre-inspection variables (inspection type, ZIP, facility type, risk level), with the Violations column excluded to avoid leakage. Models: logistic regression baseline vs random forest, both with balanced class weights, using a train/test split grouped by license number. Results: recall 70% (LogReg) / 67% (RF), precision ~30%, F1 0.415 / 0.418. Fairness audit with Fairlearn: citywide false-positive rate ~45% but 6%-68% across ZIPs; the gap persists on routine canvass-only inspections, ZIP FPR correlates 0.69 with enforcement-heavy inspection mix, and removing ZIP flips 24.6% of predictions.
summary.question: Which characteristics best predict whether a Chicago food establishment fails a health inspection, and do predicted failure rates differ across ZIP codes in a way that reflect real risk versus uneven enforcement?
summary.problem: Inspectors are limited, so prioritization matters, but models trained on past enforcement can encode uneven enforcement and concentrate false alarms on certain neighborhoods.
summary.beneficiary: City public-health departments and restaurant owners in over-flagged neighborhoods
summary.subdomain: Food safety inspection targeting and algorithmic fairness audit

summary.outputs: Predicted inspection failure (binary) and per-ZIP error-rate audit
summary.results: Recall 67-70%, precision ~30%, F1 ~0.42; per-ZIP false-alarm rate ranges 6%-68% (about 12x gap).

projects.title: Predicting Flood Events in Florida Counties Using Environmental Features
projects.title_slide: Predicting Flood Events in Florida Counties Using Environmental Features
projects.student_description: Our project develops machine learning models to predict flood events in Florida counties using environmental features such as rainfall, soil moisture, elevation, and slope.

summary.plain: This project tried to predict whether a Florida county would flood on a given day using NASA satellite data on rainfall, soil moisture, elevation and slope, with NOAA storm records as the answer key. The team compared Random Forest, XGBoost and Logistic Regression. Because floods are rare, the models caught some floods but raised many false alarms.
summary.technical: Daily county-level records were built by combining NASA GPM daily rainfall, NASA SMAP soil moisture, SRTM elevation/slope statistics (min/max/mean/std), U.S. Census county shapefiles, and NOAA Storm Events flood labels for Florida. Rainfall was log-transformed and lag-1 and 3-/7-day rolling rainfall sums were engineered. Models were trained on 2015-2021 and tested on 2022-2024 (temporal split), with random undersampling chosen over SMOTE for the rare flood class and decision thresholds tuned. Random Forest (baseline), XGBoost and Logistic Regression were compared using precision/recall/F1 (F1 the chosen metric) on 30,875 test days with 186 floods. Reported flood-class results: Random Forest precision 0.12 / recall 0.15 / F1 0.13 (accuracy 0.988); XGBoost precision 0.025 / recall 0.575 / F1 0.048 (accuracy 0.863); Logistic Regression precision 0.023 / recall 0.554 / F1 0.045 (accuracy 0.857).

projects.title: PREDICTING JET ENGINE  SYSTEM FAILURE
projects.student_description: Our project uses machine learning to predict how many flight cycles remain before a turbofan engine fails, using NASA's C-MAPSS sensor dataset. We trained and compared three models — Linear Regression, Random Forest, and an LSTM neural network — finding that thoughtful data preparation consistently mattered more than model complexity alone.

summary.plain: This project used NASA's simulated jet-engine sensor data to predict how many flights an engine has left before it fails. The team compared a simple linear model, a Random Forest and an LSTM neural network that reads the engine's sensor history, and found the LSTM made the smallest errors. They also built a Streamlit demo.
summary.technical: NASA C-MAPSS turbofan run-to-failure data (21 sensor channels; FD001 plus all four sub-datasets for validation) was cleaned, with per-unit signal detrending, pruning of constant/near-zero-variance channels, global feature normalization and windowing; features were screened with Pearson and lagged maximum correlation to RUL. Remaining Useful Life (RUL, in cycles) was predicted with a linear regression baseline, a Random Forest regressor and an LSTM sequence model trained with loss weighting by proximity to failure and learning-rate decay. Evaluation used RMSE/MAE on 25 unseen engines from a grouped split (seed 42), with K-fold cross-validation across sub-datasets claimed. Reported RMSE/MAE: Linear Regression 20.55/15.89, Random Forest 18.69/13.82, LSTM 16.59/12.20 (best validation checkpoint 15.71; 15.93-16.59 across three machines). The LSTM was deployed in a Streamlit dashboard.

summary.problem: Scheduled maintenance replaces engine parts too early (waste) or too late (danger); predicting remaining useful life enables proactive maintenance.

projects.title: Predicting Medium Article Engagement
projects.student_description:
The project predicts article engagement using both classification and regression approaches. 

For classification, it identifies whether an article has high or low engagement, while for regression, it predicts the log-transformed number of claps. The models applied include a Random Forest classifier and a Gradient Boosting regressor. Features are engineered from TF-IDF representations of titles and subtitles, VADER sentiment scores, one-hot encoded tags, and numeric metadata such as reading time and response counts. 

Model performance is evaluated using standard classification and regression metrics.

summary.plain: This project tried to predict how popular Medium blog articles would be. One model sorted articles into high or low engagement, and a second model estimated how many 'claps' an article would get. The author's past popularity, text length and positive tone mattered most for the high/low model.
summary.technical: Medium article records (source unnamed) were featurized with TF-IDF on combined title+subtitle, VADER sentiment scores, one-hot tags, author average claps, month/weekday/weekend flags, reading time and response counts. A Random Forest classifier with balanced class weights predicted whether an article was in the top 25% of engagement (stratified 80/20 split), reporting 92% accuracy, ROC AUC 0.8949, class-0 precision/recall 0.95/0.95 and class-1 0.84/0.84. A Gradient Boosting regressor predicted log-transformed claps (80/20 split) with MAE 1.25, RMSE 1.55 (log scale) and R² 0.32. Feature importances were reported for both models.
summary.question: To what extent can machine learning models predict the engagement level of Medium articles using features such as textual content, author history, and publishing metadata, and how accurately can the number of claps be estimated?
summary.problem: Writers, editors, platforms and advertisers want to know in advance which articles will engage readers.
summary.beneficiary: Writers, editors and content platforms
summary.inputs: Title/subtitle text, sentiment, tags, author average claps, publishing time, reading time, response count
summary.outputs: High/low engagement label and predicted log clap count
summary.results: Classifier: 92% accuracy, ROC AUC 0.8949; Regressor: MAE 1.25, RMSE 1.55 (log claps), R² 0.32.

projects.title: Predicting Mental Health Symptom Severity Using Behavioral and Neuroimaging Data
projects.title_slide: Predicting Mental Health Symptom Severity Using Behavioral and Neuroimaging Data
projects.student_description: We investigate if using behavioral and imaging data yields better results for prediction of mental health symptom severity than either method on its own.

summary.plain: This project asked whether questionnaire answers, brain scans (resting-state fMRI), or both together best predict how severe someone's depression, anxiety, stress or anhedonia symptoms are. Using an open research dataset, the team built dozens of Random Forest models and found questionnaire data worked best while brain-scan features alone predicted poorly. They caught and fixed a 'cheating' problem where some questionnaires measured the same symptoms they were predicting, and built a Streamlit dashboard to explore results.
summary.technical: Behavioral questionnaire and resting-state fMRI features from the Transdiagnostic Connectome Project dataset were used to predict four continuous symptom scores (QIDS, STAI-State, SHAPS, PSS). Random Forest regressors were trained on behavioral (all, relevant, category, non-symptom), imaging-only and multimodal feature sets, growing from 28 to 36 models after target leakage was found and symptom-scale predictors were removed; Spearman correlations screened features for excessive (rho >= 0.80) correlation with targets. Models were evaluated with held-out test R² and mean repeated cross-validation R², plus MAE/RMSE. Best test R² / CV R²: Stress (PSS) all behavioral 0.577/0.572; Depression (QIDS) relevant behavioral 0.636/0.588; Anhedonia (SHAPS) all behavioral -0.070/0.335; Anxiety (STAI-State) all behavioral 0.719/0.726; non-symptom behavioral for anxiety reached test R² 0.638 (MAE 6.638, RMSE 8.272). Imaging-only models gave weak or negative R², and cross-category symptom ablations quantified gains over domain-only baselines. Results are shown in an interactive Streamlit dashboard.

projects.title: Predicting Mild Cognitive Impairment in Older Adults with Type 2 Diabetes
projects.title_slide: Predicting Mild Cognitive Impairment in Older Adults with Type 2 Diabetes
projects.student_description: This project builds a supervised machine learning pipeline to classify mild cognitive impairment (MCI) in older adults with Type 2 Diabetes using clinical and MRI-derived biomarkers from the PhysioNet GE-79 dataset. Our results demonstrate that cerebrovascular features—particularly global vasoreactivity, white matter hyperintensity, and cerebral perfusion measures—emerge as the strongest predictors of MCI status alongside glycemic, cardiovascular, and inflammatory biomarkers, offering clinically interpretable insights for cognitive risk assessment in this population.

summary.plain: This project tested whether computer models could spot mild memory and thinking problems (mild cognitive impairment) in older adults with Type 2 diabetes using blood tests, blood pressure and brain MRI measurements. With only 75 people in the dataset, a Random Forest did best overall but missed many impaired cases, while a simple decision tree caught more of them. SHAP was used to show which measurements, like blood sugar and brain blood flow, drove the predictions.
summary.technical: The PhysioNet CDED GE-79 dataset (75 participants, 46 variables; 55 no impairment / 20 impaired) was cleaned by removing identifiers and leakage variables, median-imputing missing numerics and adding a diabetes-duration missingness indicator. A Random Forest was used to rank features and select 14 shared biomarker features. Logistic Regression, Decision Tree and Random Forest were evaluated with 5-fold stratified cross-validation using accuracy, macro-F1, impaired recall, ROC-AUC and PR-AUC. Reported: Logistic Regression 0.547 / 0.508 / 0.500 / 0.534 / 0.369; Decision Tree 0.627 / 0.580 / 0.550 / 0.639 / 0.370; Random Forest 0.747 / 0.594 / 0.250 / 0.648 / 0.441. SHAP summary and mean |SHAP| plots for the Random Forest highlighted fasting glucose (0.586), global vasoreactivity (0.538), whole-brain perfusion and sVCAM.

projects.title_slide: Predicting NBA Success with Pre-Draft Data
projects.student_description: Our project uses machine learning to predict NBA player success based on college basketball statistics by engineering new impact metrics, aiming to improve draft decision-making and reduce bust rates

summary.plain: This project tried to predict how much college basketball players would help their NBA teams win (measured by Win Shares) using their college stats. The team built some new combined impact stats, then tried a decision tree, linear regression and random forest. The models did poorly, and the team concluded Win Shares is hard to predict from college stats alone.
summary.technical: College basketball stats (2009-2021) and NBA stats/All-Star data (1980-2024) from Kaggle were joined, and engineered impact metrics were added (efficient usage, points per minute, impact per usage, two-way impact, versatility score) alongside stops, BPM, recruiting rank, games played and free-throw rate. An initial plan to predict four targets combined into an 'NBA Success Score' was narrowed to predicting NBA Win Shares. Decision Tree (depth 3 visualized), Linear Regression and Random Forest regressors were trained and tested on a separate validation set using RMSE and R²; no values are reported, only that performance was weak with individual stats and improved slightly with added predictors. Random Forest feature importances ranked recruiting rank, stops and versatility score highest.

projects.title: Predicting NFL Lower-Extremity Injury Risk Using Machine Learning
projects.title_slide: Predicting NFL Lower-Extremity Injury Risk Using Machine Learning
projects.student_description: The NFL Lower-Risk Injury Lab uses machine learning to analyze player movement, field conditions, weather, and game factors to estimate the risk of lower-extremity injuries during NFL plays. The project aims to help identify potential injury risk factors and support safer decision-making in football.

summary.plain: This project tried to predict whether an NFL player would suffer a leg or foot injury on a given play using tracking data on speed, acceleration and distance, workload, and whether the field was artificial turf or grass. The team used a balanced logistic regression model and built a Streamlit dashboard where users can compare players and adjust risk thresholds. Injuries were extremely rare in the data, and the model performed close to random guessing.
summary.technical: The Kaggle NFL Playing Surface Analytics data (injury record, play list and player track files; 105 injuries among more than 267,000 player-plays) was used. From player tracking data, features were engineered per play: maximum speed, maximum acceleration, maximum deceleration, total distance, daily workload and acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR), plus synthetic vs natural surface; features were standardized. A class-balanced logistic regression output injury probability and a relative risk score. Reported evaluation: ROC AUC 0.522, injury recall 40%, injury precision 0.03%. A Streamlit decision-support dashboard provides a lower-risk player board with position filters, an adjustable risk threshold and model diagnostics.
summary.question: Can machine learning accurately predict the likelihood of a lower-extremity injury during an NFL play using player movement, field surface, weather, stadium conditions, and game-related variables?
summary.problem: The NFL loses millions per year to player injuries, most commonly lower-extremity injuries, and surface type may contribute.
summary.beneficiary: NFL teams, coaches and medical/performance staff
summary.inputs: Per-play movement features (max speed, acceleration, deceleration, distance), workload/ACWR, playing surface
summary.outputs: Injury risk probability and relative risk score
summary.results: ROC AUC 0.522, injury recall 40%, injury precision 0.03%.

projects.title: Predicting Optimal Wind Farm Locations Using AI​
projects.title_slide: Predicting Optimal Wind Farm Locations Using AI
projects.student_description:
​

We built machine learning models to predict whether a location is likely to have a wind turbine based on wind
resource characteristics. Using data from NREL's Wind Toolkit and the U.S. Wind Turbine Database, we
trained two models: Logistic Regression and Random Forest to classify sites as suitable or unsuitable for
wind development.

summary.plain: This project trained models to guess whether a U.S. location is likely to have a wind turbine, based on wind speed, how much power a turbine could produce there, and usable land. The team compared logistic regression, Random Forest and XGBoost, and XGBoost did best. They discuss how learning from where turbines already are can repeat past biases.
summary.technical: Sites were labeled turbine/no-turbine using the U.S. Wind Turbine Database and joined to NREL WIND Toolkit wind-resource and economic features despite differing spatial resolutions. Four core features were used: wind speed, capacity factor, usable land area fraction and potential capacity. With a stratified train/test split and class_weight='balanced' to address imbalance, Logistic Regression, Random Forest (500 trees) and XGBoost were compared. Reported test metrics: ROC-AUC 0.732 / 0.770 / 0.847, accuracy 0.643 / 0.703 / 0.766, turbine recall 0.728 / 0.448 / 0.645, turbine precision 0.522 / 0.663 / 0.708 for LR / RF / XGBoost; XGBoost was recommended. Balanced weights reportedly raised turbine detection from 40% to 73%.
summary.question: How can ensemble tree-based classifiers use wind resource and geospatial data to identify optimal locations for future wind energy plants across the United States while balancing environmental, sociological, and economic constraints?
summary.problem: Poor wind farm siting causes environmental and community harms, and current models optimize only for wind potential.
summary.beneficiary: Renewable energy developers and planners
summary.inputs: Wind speed, capacity factor, usable land area fraction, potential capacity per site
summary.outputs: Probability that a site has / is suitable for a wind turbine
summary.results: XGBoost ROC-AUC 0.847, accuracy 0.766; Random Forest ROC-AUC 0.770, accuracy 0.703; Logistic Regression ROC-AUC 0.732, accuracy 0.643.

projects.student_description: Predicting small price changes in financial markets over short periods of time is very important in making the right trading decisions, helping to reduce loss while keeping markets efficient and fair. This project aimed to predict short-term Bitcoin price movements using high-frequency order book data.

summary.plain: This project tried to predict tiny, very short-term changes in Bitcoin's price using order book data, which lists how many people want to buy and sell at each price. The team built features like the gap between buy and sell prices and the balance of buy versus sell volume, then fit a linear regression. The model caught some patterns but still made sizable errors.
summary.technical: High-frequency Bitcoin limit order book data (Kaggle Bitcoin LOB data / Binance data collection) was explored with plots of mid-price, bid-ask spread and order book depth. Features engineered were spread, mid price, log volume imbalance (log ask volume / log bid volume) and volume-weighted mid price. A linear regression predicted the change in mid-price over a 2.5-second future window, reporting MAE 0.1951 and RMSE 0.4564 on a data subset. Random Forest and XGBoost comparisons and a web app were planned but not done.

projects.title_slide: PREDICTING STARTUP SUCCESS WITH MACHINE LEARNING
projects.student_description: A logistic regression model and Streamlit app that estimates whether an early-stage startup is more likely to be acquired/IPO or to close, based on funding history, timing, industry, and global location.

summary.plain: This project predicts whether an early-stage startup is more likely to succeed (be acquired or go public) or to shut down, using its funding history, timing, industry and region. The team tried logistic regression, random forest and a neural network and chose logistic regression because it worked as well and is easy to explain. They built an app that shows the top factors behind each prediction, and found that data quality and regional bias were the biggest challenges.
summary.technical: After discarding an earlier dataset found to be synthetic and a small US-only dataset (0.80 AUC baseline), the team rebuilt on a global 13,000+ company Crunchbase-derived Kaggle dataset. A leakage column (closed_at) was removed, features were engineered (log total funding, number of rounds, funding velocity, years to most recent round, gap between first and most recent round, continent, top-10 industry + Other), highly correlated engineered features were dropped and a multicollinearity issue fixed; missingness was analyzed by outcome. Logistic Regression, Random Forest and a Neural Network were compared; Logistic Regression was tuned with Optuna and evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation, reaching ROC-AUC 0.823 and 75% accuracy. A secondary XGBoost regressor trained on a unicorn dataset predicts valuations (R² 0.51, RMSE 0.57, MAE 0.45). A live app takes six inputs and returns a prediction with top-factor explanations.

projects.title: Predicting Stock Outperformance from Quarterly Earnings Calls
projects.student_description: Used quarterly earnings calls to identify whether there was predictive information in language with how a stock performs relative to the S&P500/market.

summary.plain: This project asked whether the way company executives talk on quarterly earnings calls hints at whether their stock will beat the S&P 500 over the next five days. The team scored the tone of each call sentence by sentence with a finance-tuned language model and a finance word dictionary, combined that with market data, and trained an XGBoost model. They found a real but weak signal (AUC about 0.63) and stress that it is not a trading strategy.
summary.technical: S&P 500 earnings call transcripts from the Hugging Face dataset Bose345/sp500_earnings_transcripts (33,000+) were filtered to Industrials from 2015 onward and matched to yfinance prices using exact call timestamps (intraday calls excluded), giving samples of 1,516 events/67 companies and 886 events/61 companies. Features (44+) included market controls (momentum, volatility, beta), FinBERT positive/negative/neutral sentiment, sentence-level chunked sentiment trajectories, Loughran-McDonald dictionary categories and company-relative historical sentiment z-scores. After a linear regression on returns gave R² ~0, the task became binary 5-day outperformance vs the S&P 500; 10+ model variants were tried. With walk-forward validation (2019-2022, holdout from 2023) and clustered bootstrap by company, a shallow XGBoost (depth 2, 150 trees) using sentence sentiment + historical features won: walk-forward AUC 0.631, holdout AUC 0.627, Brier 0.237 (95% AUC CI 0.558-0.685), versus original logistic 0.555/0.635, market-only 0.543/0.473 and historical XGBoost 0.629/0.591. MCC was about 0.19. An earnings call dashboard was demoed.

projects.title: Predicting Stock Volatility
projects.student_description: This project develops a machine learning model to predict stock price volatility using engineered features from high-frequency order book and trade data, with linear regression on features like realized volatility and bid-ask spreads.

summary.plain: The team tried to predict how much a stock's price will jump around (its volatility) over the next 10 minutes using very detailed trading data. They built many features from order-book and trade records and fit a linear regression model, which they report explains about 79% of the variation in volatility.
summary.technical: Uses the Optiver realized-volatility Kaggle competition data (order book bid/ask prices and sizes plus trade executions). The target is realized volatility computed from log returns within each 10-minute window. The team engineered 46+ features including weighted average price (WAP), bid-ask spreads, supply-demand ratios, price-level volatilities, VWAP and trade statistics. A linear regression model was trained with a sequential time split to avoid leakage. They report an RMSE of 0.001397 and R^2 of 0.79, and analyse feature-target correlations (realized-volatility features ~0.89, spreads ~0.77).

projects.title_slide: Predicting U.S. Regional Electricity Demand Using Weather Data
projects.student_description: Can we forecast hourly electricity demand 1 day, 1 week, and 1 month ahead across 8 major US grid regions using historical demand, weather, and calendar features, and how does forecast reliability vary by model and region?

summary.plain: The team collected a year of hourly electricity demand and weather data for 8 large U.S. power-grid regions and trained models to predict demand a day, a week and a month ahead. Tree-based models (XGBoost and Random Forest) predicted demand well, and they built a Streamlit app that estimates typical demand for a chosen region, time and temperature.
summary.technical: Hourly demand, solar and wind generation were pulled from the EIA Grid Monitor API and merged with Open-Meteo historical weather for a representative city per region (~70,000 hourly rows over one year). Features included sine/cosine cyclical time encodings and 24h/168h lags and rolling means/stds. Linear regression (80/20 time-based split) and an LSTM on 24-hour sequences were evaluated with MAE/RMSE/MAPE (LR MAE 5,266.84 MWh; LSTM MAE 9,079.89 MWh). XGBoost and Random Forest were trained as direct multi-horizon models (1 day/1 week/1 month) and tested on a held-out 45-day window with overall and per-region MAE, RMSE, MAPE and R^2 (e.g. XGBoost 1-day MAPE 4.30%, R^2 0.9929, degrading to ~7.5% at 1 month). For the deployed demo, models were retrained without lag features on region/time/apparent temperature with a random stratified split (XGBoost MAE 1,362 MWh, MAPE 3.70%, R^2 0.995).

projects.title: Prediction of Future Energy Usage
projects.student_description: Our Final Project is a predictive model to predict the future energy usage across all countries. We used 20 years real data to train two algorithms: Random Forest Regressor and XGBoost Regressor. Then, we evaluated both the models and deployed XGBoost as it outperformed the Random Forest model.

summary.plain: The team used 20 years of country-level data on economy, geography and electricity sources to predict how much energy each person in a country uses. They compared Random Forest and XGBoost models and chose a tuned XGBoost model, then built a Streamlit demo where users enter a country's metrics to get a prediction.
summary.technical: Data is the Kaggle 'Global Data on Sustainable Energy (2000-2020)' dataset with 20+ features (GDP per capita, CO2 emissions, energy intensity, electricity by source, access to electricity, population density, latitude/longitude). Missing values (up to 2,089 per column) were analysed with heatmaps and imputed with linear interpolation and country-grouped mean imputation; low-importance, high-missing columns were dropped and the year feature excluded to avoid leakage. Random Forest and XGBoost regressors predicted primary energy consumption per capita. RF reported R^2 0.9670 and MAE ~1,920; XGBoost R^2 0.9680 before and 0.9761 after hyperparameter tuning (MAE ~2,041, a 7.4% reduction). MAE was also segmented by low/mid/high usage, showing much larger errors for high-usage countries.

projects.title: Preventing Server Crashes
projects.student_description: Building fair and reliable AI systems to predict service crashes based on workload data to help prevent widespread harm and ensure equal performance across different servers.

summary.plain: The team tried to predict when cloud computing jobs will have a high error rate, as an early warning sign that servers could overload or crash. They trained a random forest model on a public dataset of 5,000 cloud workload jobs and looked at which measurements (CPU, memory, network) mattered most. The model's overall ability to separate risky from normal jobs was about the same as guessing.
summary.technical: Data: 5,000 job records from a public Kaggle cloud workload scheduling dataset with CPU, memory, network bandwidth, execution time, priority, scheduler type and resource allocation fields. Preprocessing: the continuous Error Rate was binarized at the 75th percentile (3.8%) into High Error vs Normal, and categorical fields were one-hot encoded. Model: a scikit-learn-style Random Forest classifier with balanced class weights. Evaluation (on an apparent 1,000-job hold-out, read from the confusion matrix): ROC AUC = 0.47, and lowering the decision threshold to 0.3 raised recall for the high-error class to about 0.57 at the cost of 452 false positives out of 751 normal jobs. Feature importances ranked CPU, memory and network metrics highest.
summary.question: How can AI predict server load spikes to prevent slowdowns or crashes, while adapting to different workloads and server types?
summary.problem: Server overloads and outages cause downtime for businesses and users; the team wants proactive rather than reactive prediction that performs fairly across server types.
summary.beneficiary: IT / cloud operations teams and the businesses and users relying on cloud services
summary.inputs: Job-level cloud workload metrics (CPU, memory, network bandwidth, execution time, throughput) and categorical job attributes
summary.outputs: Binary label: high-error (overload risk) vs normal job
summary.results: ROC AUC 0.47 (at or below chance); at threshold 0.3 the confusion matrix shows 143/249 high-error jobs caught (recall ~0.57) with 452 false positives.
