projects.title: Prompt Injection Detector
projects.student_description: We made a model that detects malicious input designed to hijack or manipulate a large language model: overriding its instructions, extracting hidden prompts, or bypassing safety rules.

summary.plain: Prompt injection is when someone writes text designed to trick an AI chatbot into ignoring its rules. The team trained four models to flag such prompts and found that near-perfect test scores hid a blind spot: simple character tricks fooled the models until they retrained on real human-written attacks.
summary.technical: Four binary classifiers (safe vs injection, with confidence) were built: fine-tuned DistilBERT, logistic regression on TF-IDF and on all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, a linear-kernel SVM on TF-IDF, and a Random Forest on TF-IDF tuned with GridSearchCV. In iteration 1 on a synthetic dataset, all models scored ~99% accuracy and ~0.98-0.99 injection-class F1, but Unicode obfuscation (homoglyphs, tag smuggling, spacing) got 0% detection. In iteration 2 the models were retrained on xTRam1 plus Tensor Trust (280,000+ human-submitted adversarial prompts) and robustness was tested with Mindgard evaded samples across 20 evasion techniques, with detection rates of roughly 93.8-100% shown in the chart. A live app lets users test any of the four models and view a robustness dashboard.
summary.question: How robust is a transformer-based prompt injection detector against attacks specifically designed to evade it — and what does that reveal about the role training data plays in that robustness?
summary.problem: LLM applications are vulnerable to inputs that override instructions, extract hidden prompts or bypass safety rules.
summary.beneficiary: Developers deploying LLM-based applications
summary.inputs: A single raw text prompt
summary.outputs: Binary label (safe / injection) plus a confidence score
summary.results: ~99% clean-test accuracy for all models; 0% detection on Unicode attacks in v1; after retraining on real attacks, ~94-100% detection across 20 evasion techniques.

projects.title: PROMPT SHIELD
projects.student_description: Fine-tuned DistilBERT for text classification (prompt detection), achieving a strong validation F1 score of 0.969 on the baseline model and tested how this generalized to new ai generated adversarial and benign prompts.

summary.plain: The team built a classifier that sorts prompts sent to AI chatbots into four types: normal, prompt injection, jailbreak, or attempts to leak the hidden system prompt. It scored very well on test data from the same sources, but when tested on new prompts written by other AI models, its score dropped sharply, showing it had mostly memorized its training data.
summary.technical: Four public prompt-attack datasets (Neuralchemy prompt-injection, TrustAIRLab in-the-wild jailbreaks, jackhhao jailbreak-classification, gabrielchua system-prompt-leakage; 383,811 rows) were unified to text/label, 30+ subcategories collapsed into 4 classes, benign and extraction downsampled to 2,500, and duplicates removed, giving 10,117 rows. distilbert-base-uncased was fine-tuned (3 epochs, batch 16, LR 2e-5, 256 max tokens) on a 70/15/15 stratified split with macro F1 as the selection metric. In-distribution test macro F1 was 0.97 (per-class F1 0.93-0.99), with confusion mostly between jailbreak and prompt injection. A 400-prompt out-of-distribution set generated by two LLMs (GPT-5.5 Instant and Claude 4.6 Sonnet) gave macro F1 0.43; extraction F1 fell from 0.99 to 0.00.
summary.question: Does a prompt-attack classifier trained on existing datasets genuinely learn to recognize attacks, or does it just memorize the patterns of its training data?
summary.problem: Lightweight input filters for LLM apps may overfit to the datasets they were trained on and give false security.
summary.beneficiary: Developers of LLM-based applications
summary.subdomain: Prompt attack classification and generalization testing
summary.inputs: Prompt text
summary.outputs: One of four labels: benign, prompt_injection, jailbreak, extraction
summary.results: Macro F1 0.97 in distribution vs 0.43 on synthetic OOD prompts; extraction class 0.00 OOD.

projects.title: Readability Assessment Project
projects.student_description: Our project aims to ascertain if we can train AI/ML models that better predict readability scores with the incorporation of semantics as compared to traditional methods like the Flesch-Kincaid algorithm.

summary.plain: The team tried to predict how hard a passage is to read using machine learning instead of classic formulas like Flesch-Kincaid that only count word and sentence length. They compared simple word-count features, BERT text embeddings and a further-trained BERT language model, and found the language-model approach gave the lowest error.
summary.technical: Using the CommonLit Readability Prize (Kaggle) data and the CLEAR corpus, the team explored text embeddings with PCA and KMeans clustering and pairwise cosine similarity. Three regression approaches were tried: a TF-IDF baseline with gradient-boosted trees (LightGBM/XGBoost), BERT embeddings fed to a regressor (output shows Random Forest) plus spaCy cohesion metrics, and masked language modeling (MLM) followed by regression. Reported RMSE: TF-IDF 5-fold CV mean 0.9151, embeddings + regression average K-fold CV 0.4666, and MLM + regression 0.3386 (fold 1, epoch 2). Traditional formulas were not reported numerically.
summary.question: Can ML models incorporating semantics predict readability scores better than traditional methods like Flesch-Kincaid?
summary.problem: Traditional readability formulas rely on surface features and many tools are proprietary.
summary.beneficiary: Educators matching students in grades 3-12 with appropriate texts
summary.inputs: Text excerpts
summary.outputs: Predicted readability score
summary.results: RMSE 0.9151 (TF-IDF), 0.4666 (embeddings + regression), 0.3386 (MLM + regression, single fold).

projects.title: Reading the Room
projects.student_description: Turning a webcam into an honest measure of how people really react to ads.

summary.plain: The team built a web app that watches a person's face through a webcam while they watch an ad and scores six emotions live, second by second. It reads 52 facial muscle movements and uses a Random Forest model to turn them into emotion scores, so advertisers can see which moments of an ad people actually react to.
summary.technical: MediaPipe extracts 52 named facial blendshape scores; a multi-output Random Forest regressor maps a half-second window of these to six emotion intensities on a 0-3 scale. Training mixed acted clips with graded intensity labels (CREMA-D) and candid in-the-wild photos (AffectNet), which nearly tripled sadness accuracy. On 5,522 held-out faces never seen in training, they report 0.98 detection quality for happiness, 76% less error than a naive guess, and ±0.02 variation across reruns; 5-fold splits and a calibration check were used. Recall is weak for sadness (17%), disgust and fear. SHAP attributions match FACS regions, and a fairness audit on held-out CREMA-D actors found similar error across sex/race/ethnicity but 14% worse accuracy for faces over 50. The model was capped at 47.8 MB and deployed on Render on a free CPU.
summary.question: How can we measure the performance of an advertisement or new product by turning a webcam into an honest measure of how people really react to ads?
summary.problem: Ad testing relies on after-the-fact surveys that are unreliable and cannot locate which second of an ad landed.

projects.title: ReadMe
projects.student_description: We live in a world where AI helps us find everything, but when it comes to books, it’s still surprisingly hard to get recommendations that really fit your interests or mood so we created ReadMe, a machine-learning-powered system that understands what kind of stories speak to you and helps you discover more of them effortlessly.

summary.plain: ReadMe is a book recommendation website: you type what you're in the mood for and it suggests 5 books. It uses a k-nearest-neighbors approach on a Goodreads book dataset to find books that are similar to each other, and the team compared it against a few other simple models.
summary.technical: Data: a Goodreads books dataset (May 2024) with book features such as genre and rating; no user profiles, so recommendations are item-to-item. Models: k-nearest neighbors combined with PCA was the chosen approach; linear regression, a decision tree and a random forest regressor were also run as regression benchmarks. Evaluation (p9 table): KNN+PCA MSE 0.0925, R² 0.4511, average cross-validated RMSE 0.3055; Linear Regression 0.0989 / 0.0486 / 0.32; Decision Trees 0.1734 / 0.6825 / 0.42; Random Forest 0.0945 / 0.1001 / 0.3023. A web front end takes a mood/theme prompt and returns 5 books. The regression target and how prompts map to features are not stated.
summary.question: How can kNN algorithms improve book recommendation accuracy and help users find books using a prompt?
summary.problem: Readers struggle to find books matching specific themes, tones or moods, and ordinary search engines and popularity-driven recommendations don't capture this.
summary.beneficiary: Readers, and potentially libraries and online reading platforms
summary.inputs: Book features (e.g. genre, rating) from Goodreads data; a user's free-text prompt describing mood/themes
summary.outputs: Five recommended books
summary.results: KNN+PCA: MSE 0.0925, R² 0.4511, CV RMSE 0.3055 (as reported); team chose KNN citing lower RMSE than decision trees.

projects.student_description: Automate rapid and accurate human detection in aerial drone images for Search and Rescue (SAR) operations.

summary.plain: The team trained an object-detection model to spot people in aerial drone photos, to help search and rescue teams find missing people faster. Using a YOLOv11 model trained on a labeled search-and-rescue drone dataset, they report finding people with about 94% mean average precision on validation images.
summary.technical: The SARD (search and rescue drone) dataset from Roboflow, with human-annotated bounding boxes of (acted) people in wilderness drone imagery, was cleaned and organized (4,000+ training images; 5,000+ annotated images overall). A YOLOv11 detector was trained for 60-80 epochs and evaluated on validation and test sets. Validation metrics: mAP 94%, precision 94.6%, recall 89.9%, F1 92%, with an F1-confidence curve; an additional unlabeled 0.64 value is shown (possibly mAP50-95).

projects.title:
Topological Data Analysis of Market Sentiment, Volatility, and Returns
Detecting Nonlinear Regime Structure in Financial Time Series
projects.student_description: We examine how Twitter sentiment and volatility shape stock returns, finding that sentiment predicts returns only during volatile market regimes.

summary.plain: The team asked whether the mood of tweets about a stock helps predict its returns over the next five days, and whether that changes when the market is calm versus jumpy. Using a public dataset of tweets and stock prices, they ran statistical regressions and found that tweet sentiment did not reliably predict returns in any volatility regime, while past returns showed a small reversal effect.
summary.technical: The StockNet dataset (two years of tweets aligned with daily prices for 88 U.S. equities) was used with a daily aggregated sentiment measure, 5-day volatility, lagged 5-day return and 5-day return target. Rows with missing values were dropped, variables winsorized at the 1st/99th percentiles, and observations split into three equal-count volatility regimes (~3,461 each). A pooled OLS with a sentiment x volatility interaction and HAC/Newey-West standard errors (5 lags) found only past return significant (beta = -0.0554, p < 0.001; R^2 = 0.005). Regime-specific regressions gave non-significant sentiment coefficients (p = 0.321, 0.916, 0.352). Binned decile plots showed rising return dispersion with volatility and short-horizon mean reversion.
summary.question: How do 5-day stock returns behave across volatility regimes, and does Twitter sentiment have different predictive value in low vs high volatility environments (after controlling for past returns / mean reversion)?
summary.problem: Pooled models may hide regime-dependent relationships between sentiment and returns.
summary.beneficiary: Investors and quantitative finance researchers
summary.subdomain: Social media sentiment and stock returns
summary.inputs: Daily tweet sentiment, recent volatility and lagged returns per stock
summary.outputs: Regression coefficients and significance for 5-day returns
summary.results: Sentiment not significant pooled (p = 0.156) or within any regime; past return negative and significant (mean reversion); R^2 = 0.005.

projects.title: SafeInbox: Phishing Detection Project
projects.student_description: We created a Phishing email detector as a browser extension.

summary.plain: The team built a phishing detector that checks emails and the links inside them for signs of a scam, with the goal of warning users before they click. They compared several machine learning models and found that logistic regression worked best, and demonstrated it as a browser extension.
summary.technical: Two datasets were prepared: a URL dataset of 800k+ phishing and legitimate URLs with 48 hand-made features (e.g. url length, digit ratio, is_https), deduplicated and cleaned, and an email dataset combining seven public email datasets with 21 hand-made features plus 768 BERT embedding features. Class imbalance was handled by balanced sampling (50% of each class) and a stratified train-test split, with precision, recall and F1 reported. K-fold cross-validation was used to choose among XGBoost, Random Forest, Logistic Regression and Naive Bayes; logistic regression was best (F1, precision, recall and accuracy all shown as 0.9670) and was tuned over C, penalty and max_iter (best C=1.0, L1, 300 iterations; CV F1 0.9671).
summary.question: How easily and accurately can phishing urls be detected in emails and websites to notify the user even before the url is accessed?
summary.problem: Phishing emails and URLs trick users into visiting malicious sites.
summary.beneficiary: Email users, especially those less familiar with online threats
summary.inputs: Email content and URLs (hand-made features and BERT embeddings)
summary.outputs: Phishing vs legitimate prediction
summary.results: Tuned logistic regression best with cross-validation F1 0.9671.

projects.title: Safety-Aware Navigation
projects.student_description: user inputs a route, model gives it a safety-score from 1-100 based on features of the immediate surrounding area

summary.plain: The team built a Streamlit app that gives a walking route in Los Angeles a safety score from 1 to 100, based on crime and streetlight data near the route. They used crime severity scores and linear regression to predict how safe neighborhoods feel, and found the model beat simply guessing the average, but only by a small and unstable margin.
summary.technical: LA crime data (2010-2019) were mapped to Cambridge Crime Harm Index (CCHI) severity scores via a crosswalk generated with a 'foundational model' during preprocessing; features such as crime density, average CCHI and streetlight density were computed per area. The target was a perceived-safety score from an 'LA neighborhoods considered safe for walking' source. Linear regression was the main model; a Random Forest regressor and extra features (crime per capita, interaction terms) did not improve results. 5-fold cross-validation gave mean RMSE 9.9 vs an always-predict-the-mean baseline RMSE of 12.1, with fold instability; an 'accuracy rate' of ~78% is also reported. A Streamlit app scores a typed address route or uploaded map file.

summary.beneficiary: Pedestrians in Los Angeles

summary.outputs: Safety score (1-100) for the area around the route

projects.title: Scam Detector
projects.student_description: We built a scam detector using a supervised ML Model - Logistic Regression. With irresponsible use of AI increasing worldwide, we build a model to help classify messages into 3 categories - spam, smishing, ham.

summary.plain: The team built a tool that reads a text message and decides whether it is a normal message (ham), junk advertising (spam), or a scam trying to steal personal information (smishing). They trained three simple machine learning models on about 6,000 labeled SMS messages and found they all got around 94-96% of messages right.
summary.technical: A Mendeley SMS phishing dataset of 5,971 messages labeled ham/spam/smishing was used; the plan was to drop the Email column and convert Phone and URL columns into binary features alongside the message text. Data was split 80/20 for training and testing. Logistic regression, decision tree and random forest classifiers were compared using confusion matrices and per-class precision/recall/F1. Reported accuracies were 0.957 (logistic regression), 0.958 (random forest) and 0.941 (decision tree); the spam class was hardest (F1 0.77, 0.76, 0.67). A demo UI lets a user enter a message and flag whether it contains a URL or phone number.

projects.title: Scarlet.AI
projects.student_description: An Explainable AI Chatbot for College Students, focused on providing reliable information about Rutgers University.

summary.plain: Scarlet.AI is a chatbot that answers college students' questions about their university (deadlines, dining, housing, financial aid and more) and shows where each answer came from so students can judge whether to trust it. The team collected information from hundreds of official university web pages and built a web app with extra features like quick questions and emergency contacts.
summary.technical: Data: content scraped from 300+ official university web pages and PDFs using Docling, converted to structured documents and split with Docling's HybridChunker (0.8 merge threshold); the demo shows 2,299 documents loaded. Chunks were embedded with SentenceTransformers and stored in ChromaDB for retrieval-augmented generation. An 'explainability, safety and evaluation layer' adds retrieval-distance confidence scores, hallucination detection, claim-level verification against the vector store, topic classification with risk levels and policy-aware responses (disclaimers, crisis routing). The system runs as a Streamlit app with an Explainable-AI vs Black-Box mode. A small user survey reported 83.3% 'Yes' / 16.7% 'Somewhat' on helpfulness, and the Black Box mode received higher average trust and accuracy ratings (about 5/5) than the Explainable mode (about 3.8/5).
summary.question: Can a university-specific chatbot that shows its sources give students reliable, transparent answers about campus resources?
summary.problem: Students struggle to navigate scattered campus information and may not be able to judge whether chatbot answers are reliable.
summary.beneficiary: College students (including potentially underserved groups such as international, graduate and commuter students)
summary.subdomain: Campus information assistant with source attribution

summary.outputs: Generated answers with cited sources, confidence scores and safety disclaimers
summary.results: User survey: 83.3% found answers helpful, 16.7% somewhat; Black Box mode rated ~5/5 vs Explainable mode ~3.8/5 on trust and accuracy (sample size not stated).

projects.title: Sentiment Analysis of User Feedback Using Machine Learning
projects.title_slide: Sentiment Analysis of User Feedback Using Machine Learning
projects.student_description: This project uses machine learning to classify written user feedback as positive or negative sentiment using real-world review data. It compares multiple models and demonstrates how addressing class imbalance improves the detection of negative feedback, which is critical for responsible and effective feedback analysis.

summary.plain: This project teaches a computer to read Amazon food reviews and decide if each one is positive or negative. Because most reviews are positive, the first models almost never caught negative ones, so the student told the model to pay extra attention to negative reviews, which made it catch most of them.
summary.technical: Amazon Fine Food Reviews (Kaggle) were labeled positive (rating >= 4) or negative (rating <= 2), with neutral reviews removed, giving a highly imbalanced dataset. Text was represented with TF-IDF. Multinomial-style Naive Bayes, logistic regression and class-weighted logistic regression were compared using accuracy, precision, recall and confusion matrices, with a focus on negative-class recall. Negative recall rose from about 0.02 (Naive Bayes) and about 0.46 (logistic regression) to about 0.84 with class weighting; the final confusion matrix shows 1,323 of 1,571 negatives correctly identified.
summary.question: Can machine learning reliably detect negative user feedback in imbalanced real-world review data?
summary.problem: Organizations rely on feedback, and missing negative feedback can have serious consequences; imbalanced data makes models ignore negatives.
summary.beneficiary: Organizations analyzing customer or user feedback
summary.inputs: Written review text
summary.outputs: Positive or negative sentiment label
summary.results: Class-weighted LR negative recall about 0.84 (1,323/1,571) vs about 0.46 for plain LR and about 0.02 for Naive Bayes (read from charts).

projects.title: Sentiment Analysis on 2024 Election
projects.student_description: Our project applies AI-driven sentiment analysis to U.S. 2024 Election tweets, using a custom override layer to improve classification accuracy. By anonymizing candidate names and detecting negation cues, the model helps uncover deeper sentiment patterns in political discourse.

summary.plain: The team trained several simple text classifiers to label tweets about the 2024 U.S. election as positive, neutral or negative. On a small test set, the models got between 91% and 99% of tweets right, with a Naive Bayes model doing best.
summary.technical: A Kaggle dataset of 2024 U.S. election tweets with pre-assigned positive/neutral/negative labels was used, keeping only tweet text and label. Text was cleaned with regex, tokenized and filtered of high-frequency words; features were NLTK word features for NLTK Naive Bayes and TF-IDF vectors for scikit-learn Naive Bayes, logistic regression and LinearSVC. Models were evaluated with accuracy, F1 and confusion matrices on a test set of 101 tweets. Reported accuracy/F1: NLTK Naive Bayes 99%/0.99, sklearn Naive Bayes 97%/0.96, logistic regression 91%/0.90, LinearSVC 97%/0.97.
summary.question: How accurately can sentiment analysis models trained on historical social media data classify sentiment in tweets about the 2024 US election, and which metrics and deployment strategies are most effective?
summary.problem: Social media sentiment influences public opinion during elections, but tweet data is noisy and biased.
summary.beneficiary: Political campaigns, journalists and public-opinion researchers

projects.title: Sentiment-Based Stock Direction Classifier
projects.student_description: Our project investigates whether Twitter sentiment analysis and certain market features can predict stock price direction for major technology companies.

summary.plain: The team asked whether the mood of tweets about big tech companies can predict if their stock will go up or down the next day. They scored each tweet's mood with a ready-made sentiment tool and trained several models; the best results got roughly 65-86% of days right depending on the stock, using small test sets.
summary.technical: Kaggle's Stock Tweets for Sentiment Analysis and Prediction dataset (tweets plus daily prices) was used; VADER assigned negative/neutral/positive/compound scores to each tweet. Features combined the previous day's VADER compound score with previous-day close, volume, technical indicators and trading-day information to predict next-day direction (up/down), described as a fix for data leakage. An RBF-kernel SVM (accuracy 65-82% per stock), k-nearest neighbors (46-56%) and a 3-hidden-layer neural network (64-32-16) were reported, and random forest and decision trees were also mentioned as tested. Per-stock confusion matrices on roughly 26-50 test days imply accuracies of about 65-86%.

projects.title: SIGN BUDDY
projects.student_description: A bidirectional CNN system that translates ASL alphabet signs to English text and provides visual ASL demonstrations from text input, addressing the critical shortage of qualified ASL instructors affecting deaf children's education. Applied advanced computer vision techniques including transfer learning and performance optimization within a comprehensive machine learning project.

summary.plain: Sign Buddy is a learning app that recognizes American Sign Language alphabet signs from a photo or webcam and turns them into English letters, and can also show the sign for typed text. It got 26 of 28 test pictures right, but only about a quarter to half right on new photos from the internet or a webcam.
summary.technical: The Kaggle ASL Alphabet dataset (87,000+ images, 29 classes including space, delete and nothing) was used. Images were transformed to reduce lighting variance and cropped to the hand before training. A CNN using transfer learning from ResNet-50 was trained in Colab, with training time cut from 7+ hours to 30 minutes by copying data locally and increasing batch size. Evaluation: 26/28 (92.86%) on the dataset's test images, 8/29 (27.59%) on random internet images uploaded to the Streamlit app, and 15/29 (51.72%) via webcam; motion letters (J, Z) and similar signs (V/K) were misclassified.
summary.question: Can a bidirectional CNN system (ASL <-> English) achieve sufficient accuracy in alphabet recognition to be an effective educational tool for children, addressing ASL instructor shortages?
summary.problem: Deaf children face language deprivation partly because few families learn ASL from qualified instructors.
summary.beneficiary: Deaf and hearing children learning the ASL alphabet, and their families

projects.title_slide: Skin Disease Diagnosis Using Computer Vision
projects.student_description: With a dataset of dermatoscopic image lesions, we used convolutional neural networks, ResNet, ViT and EfficientNetB0 to create models to classify the images into 4 categories of diseases, including melanoma.

summary.plain: The team trained computer vision models to look at close-up pictures of skin spots and decide which of four common types they are, including the dangerous skin cancer melanoma. The best model (EfficientNetB0) got about two-thirds of images right and found melanoma much more often than a simple custom network did.
summary.technical: The ISIC 2019 dermatoscopic dataset (25,331 images, nine diagnoses plus age, sex and anatomical-site metadata) was restricted to the top four diagnoses (NV, MEL, BCC, BKL) plus an 'other' class, with train/val/test splits. A custom CNN (images only) was compared with ResNet, ViT and EfficientNetB0 models using images plus metadata. Overfitting in EfficientNetB0 was handled by freezing base layers, fine-tuning at learning rate 1e-5 and early stopping with best-weight restoration. Test accuracy was 0.52 (CNN), 0.67 (ResNet), 0.51 (ViT) and 0.66 (EfficientNetB0); EfficientNetB0 raised melanoma recall from 7% to 43% and BCC F1 from 0.33 to 0.61 versus the CNN.
summary.question: Which supervised model (CNN, ResNet, ViT or EfficientNet) most accurately classifies skin lesions from dermatoscopic images, and how does including patient metadata affect performance?
summary.problem: Manual skin lesion diagnosis is slow, subjective and limited by access to specialists.

projects.title: Skin Lesion Classifier
projects.student_description: Our project combines machine learning and computer vision techniques with two datasets—HAM10000 and the Diverse Dermatology Images dataset—to build and evaluate a fair and reliable skin lesion detector for everyone, regardless of skin tone.

summary.plain: The team trained neural networks to recognize seven kinds of skin spots from photos, aiming for a tool that works fairly for people with all skin tones. Their image models got around 75-82% of test images right, and they also compared several EfficientNet versions on two skin datasets.
summary.technical: HAM10000 (Kaggle) and the Stanford Diverse Dermatology Images (DDI) dataset were used; EDA removed 57 null values and 25 IQR outliers from HAM10000 metadata, and DDI was augmented. An ANN baseline (HAM10000: accuracy 70.99%, precision 72.14%, recall 70.19%) was compared with a CNN (HAM10000: 75.74% / 84.02% / 69.85%; DDI: 81.57% / 88.07% / 78.76%). EfficientNet B0 and B3 were fine-tuned and benchmarked on HAM10000 and ISIC 2019 with accuracy, macro precision/recall/F1, ROC-AUC and training time (HAM10000 B3 adjusted 0.7493 accuracy, B0 0.7428 with ROC-AUC 0.9181; ISIC 2019 B0 0.6088). Per-skin-tone recall analysis and Grad-CAM are listed as next steps.
summary.question: Can existing deep learning architectures be fine-tuned to classify skin lesions with equitable accuracy and recall across light and dark skin tones?
summary.problem: Skin lesion diagnosis is often delayed, and dermatology AI performs worse on darker skin tones due to dataset underrepresentation.
summary.beneficiary: Patients with diverse skin tones and clinicians screening skin lesions
summary.inputs: Dermatoscopic / clinical skin lesion images
summary.outputs: Lesion type (seven classes) or benign/malignant
summary.results: CNN HAM10000 accuracy 75.74%, recall 69.85%; CNN DDI accuracy 81.57%, recall 78.76%; ANN baseline 70.99%; EfficientNet B3 (adjusted) 0.7493 on HAM10000.

projects.title: Sleep Doctor
projects.student_description: Sleep Doctor uses linear regression to predict a person's sleep quality (1–10) from their age, stress, and activity level. We found that stress is the only strong predictor, age and activity had almost no effect, giving an honest, interpretable answer to whether these everyday factors shape sleep.

summary.plain: Sleep Doctor predicts how well someone will sleep from their age, stress level and physical activity. Using a large synthetic dataset, the team found that stress is the only one of these that really matters, and they built a web app that shows which factors pushed a person's predicted score up or down.
summary.technical: A synthetic Kaggle dataset (Sleep Health and Daily Performance; 100,000 records, 32 columns) was used. Two supervised paths took age, stress and physical activity as inputs: linear regression predicting a 1-10 sleep-quality score, and a random forest classifying Low/Medium/High quality. Validation used stratified 70/15/15 splits, 5-fold cross-validation, permutation feature importance, a 44.5% majority-class baseline and a fairness audit across occupation and gender. Both models reached about 61% class accuracy (R² 0.41); an extended model with lifestyle/context factors reached about 68% (R² 0.60). Stress correlated with sleep quality at r = -0.64 while age and steps showed near-zero correlation. A Streamlit app (with Docker) shows per-feature contribution bars.

projects.title: Smart Restaurant Investment Advisor
projects.student_description:
Our initial project idea was a recommendation system for ideal areas to open a restaurant and underserved restaurants in those areas. This tool can be used by small business owners and investors alike to gain insight into where to invest their capital based on existing market data. 

After further discussion and exploration, we realized that our project would not be able to act as a recommendation system, but rather serve as the foundation for one. Predicting the success of a business can feel mostly like guesswork, so we approached our project with the question: What actually determines a restaurant’s success?

summary.plain: The team wanted to know what makes a restaurant successful so investors could choose where to open one. They predicted each restaurant's rating (adjusted so places with few reviews are not over-trusted) from its cuisine and price, and found that being fast food was the strongest signal of lower ratings, though these factors explain only about a quarter of the differences.
summary.technical: A Kaggle restaurant dataset was filtered to businesses tagged 'restaurant'; cuisine categories were one-hot encoded and a 1-4 price tier extracted. The target was a Bayesian-average adjusted rating combining star rating with review count. Linear regression and a random forest regressor were compared against a mean-prediction baseline using RMSE: baseline 0.3783, linear regression 0.3360 (~11.2% reduction), random forest 0.3319 (~12.3% reduction), with R² 0.2303. Random forest feature importances ranked Fast Food (0.256), price (0.065) and Sandwiches (0.045) highest.

projects.title: SmartHome Energy IQ
projects.student_description: SmartHome Energy IQ is a household energy analyzer and optimizer designed to provide clear, actionable insights into daily power consumption. By leveraging machine learning models, it helps users efficiently monitor and optimize their home energy usage.

summary.plain: SmartHome Energy IQ is a web app that helps families understand and cut their home electricity use. It predicts upcoming appliance energy use, flags unusual spikes, and lets users try 'what-if' changes like adjusting the thermostat to see estimated savings. The team found that simply assuming the next reading equals the last one beat their trained models on new data, and they reported this honestly.
summary.technical: The UCI Appliances Energy Prediction dataset (19,735 ten-minute readings from one Belgian home, 28 features) was used. Features included room temperatures/humidity, weather, cyclical time encodings and lag/rolling energy features; validation used a chronological 70/15/15 split and 5-fold time-series cross-validation. A persistence baseline (test R² 0.459, MAE 26.76 Wh) beat a random forest (CV R² ~0.49 but test R² 0.079, MAE 62.56 Wh); XGBoost was also tuned. An Isolation Forest on usage, change and rolling variability flagged 592 of 19,729 readings (3% contamination). An LSTM sequence pipeline (36-step windows, 17 features, MinMax/log1p scaling) was prepared but training is listed as a next step. Models were exported as joblib artifacts and served via a FastAPI app with graceful fallbacks, deployed with Docker on Railway.
summary.question: Can we predict appliance energy use from environmental conditions, automatically detect abnormal usage, and quantify how temperature changes affect total consumption?
summary.problem: Household energy use is expensive and opaque; meter totals hide which habits drive bills and emissions.
summary.beneficiary: Homeowners and households wanting to reduce energy costs
summary.subdomain: Household appliance energy forecasting and anomaly detection
summary.inputs: 10-minute indoor temperature/humidity, outdoor weather, time features and recent appliance energy history
summary.outputs: Short-term energy forecasts, anomaly flags, what-if savings estimates
summary.results: Persistence test R² 0.459 vs random forest 0.079; RF CV R² ~0.49; Isolation Forest flagged 592 anomalies (avg 466 Wh vs 86 Wh normal).

projects.title: Smartphone Addiction Risk Prediction
projects.student_description: Our project uses supervised machine learning to predict smartphone addiction risk based on users' smartphone usage patterns, including screen time, app usage, battery consumption, and data usage. We compared multiple classification models, selected a Random Forest classifier for deployment, and built an interactive Streamlit web application that provides risk predictions, confidence scores, and personalized recommendations.

summary.plain: The team built a web app that guesses how heavily someone uses their smartphone (on a 1-5 scale) from things like screen time, app usage, battery drain and data use. Their tree-based models scored 100% on the test data, which they flagged as suspicious and explained as a sign the dataset is small and its classes are very easy to separate.
summary.technical: The Kaggle Mobile Device Usage and User Behavior dataset (700 users, 11 variables, no missing values, balanced classes) was used with User Behavior Class (1-5) as the target. Inputs were age, gender, device model, OS, app usage time, screen-on time, battery drain, number of apps and data usage. Logistic regression (68.6% accuracy), a decision tree (100%) and a random forest (100%) were compared; cross-validation also gave 1.0 and confusion matrices and feature importance were inspected. The random forest was deployed in a Streamlit app that returns a predicted class, confidence and recommendations.
summary.question: Can machine learning models predict smartphone usage behavior patterns based on a user's device usage habits and demographic information?
summary.problem: Excessive smartphone use is linked to reduced productivity, sleep disruption and attention problems.
summary.beneficiary: Smartphone users and digital-wellness educators
summary.inputs: Demographics, device information and daily usage metrics
summary.outputs: User behavior class 1 (very low) to 5 (very high usage), with confidence
summary.results: Logistic regression 68.6%; decision tree and random forest 100% accuracy; cross-validation 1.0.

projects.student_description: Describing our model which is predicting the energy output for solar panel installations to help governments increase renewable energy.

summary.plain: The team used weather and location data from 12 sites to predict how much power a horizontal solar panel would produce. They compared several regression models and found XGBoost worked best, then built a small web app so people could try the predictor.
summary.technical: A public Kaggle/Mendeley dataset of horizontal photovoltaic power output with weather and location features (Northern Hemisphere sites, 2017-2018) was cleaned by converting date/time fields to numeric values and dropping redundant columns. Linear regression, Ridge, Lasso and XGBoost regression were trained to predict power output (PolyPwr). XGBoost performed best with R-squared about 0.68 (RMSE 16.29, MAE 2.71) versus about 0.47 for the linear models. The model was wrapped in a Streamlit app titled Solar Panel Suitability Predictor. The team earlier tried classification and switched to regression.
summary.question: Using a model trained on 2017-2018 Northern Hemisphere weather data, where in the U.S. would new solar panel projects have the highest energy output?
summary.problem: Companies and policymakers need a simpler way to find locations where large solar projects would produce the most energy.
summary.beneficiary: Governments, policymakers and companies planning solar installations
summary.inputs: Date, time, latitude, longitude, altitude, month, humidity, ambient temperature, wind speed, visibility, pressure, cloud ceiling
summary.outputs: Predicted solar panel power output
summary.results: XGBoost regression R-squared 68.0% (RMSE 16.29, MAE 2.71); linear regression and Ridge R-squared 47.5%, Lasso 46.7%.

projects.title: Solar Energy Yield Predictor
projects.student_description: We created a ML model that predicts solar energy output yield using weather API's and physics.

summary.plain: The team predicted how much electricity a solar power plant would make from weather data. They first used physics formulas to estimate the expected power, then trained a machine learning model to fix the gap between that estimate and what the plant really produced, and built a dashboard to run forecasts.
summary.technical: Kaggle solar plant generation data (22 inverters, one plant, May 15 - Jun 17, 2020) was aggregated to plant level and matched by timestamp with weather sensor data, enriched with wind speed and cloud cover from the Open-Meteo API, giving 3,259 synchronized observations. Physics features were computed (Faiman thermal model for module temperature, PVWatts-style power equations for theoretical AC/DC power, per-kWp normalization, cyclical time encoding), and residual targets were built as actual minus physics-predicted power. An XGBoost regressor learned the residual correction, with physical constraints (non-negative power, efficiency limits). On a hold-out test the gap-correction model reached R-squared 0.8009 and the reconstructed AC output R-squared 0.9642 (MAE 469.4 kW, RMSE 1,191 kW plant level). Feature importances showed irradiation dominates, followed by cyclical time features.
summary.question: Can combining a physics-based solar power baseline with machine learning residual correction give reliable solar output forecasts from weather data?
summary.problem: Weather-driven fluctuations in solar output make grid balancing and energy planning difficult, and traditional methods struggle with nonlinear effects.
summary.beneficiary: Grid operators and solar plant operators
summary.inputs: Irradiation, ambient and module temperature, wind speed, cloud cover, time features, plant capacity
summary.outputs: Forecast plant AC power / energy yield
summary.results: Gap-correction model R-squared 0.8009; final reconstructed AC output R-squared 0.9642; hold-out MAE 0.0199 per kWp and RMSE 0.0476 per kWp.

projects.title: Solar Panel Defect Detection
projects.student_description: Our project uses machine learning to help identify defects in solar panels.

summary.plain: The team trained an image model to look at photos of solar panels and say what is wrong with them, such as dust, snow, bird droppings or damage. Balancing how often each category appeared during training raised accuracy from about 79% to about 95%.
summary.technical: Solar panel images from a public Kaggle dataset in six classes (bird-drop, clean, dusty, snow-covered, electrical damage, physical damage) were used for multi-class classification with a ResNet-18 CNN. Because classes were imbalanced, the team compared simple random sampling with stratified random sampling so minority classes appear in every epoch. Total accuracy was 14.69% for an untrained ResNet-18 baseline, 79.10% with simple random sampling and 95.48% with stratified sampling, with per-class accuracy charts and confusion matrices. Grad-CAM was used to check the model focuses on the panel surface. A Streamlit upload demo classifies a single image.

projects.title: Sounding Out Parkinson’s Disease
projects.student_description: Built an end-to-end pipeline that turns one sustained “ah” sound into a high-accuracy Parkinson’s disease screen, applying feature selection, class balancing, and machine learning modeling skills.

summary.plain: Parkinson's disease often changes a person's voice early on. The team used measurements from recordings of people saying a long 'ah' sound to train models that flag who might have Parkinson's, testing many combinations of feature selection, class balancing and models.
summary.technical: The Sakar et al. (2019) Parkinson's speech dataset (252 individuals: 188 PD, 64 healthy; 3 sustained /a/ recordings each, with baseline, MFCC, wavelet/TQWT and vocal fold features) was aggregated to one row per individual to prevent leakage. Pipelines (imblearn) combined feature selectors (correlation filter, SelectKBest ANOVA/mutual information, RFE, random forest importance, L1-logistic; top 20 features), scaling, samplers (none, SMOTE, SMOTE-ENN) and models (logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost), tuned with GridSearchCV using PD recall as the refit metric. CV ROC-AUC was about 0.83 (LR), 0.86 (RF) and 0.85 (XGBoost), AUPRC 0.94-0.95. The best-recall XGBoost pipeline was retrained and evaluated on held-out test speakers with weighted-utility threshold tuning (threshold 0.79): test ROC AUC 0.812, accuracy 0.83, PD recall 0.87, non-PD recall 0.69. SHAP showed MFCC features dominate.
summary.question: Which supervised learning model best identifies early-stage Parkinson's disease from speech features?
summary.problem: Parkinson's disease is often diagnosed late, yet about 90% of patients show vocal symptoms early.
summary.beneficiary: People at risk of Parkinson's disease and clinicians doing screening
summary.inputs: Acoustic features extracted from sustained /a/ phonation (MFCCs, TQWT, jitter, shimmer, etc.)
summary.outputs: PD vs healthy prediction

projects.title: SoundsLike: Identifying Similar Songs and Emotions from Prompt-Based Queries
projects.title_slide: SoundsLike: Identifying Similar Songs and Emotions from Prompt-Based Queries
projects.student_description: SoundsLike is a music recommendation system that suggests songs based on a user’s textual input, identifying moods, song titles, or artist names.

summary.plain: SoundsLike lets you type something like 'chill songs like Let It Happen' and recommends similar songs. A language model picks out the mood, song and artist from your sentence, and then the system finds songs with the closest audio features such as energy and danceability.
summary.technical: A Kaggle Spotify dataset (500K+ songs with audio features and emotion labels) was reduced to 7 key standardized audio attributes forming song vectors. User prompts are parsed by a DistilBERT token-classification (NER) model trained on token/label examples (B-MOOD, B-SONG, B-ARTIST) to extract mood, song and artist, with optional fuzzy matching; these are mapped into the same feature space and a k-nearest-neighbor search (Euclidean or cosine) returns the top-k songs. The team initially tried K-means clustering and switched to KNN. NER evaluation reported scores of 0.8930, 0.7542, 0.7479 and 0.7511 (precision, recall, accuracy and likely F1). A web demo shows detected entities, recommendations and radar-style feature comparisons.
summary.question: How effective is the K-Nearest Neighbors algorithm at recommending songs with similar style and mood using only Spotify audio features?
summary.problem: Listeners want music matching their mood or vibe without needing exact filters or popularity-driven playlists.
summary.beneficiary: Music listeners
summary.inputs: Natural-language prompt (mood, song title, artist); song audio feature vectors
summary.outputs: Top-k similar song recommendations with detected entities
summary.results: NER scores reported as 0.8930, 0.7542, 0.7479, 0.7511; no quantitative evaluation of recommendation quality.

projects.title: SpeakNoLie
projects.student_description: Our final project explores whether a machine learning model trained on text transcript features can accurately detect deepfake audio. We used the BERT language model to identify patterns that distinguish real (bona-fide) speech from synthetic (spoofed) speech.

summary.plain: SpeakNoLie tries to tell real recordings from AI-generated (deepfake) voice recordings by first turning the audio into text and then checking whether the words themselves give the fake away. The team compared two ways of representing the text and found the BERT language model approach was slightly more accurate (81.5%) than a simpler word-counting approach (78.9%).
summary.technical: Data: 31,000+ .wav clips from the In-the-Wild Audio Deepfake dataset (Kaggle) labeled bona-fide or spoof. Preprocessing: clips were converted to text transcripts (transcription tool not stated). Features: TF-IDF vectors of transcripts vs BERT contextual embeddings, each fed to a feed-forward neural network classifier. Evaluation on an apparent ~6,340-clip hold-out (from confusion matrices): TF-IDF accuracy 0.789, precision 0.790, recall 0.789, F1 0.781; BERT accuracy 0.815, precision 0.813, recall 0.815, F1 0.813. Both models miss many fakes (989 and 701 fake clips predicted as real, respectively).
summary.question: Can a machine learning model trained on text transcript features effectively distinguish between bona-fide and spoofed speech?
summary.problem: Deepfake audio threatens trust in media, security and personal privacy, and detection methods struggle to keep up.

projects.student_description: Using supervised machine learning to predict the success or failure of startups.

summary.plain: The team used real Crunchbase data on tens of thousands of companies to predict whether a startup is still operating or has closed, based on its country, industry and funding. They found the data was very unbalanced, tried a balancing technique, and built a website where users can try the predictor.
summary.technical: A Kaggle Crunchbase startup success/fail dataset (~66k rows, 14 columns) was reduced to status, country, funding rounds/amounts and category, with category frequency encoding and one-hot country codes. A random forest classifier with weighted classes was trained; the initial model reached about 0.89 accuracy but recall of only 0.07 on closed startups. SMOTE-ENN resampling was applied, improving prediction of closed startups (reported as a 134% improvement). A later comparison reported accuracy 0.7393 / weighted F1 0.7090 on the original imbalanced data, 0.6283 / 0.6558 after resampling, and 0.5307 / 0.5936 after resampling with tuned hyperparameters. Random forest feature importances ranked total funding, funding rounds and founding year highest. The model was deployed with a FastAPI backend and React/TypeScript frontend.

projects.title: Stock Market Predictions of S&P 500 companies
projects.title_slide: Stock Market Predictions of S&P 500 companies
projects.student_description: Used multiple models to predict stock prices, comparing them to find the best.

summary.plain: The team tried to predict the next day's closing price of S&P 500 stocks using past prices. They compared four models on a single stock (Apple) and on all stocks together, and found that models did much worse on later, more volatile years and when one model had to cover all 500 companies.
summary.technical: A Kaggle S&P 500 daily stock dataset (2013-2018, >600k rows; open, high, low, close, volume) was cleaned, stock tickers one-hot encoded, highly correlated columns dropped, features scaled, and lag and rolling mean/std features created. Data was split chronologically (60/20/20; train ~2013, validation ~2015, test ~2018). Linear regression, random forest, XGBoost and a CNN-LSTM (10-day window) were trained. On a single stock, test MSE was 3.72 (linear regression), 10.81 (CNN-LSTM), 860.38 (XGBoost) and 877.09 (random forest); across all stocks only XGBoost stayed moderate (test MSE 208.06) while the others exceeded 15,000. The team attributes tree-model failure to extrapolation on unseen price ranges.

summary.beneficiary: Retail investors and policymakers

summary.results: Single stock test MSE: LR 3.72, CNN-LSTM 10.81, XGBoost 860.38, RF 877.09; all stocks test MSE: XGBoost 208.06, others 15,000+.

projects.student_description: This project examines the accuracy of predicting short-term stock price direction using daily financial news headlines. We applied NLP and ML techniques to extract features like sentiment scores & keyword frequency from news, training a supervised XGBoost & FinBert model.

summary.plain: The team checked whether daily news headlines about big tech companies can predict if their stock price goes up or down the next day. They used a finance-trained language model to score how positive or negative each headline is and fed those scores into a classifier that was about 80% accurate.
summary.technical: A Kaggle FAANG stock price dataset was merged with a financial news headlines dataset (S&P 500 companies) by publish date and ticker, filtered to FAANG companies, with headlines lowercased and stripped of punctuation. A next-day PriceUp label was generated. Features were FinBERT sentiment scores (-1 to +1) from a pretrained model, counts of finance keywords, and 3/5/7-day rolling sentiment averages. An XGBoost classifier predicted up/down direction, reaching about 80% accuracy; precision, recall and F1 are mentioned but not reported.

summary.technical: Data: historical daily open/close prices for Apple, Microsoft, Intel and IBM (Kaggle), the S&P 500, and macroeconomic indicators (Federal Funds rate, GDP, unemployment, inflation). EDA covered close-open correlations, 60-day rolling correlations with the Fed Funds rate, 30-day lagged cross-company correlations and correlation with the S&P 500 (e.g. Apple vs S&P 500 r = 0.948). Days were labeled Buy/Hold/Sell from derived return thresholds; 20+ features including rolling and lagged correlations were engineered and class imbalance was addressed. After moving from next-day price regression to classification, an ensemble of Logistic Regression and XGBoost was selected. Reported results: 75% overall accuracy across companies, 92% Apple Buy recall, and a +29% boost in macro-averaged F1; per-class charts show weak Hold performance. The model is served in a Streamlit app linked to a daily-updating dataset.

projects.student_description: Developed a GRU and LSTM model to see which one performs better when analyzing future stock prices.

summary.plain: The team built two kinds of neural networks that read the last 30 days of a stock's prices and guess the next day's opening and closing price. They compared a GRU and an LSTM and found the LSTM was slightly better.
summary.technical: A World Stock Prices CSV was filtered to a single ticker (e.g. AAPL), using Open, High, Low, Close and Volume, sorted by date and Min-Max normalized. 30-day input sequences were built in a custom PyTorch Dataset with an 80/20 train/test split and DataLoader batching. Two models (GRU and LSTM; 2 layers, hidden size 64, 5 inputs, 2 outputs for next-day open and close) were trained with MSE loss and Adam (lr 0.001, 50 epochs, batch 32). Predictions were inverse-transformed and evaluated by MSE and actual-vs-predicted plots; the LSTM had slightly lower MSE, especially in volatile regions, but numbers are not shown.

projects.title: StockLens
projects.student_description: StockLens is a machine learning project that predicts a stock's annual price change using over 200 financial indicators from company 10-K filings, training Linear Regression, Decision Tree, and Random Forest models on 2014 to 2017 data and testing them on a held-out 2018 dataset. Our best model, a Random Forest Regressor, achieved a 32.79% mean absolute error after filtering out volatile penny stocks, showing that real financial fundamentals can give everyday investors a data-driven second opinion on a stock.

summary.plain: StockLens tries to predict how much a company's stock price will change over the next year using over 200 numbers from its annual financial reports. A random forest model did best, though its average error was still about 33 percentage points, and the team built a web app to explore predictions.
summary.technical: The Kaggle '200+ Financial Indicators of US Stocks (2014-2018)' dataset (10-K derived ratios) was used with 2014-2017 for training and 2018 as an unseen holdout. Extreme 12-month returns were trimmed to (-90%, 200%) to remove volatile penny stocks, and missing values and sector imbalance were examined. Linear regression, decision tree and random forest regressors were compared with 5-fold cross-validation MAE and 2018 holdout MAE/RMSE. Random forest performed best (CV MAE 28.20%, holdout MAE 32.79%, RMSE 44.26%) versus linear regression (holdout MAE 34.77%) and decision tree (35.10%). A per-sector MAE bias audit was performed, and a Streamlit app lets users search companies.

projects.title: Student AI Journal
projects.student_description: We created a AI-powered journaling tool for students to support in their mental health.

summary.plain: The team built an AI journaling helper for students. A student writes a journal entry, the tool labels its mood as positive, neutral or negative, and an OpenAI language model writes back a supportive, non-clinical reflection. The team stresses that it is not a replacement for a therapist.
summary.technical: The team generated a synthetic journaling dataset with the OpenAI API (about 1,000 entries labelled positive/neutral/negative, with mood, stress and user-trait fields). Entries pass through a pipeline of sentiment classification followed by a GPT-generated response, written row-by-row to a labelled CSV, with prompt engineering and post-processing rules to reclassify ambiguous entries. Additional generated features include mood summaries, affirmations, weekly insights and grounding exercises, plus a dashboard of sentiment distribution (410 positive, 368 neutral, 225 negative). No accuracy or user-study metrics are reported; evaluation is limited to example outputs and manual review of a sample set.
summary.question: Can an AI journaling assistant improve student well-being through empathetic, bias-aware support without replacing human therapists?
summary.problem: Many students face mental health challenges and do not know where to start with reflective journaling.
summary.beneficiary: Students seeking self-care and emotional reflection support
summary.inputs: Free-text journal entries from students
summary.outputs: Mood/sentiment label (positive, neutral, negative) and an LLM-generated supportive reflection; mood dashboards
summary.results: Produced labelled CSV outputs and example responses; synthetic dataset sentiment distribution 40.9% positive, 36.7% neutral, 22.4% negative. No performance metrics reported.

projects.title: StyleSync
projects.student_description: An AI tool that helps anyone select stylish outfits.

summary.plain: StyleSync tries to suggest clothing items that go well with a piece you already own, to encourage people to re-wear their clothes instead of buying into trends. The team trained an image model to place matching fashion items close together, then used it in a small 'Outfit Completer' upload tool. Their own charts show the model did not yet learn the matches well.
summary.technical: Outfit images with item bounding boxes from a Pinterest-sourced complementary-fashion dataset (called both the 'A100' and 'CTL' dataset) were turned into anchor/positive/negative triplets. A pretrained ResNet-18 was trained with triplet loss to produce 128-dimensional embeddings for deep metric learning, and recommendations come from items close in embedding space. Diagnostics included training/validation loss curves, anchor-positive vs anchor-negative distance histograms and a t-SNE plot. The triplet loss rose across 3 epochs, validation loss rose while training loss fell (overfitting), and t-SNE showed no clustering; the 75% top-1 retrieval target was not reported as met. Hard/semi-hard triplet mining is proposed as the fix.
summary.question: Can a CNN-based deep metric learning model achieve at least 75% top-1 retrieval accuracy for compatible outfit recommendation from a single input item image while promoting sustainable fashion?
summary.problem: Trend-driven clothing purchases contribute to fashion's environmental footprint; people need help pairing clothes they already own.
summary.beneficiary: Consumers wanting to style their existing wardrobe
summary.inputs: A single fashion item image
summary.outputs: Recommended compatible fashion items
summary.results: Triplet loss increased over epochs, validation loss rose (overfitting) and embeddings did not cluster; most anchor-positive distances were smaller than anchor-negative distances with some overlap. No top-1 accuracy reported.

projects.title: Synthetic Sight
projects.student_description: Our project, Synthetic Sight, uses a transfer learning approach with a pre-trained ResNet-50 Convolutional Neural Network to classify 224×224 RGB images as real human faces or StyleGAN-generated synthetic faces. It aims to support digital literacy and human review by serving as a reliable baseline tool for flagging potential AI generated media.

summary.plain: This project trained a computer program to tell whether a face photo is a real person or a fake face made by AI. It reached very high accuracy on a standard test set, and the team built a simple upload app while warning that the tool should help people review images, not act as proof.
summary.technical: The team used the Kaggle '140k Real and Fake Faces' benchmark (real FFHQ faces vs StyleGAN-generated faces), sampling a balanced training set (about 10k per class), a smaller validation set and the locked official 20,000-image test split, with path-overlap checks and a file manifest. Images were resized to 224x224 RGB and augmented with horizontal flips and light colour jitter. An ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 was trained in two stages (frozen backbone head training for epochs 1-3, then layer4 fine-tuning for epochs 4-15), selecting epoch 13 by lowest validation loss and choosing a 0.51 decision threshold on validation only. On the test split it reported 99.69% accuracy, 99.69% fake F1, ROC-AUC 0.99995 and AP 0.99995, with 39 false positives and 23 false negatives, which were inspected visually. A facial lightness (CIE L*) audit compared real vs fake sets, and the model was wrapped in a Streamlit app and FastAPI inference endpoint.
summary.question: Can a CNN classifier distinguish real human faces from StyleGAN-generated synthetic faces well enough to help flag possible misinformation?
summary.problem: Humans are near chance at telling AI-generated faces from real ones, enabling misinformation.
summary.beneficiary: People and reviewers assessing whether online face images are authentic (digital literacy)
summary.inputs: Face images (224x224 RGB)
summary.outputs: Probability the image is synthetic and a real/fake label with caution text
summary.results: Test accuracy 99.69%, fake F1 99.69%, ROC-AUC 0.99995, 39 FP and 23 FN on 20,000 test images; authors caution results may not generalize to other generators.

projects.title: Tackling the "Taboo": An ML Solution for Foods That Break Traditional T1D Therapy
projects.title_slide: TACKLING THE "TABOO": An ML Solution for Foods That Break Traditional T1D Therapy
projects.student_description: Standard Type 1 Diabetes dosing fails on complex meals because it myopically focuses on carbohydrates; this project shifts the paradigm by training a machine learning 'wrapper' to analyze the critical, overlooked impact of fat, protein, and fiber. By accurately classifying 'taboo' foods as high-risk before insulin delivery, the model serves as a predictive safety net for stable blood sugar where current treatments—whether manual or automated—consistently fall short.

summary.plain: People with Type 1 diabetes usually dose insulin by counting carbs, but fat, protein and fibre also change blood sugar. This project trained a model to flag meals as high or low risk using all of these nutrients. Because the patient data had no real high-blood-sugar failures, the risk labels had to be simulated, which the student openly calls a proof of concept.
summary.technical: Data came from a 16-person UK Type 1 diabetes dataset of self-reported food logs and injection (MDI) insulin records. Because the cohort showed no natural high-risk events (>180 mg/dL), a binary 'artificial label' was programmed from total meal mass. Twelve features were built, including carbs, fat, protein, fibre, fat/protein-to-carb ratios (FCR, PCR), insulin on board and sine/cosine time-of-day encodings. A Random Forest classifier was trained with K-fold cross-validation; feature importances showed total_mass and carbs dominating. The student reports 100% recall, explicitly labelled a proof of concept rather than clinical truth.
summary.question: To what extent can a machine learning 'wrapper' utilizing fat, protein, and fiber overcome the myopic focus on carbohydrates in standard therapy to serve as a predictive safety net where current Type 1 Diabetes treatments consistently fall short?
summary.problem: Standard T1D insulin dosing focuses on carbohydrates and fails for high-fat/high-protein ('taboo') meals.

projects.title: Tax Burden Equity Analyzer
projects.student_description: Our project tries to figure out which pre-tax characteristics drive differences in effective federal tax rate between filers using machine learning.

summary.plain: People with the same income can pay very different federal tax rates. This project trained a model on U.S. survey data to predict a filer's effective tax rate, explain which traits pushed it up or down, and test 'what if' twins who differ in just one trait, such as earning from investments instead of wages.
summary.technical: IPUMS CPS ASEC 2024 (income year 2023) person records (64,696 rows, 59 columns) were collapsed into 61,231 filer units after dropping dependent filers; whole-return income (unit_inctot) was rebuilt by recovering a missing spouse's income as a family residual, raising correlation with AGI from 0.815 to 0.983. The target is effective rate = federal income tax after credits / AGI (can be negative), with 16 features (income, income-mix shares, filing status, age, dependents, household, state) and an 80/20 fixed-seed split frozen before modelling. A 500-tree Random Forest regressor reached test R² 0.900 and MAE 1.28 points (train R² 0.970, OOB R² 0.909) and was compared against IRS SOI published rates by income band. SHAP gave per-filer and global explanations, and counterfactual 'twin tests' flipping one attribute found median -2.35 points for wages→investments, -4.85 points for single→joint, and ≈0 for adding dependents.
summary.question: Which pre-tax characteristics drive differences in effective federal tax rate between filers, and how much of the gap between two economically similar people is attributable to a single attribute?
summary.problem: Filers with similar incomes face very different effective federal tax rates, and the drivers are not transparent.
summary.beneficiary: Policy analysts and the public interested in tax equity
summary.subdomain: Effective federal income tax rate equity analysis
summary.inputs: Pre-tax filer characteristics: income, income mix, filing status, age, dependents, household size, state
summary.outputs: Predicted effective federal tax rate with SHAP breakdown and single-attribute counterfactual differences
summary.results: Test R² 0.900, MAE 1.28 percentage points; predicted 5.5% vs IRS 6.1% in the $50k-$75k band; twin tests: wages→investments median -2.35 points, single→joint median -4.85 points, dependents ≈0.

projects.title: Telco Churn Predictor
projects.student_description: Our Telco Customer Churn Prediction project is a machine learning project which predicts which telecom customers are likely to churn. This is important because customer churn is a major cost for any subscription-based businesses. A company will lose on recurring revenue and the expense in obtaining that customer. Therefore, being able to flag customers that are likely to leave will allow the company to try retaining them before they completely cancel.

summary.plain: Telecom companies lose money when customers cancel. This team used a public dataset of about 7,000 telecom customers to train models that flag who is likely to leave, and found XGBoost caught the most leavers. They also built a Streamlit demo and looked at whether the model might unfairly stereotype senior customers.
summary.technical: The Kaggle Telco Customer Churn dataset (~7,000 customers, 20+ attributes such as contract type, tenure, monthly charges and payment method) was split 75/25 into training and test sets (1,750 test customers). EDA showed month-to-month customers churn far more (75% vs 13% and 3% for one- and two-year contracts) and seniors churn more across subgroups. Logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost were compared on recall, average precision and ROC-AUC: XGBoost achieved recall 85.3%, AP 0.63 and ROC-AUC 0.83 versus 53%/0.60/0.82 (logistic) and 45%/0.57/0.81 (random forest). The model was deployed as a Streamlit app.

summary.beneficiary: Telecom and subscription businesses seeking to retain customers

summary.outputs: Churn prediction / risk
summary.results: XGBoost: recall 85.3%, average precision 0.63, ROC-AUC 0.83 on 1,750 test customers, outperforming logistic regression and random forest on recall.

projects.title_slide: The Signal and the Noise: Measuring Market
projects.student_description: Can StockTwits sentiment and market data predict next-day stock direction?

summary.plain: This team tested whether the mood of posts on StockTwits (a social network for stock traders) can predict whether a stock goes up the next day. Their models did no better than always guessing 'up', so crowd sentiment was mostly noise. Grouping trading days showed that on the loudest hype or panic days, the next day tended to move slightly the other way.
summary.technical: About 4.2 million StockTwits posts (2020-2022; 2.1 million with self-tagged Bullish/Bearish labels) were filtered to AAPL, AMZN, NVDA and TSLA, rolled up into daily sentiment features (bullish/bearish ratios, post volume) and merged with Kaggle World Stock Prices market features (daily return, volume change, price range, volatility), keeping 3,936 ticker-days with actual post activity. Logistic regression and random forest predicted next-day up/down using a chronological 80/20 split and were compared with a majority baseline: accuracy 0.506 and 0.526 vs baseline 0.536, ROC-AUC ~0.50. Feature importances showed market features (~0.14 each) dominating sentiment (~0.02-0.03). K-Means (k=5, chosen by elbow and silhouette 0.330) on standardized sentiment/market features, with next-day return deliberately excluded to avoid leakage, found 'loud hype' days averaged -0.27% and 'loud panic' days +0.81% next-day returns.
summary.question: Can StockTwits sentiment and market data predict next-day stock direction?
summary.problem: Young retail investors increasingly rely on social media for investment decisions, but it is unclear whether crowd sentiment carries predictive signal.
summary.beneficiary: Retail investors and students studying social-media-driven investing
summary.subdomain: Social sentiment and stock direction prediction
summary.inputs: Daily market features and aggregated StockTwits sentiment features per ticker
summary.outputs: Next-day up/down prediction; trading-day cluster labels
summary.results: Neither model beat the 53.6% majority baseline (LR 0.506, RF 0.526 accuracy; ROC-AUC ~0.50). K-Means found small contrarian next-day moves after extreme hype (-0.27%) and panic (+0.81%) days.

projects.title: Training Models to Recognize ABCD Criteria for Early Diagnosis of Melanoma
projects.title_slide: TRAINING MODELS TO RECOGNIZE ABCD CRITERIA FOR EARLY DIAGNOSIS OF MELANOMA
projects.student_description: We are training a combined CNN model on ABCD features which are used to diagnose melanoma for accuracy and early detection as well as deployment to Streamlit.

summary.plain: This team tried to spot melanoma (a dangerous skin cancer) in photos using the ABCD warning signs: asymmetry, border, colour and diameter. They compared an image model, a model built on measured ABCD features, and a combination of both; the combined model did best on their small test set. They also built a Streamlit app for education, not medical advice.
summary.technical: A 1,000-image dataset combined 500 melanoma images from the Kaggle Skin Cancer dataset with 500 healthy-skin images produced from ~60 photos the team took, expanded with Albumentations (flips, brightness/contrast, noise, blur). Data were split 70/15/15. Lesions were segmented with Gaussian blur and Otsu thresholding to compute 17 ABCD features (asymmetry, border roughness, colour statistics, diameter). Three models were trained: an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 image model, a neural model on ABCD features, and a fusion model combining CNN image features with ABCD features. On 150 test images, test accuracy/AUC were 0.513/0.795 (CNN, which predicted every image benign), 0.800/0.890 (ABCD) and 0.880/0.951 (combined). Deployment to Streamlit Cloud ran into TensorFlow/Keras version issues.
summary.question: How well can a CNN model trained on ABCD visual criteria detect early signs of melanoma?
summary.problem: Melanoma is deadly but highly survivable when detected early; dermatology ML datasets lack skin-tone diversity.
summary.beneficiary: People screening for skin cancer, especially in underserved regions
summary.inputs: Skin lesion / skin images and derived ABCD features
summary.outputs: Benign vs malignant (melanoma) prediction
summary.results: Combined model test accuracy 0.880, AUC 0.951; ABCD model 0.800/0.890; CNN-only 0.513/0.795 (all predicted benign).

projects.title: Trust Cues and Online Product Popularity
projects.title_slide: Trust Cues and Online Product Popularity
projects.student_description: Our project uses machine learning to analyze 37K+ Amazon product listings and identify which trust cues such as reviews, ratings, discounts, and badge, most accurately predict high purchase volume. By comparing genuine consumer trust signals to platform-driven visibility cues, we built a predictive model and generated insights into what actually drives product popularity.

summary.plain: This team asked which 'trust signals' on Amazon, such as review counts, star ratings, discounts and badges like Best Seller, best predict whether a product sells a lot. Using about 37,700 products, they trained models to label products as high or low purchase volume and found review count and rating mattered most.
summary.technical: The Kaggle 'Amazon Products Sales Dataset (42K items, 2025)' was cleaned to 37,718 products x 47 features by dropping duplicates and rows missing title, rating or discounted price. Engineered features included a brand popularity (frequency) score, low/medium/high price tiers and a composite trust_score from review metrics. The binary target high_purchase marks products at or above the median purchase volume (~898). A scikit-learn pipeline (median imputation + scaling for numeric, most-frequent imputation + one-hot for categorical) with an 80/20 split was used to test Random Forest and Gradient Boosting classifiers; Random Forest was best at 96.05% accuracy. Feature importances ranked total reviews and product rating highest, then price/discount signals, then badges, sponsored tags and category.
summary.question: Which trust cues are the strongest predictors of high purchase?
summary.problem: Shoppers rely on ratings, reviews and badges, but it is unclear which cues actually signal product performance versus manipulated visibility.
summary.beneficiary: Online shoppers and sellers
summary.subdomain: Product popularity and trust signals on Amazon
summary.inputs: Product listing features: reviews, ratings, prices, discounts, badges, sponsored tags, category
summary.outputs: High vs low purchase volume prediction and feature importances
summary.results: Random Forest accuracy 96.05%; total reviews and product rating were the strongest predictors.

projects.title: TrustFall
projects.student_description: TrustFall is a machine learning project that uses wearable sensor and vital sign data to distinguish normal movement from near-fall and fall events in older adults, aiming to shift elder care from reactive emergency response toward proactive, early intervention. Using three datasets and models including Logistic Regression, Decision Trees, and K-Means Clustering, the project demonstrates how sensor-based fall-risk prediction could help caregivers catch mobility decline before a crisis occurs.

summary.plain: TrustFall explores whether wearable sensor and vital-sign data can tell normal movement apart from near-falls and falls in older adults, so families and caregivers can step in earlier. The team used three datasets, found that a perfect score on one dataset meant the data was fake, and fixed a model that missed elderly people's falls by giving those cases more weight.
summary.technical: Three datasets were used: a simulated 'Diagnostic' (cStick) dataset pairing vitals (distance, HRV, blood sugar, SpO2) with normal/near-fall/fall labels; SisFall, real motion sensor data from 38 younger and older adults with simulated falls; and HAR70+, accelerometer recordings from 18 older adults. Logistic regression served as a baseline, decision trees were chosen for SisFall based on real-fall recall, and K-Means (k=3) clustered unlabelled HAR70+ movement windows. The cStick model hit 100% accuracy, which the team traced to non-overlapping synthetic class ranges; SisFall reached 93% overall accuracy and 92% fall recall, and reweighting under-represented elderly falls raised elderly fall recall from 58% to 79% across 5-fold cross-validation. HAR70+ clusters matched sedentary, moderate and vigorous activity. A Streamlit app takes manually entered values and returns a fall-risk prediction with the decision-tree path as reasoning.
summary.question: Can wearable sensor data and vital sign measurements be used to distinguish normal movement from near-fall and fall events in older adults?
summary.problem: Falls are a leading cause of injury for older adults, and current systems react only after a fall happens.

projects.title: Uncovering Hidden Archaeological Sites in the Amazon Rainforest
projects.title_slide: Uncovering Hidden Archaeological Sites in the Amazon Rainforest
projects.student_description: Our project used an autoencoder and computer vision model to try and find hidden archaelogical sites in the Southwest moist Amazon forest region.

summary.plain: This team searched for hidden archaeological sites under the Amazon rainforest using elevation data from space. They downloaded terrain maps from Google Earth Engine, prepared them, and ran an image model and an anomaly-finding model over 25 map tiles. In the end, no tiles were flagged as containing likely sites.
summary.technical: SRTM elevation data (USGS/SRTMGL1_003, ~90 m/pixel) for the Southwest Amazon moist forests ecoregion were exported from Google Earth Engine via Python as 25 GeoTIFF tiles (5x5 grid). Rasterio was used to mask nodata; tiles were resized to 100x100, normalised to 0-1, banded by elevation, and augmented with slope and hillshade features. A modular pipeline (data acquisition, terrain processing, feature detection, model training) trained a supervised CNN and an unsupervised autoencoder. Dashboards report CNN precision/recall/F1 of 1.000 and autoencoder precision 1.000, recall 0.800, F1 0.889, but 0 of 25 tiles were found to contain features or high-potential sites.

summary.problem: Archaeological sites in the Amazon are hidden under dense canopy, making them hard to find and protect.
summary.beneficiary: Archaeologists, conservation groups and Indigenous communities
