projects.title: Using ML To Classify Bias in News Articles
projects.title_slide: USING ML TO CLASSIFY BIAS IN NEWS ARTICLES
projects.student_description: Investigates how machine learning can automatically classify political bias (left, center, right) in news articles to promote transparency.

summary.plain: The team built a program that reads a news article and guesses whether it leans left, center, or right politically. They tried several text classifiers and combinations of them, and the best ones were right about half the time.
summary.technical: News articles labeled left/center/right (roughly 16-17k articles, with left over-represented per the class-distribution chart) were converted to TF-IDF feature vectors. Logistic Regression and Linear SVM were trained, then combined via hard voting, soft voting, stacking (logistic-regression and decision-tree meta-learners) and a weighted ensemble. Models were compared on accuracy, precision, recall and F1, with confusion matrices for LR and SVM. Stacking with an LR meta-learner had the highest accuracy (0.5114) and Logistic Regression the highest F1 (0.485); Linear SVM was weakest (0.4745 accuracy).
summary.question: How effectively can machine learning classify news articles as left, center, or right, and what is its potential to help users identify bias and promote transparency in news consumption?
summary.problem: Readers often cannot tell where a news article falls on the political spectrum, which contributes to polarization.

projects.student_description: Using Spotify’s audio features to build a model that predicts mood of songs and improve personalized, emotionally-aware music recommendation systems.

summary.plain: The team grouped songs by how they sound (happiness, energy, danceability, acoustic sound and tempo) to find mood groups like 'happy and energetic' or 'sad and calm'. They then used simple rules to give each group a mood name that a music app could use to recommend songs.
summary.technical: Spotify audio features (valence, energy, danceability, acousticness, tempo) from the Kaggle Spotify Tracks dataset were clustered with K-Means, with k chosen via the elbow method (4 clusters shown). Cluster centers were interpreted and a threshold-based rule system (e.g., valence > 0.5 = Happy, energy > 0.7 = Energetic, tempo > 120 = Fast Tempo) generated mood names for each cluster. Clustering quality was measured with silhouette score on train and test splits (~0.22 each).

projects.title: Video Game Recommender
projects.student_description: Built an interactive recommendation system using machine learning and natural language processing to suggest video games based on user preferences. Integrated sentiment analysis and a logistic regression model to predict game likability.

summary.plain: The team built a video game recommender that suggests games similar to what a user likes, based on genre and game descriptions. It also looks at whether player reviews sound positive and uses a simple model to guess whether a user would like a game.
summary.technical: Game metadata (titles, genres, teams, summaries, user reviews) from Kaggle's Popular Video Games 1980-2023 dataset was cleaned (HTML parsing, text normalization). Genres were binary-encoded and summaries turned into 300-dimensional TF-IDF vectors; cosine similarity ranks content-similar games. VADER sentiment scores of user reviews feed a logistic regression model that predicts like probability, combined with similarity in a hybrid score. The logistic regression reported ROC AUC 0.70; the confusion matrix (p6) shows 266 likes and 30 dislikes predicted as 'like' and only 4 dislikes correctly identified.

projects.title: Wastewater Outbreak Prediction
projects.student_description: Our final project dealt with predicting wastewater outbreak prediction based on the surge in hospital admissions. We used XGBoost as our model because it was the best pick for our model based on our model evaluation results.

summary.plain: The team used levels of the COVID-19 virus measured in sewage to predict whether hospital admissions in a U.S. state would surge the following week. Their best model catches some surges far better than guessing, and they explain clearly why plain accuracy is misleading and where the data can be biased.
summary.technical: CDC wastewater SARS-CoV-2 concentration data were aggregated to state-weeks and joined with CDC/NHSN weekly hospital respiratory data on state and Saturday-ending epiweek (10,195 rows, 52 jurisdictions), after fixing a week-alignment bug and dropping the voluntary-reporting window. Seventeen features were built, including site-normalized concentration z-scores, 1-3 week lags, week-over-week deltas, rolling means, coverage and seasonality; the target is a custom surge label (>10% rise and above the state median). A majority-class baseline, Logistic Regression (class_weight balanced), Random Forest and XGBoost were trained with a time-based split and evaluated on a 2022+ hold-out (2,269 state-weeks, 88 surges). XGBoost was shipped: accuracy 0.958, recall 0.227, precision 0.426, F1 0.296, PR-AUC ~0.30 vs a 0.039 floor, ROC-AUC 0.871. SHAP analysis showed the normalized wastewater signal outranks raw concentration and exposed confounding from data-quality features and a miscomputed admissions-per-100k feature; a dashboard app was deployed.
summary.question: Can rising SARS-CoV-2 concentrations in wastewater predict a COVID-19 hospital-admission surge in the following week?
summary.problem: Public health officials and hospitals need earlier warning of COVID-19 hospital surges than individual testing provides.

projects.title: Water Quality Prediction Using Machine Learning
projects.title_slide: Water Quality Prediction Using Machine Learning
projects.student_description: This project looks at water-quality data from public sources and uses it to estimate the Water Quality Index for different ZIP codes. It helps people see current conditions and how their local water quality may shift over time.

summary.plain: The team built a web app where you type a U.S. ZIP code and it pulls real government water measurements, calculates a water quality score, and predicts whether the water looks safe. They also tested it on lead-crisis scenarios like Flint and found it wrongly called that water safe, because the score it learned from ignores lead.
summary.technical: Random Forest classifier and regressor were trained on ~2,900 samples (1991-2017, mostly European sites) from a Kaggle water quality dataset using 18 features: raw pH, dissolved oxygen, temperature, nitrate and conductance plus temporal, derived (pH deviation, DO/temp ratio), interaction and binned features. Targets are the NSF Water Quality Index (0-100) and a SAFE/UNSAFE label (WQI >= 70). On the test set the classifier reported 98.27% accuracy, 98.47% F1, 99.82% ROC-AUC and Brier 0.0141; the regressor R^2 0.9676, MAE 1.67, RMSE 5.09, all with 95% CIs. SHAP explains predictions. A Streamlit Cloud app geocodes a ZIP (pgeocode), queries USGS and Water Quality Portal APIs for live data, computes WQI and predicts; a stress test on 6 Flint/Jackson lead scenarios produced a 100% false negative rate.
summary.question: How can we use real-world water quality data to support awareness about drinking-water safety, while being honest about uncertainty and bias?
summary.problem: Government water quality data is fragmented and hard for the public to interpret.
summary.beneficiary: Members of the public and communities concerned about local water quality
summary.subdomain: Water Quality Index estimation from monitoring data
summary.inputs: US ZIP code; water parameters (pH, DO, temperature, turbidity, nitrate, conductance) from USGS/WQP
summary.outputs: Predicted WQI score (0-100), SAFE/UNSAFE label, SHAP explanations
summary.results: Classifier accuracy 98.27%, F1 98.47%, ROC-AUC 99.82%; regressor R^2 0.9676, MAE 1.67; 100% false negative rate on lead-contamination scenarios.

projects.title: Wealth of Nutrition & Body
projects.student_description: Identifying current project-defined metabolic-health status and translating observed gaps into safe, practical guidance.

summary.plain: The team used a large U.S. national health survey to estimate whether an adult currently meets a project-defined metabolic-health warning label (based on waist, blood pressure, blood fats and blood sugar). They found that diet and behavior answers alone predicted this only moderately, while body measurements helped a lot, and they built a prototype that gives at most two safe, guideline-based suggestions or says 'inconclusive' when it lacks information.
summary.technical: NHANES 2013-2018 adults (17,057 cleaned; 9,478 final development participants) were labeled positive when at least 3 of 5 metabolic-syndrome components were positive, using HbA1c as a glucose proxy, with logic-based recovery of rows with missing components. An expanded behavior-only Random Forest (23 features) reached development OOF AUC 0.676 and locked historical test AUC 0.654; a food-pattern ablation gave ΔAUC -0.0013 (95% CI -0.0066 to 0.0038). K-means (k = 3) was used exploratorily to profile demographic context. The final tiered Risk Engine uses logistic regression with fold-safe preprocessing and calibration per information tier, outputting qualitative bands or 'Inconclusive'. Evaluated once on the untouched NHANES 2011-2012 cycle: R3 (body-supported) ROC-AUC 0.850 (95% CI 0.838-0.862) and R4-D3 (measurement-supported) 0.896 (0.882-0.909); R1/R2 remained inconclusive. A rule-based recommendation engine combines observed gaps, safety checks, official guidance and RF support in a local Streamlit prototype.

projects.title: County Clustering for Recognizing Vulnerability
projects.title_slide: What Kind of Place Is Your County?
projects.student_description: Our projects aims to find how different counties are vulnerable and what are the primary factors driving this.

summary.plain: The team grouped all 3,128 U.S. counties into four types (like 'rural hardship' or 'costly big metros') based on measures of social vulnerability and how well poor kids do economically as adults. They then checked whether the groups were meaningful, tested what happened when race and language measures were removed, and showed the same measures can predict upward mobility fairly well.
summary.technical: CDC Social Vulnerability Index (16 measures), Opportunity Atlas upward mobility and the NCHS urban-rural code were joined on county FIPS (3,128 counties). K-Means with k = 4 was run on 17 standardized features, with k chosen by inspecting elbow, silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz and Davies-Bouldin curves; clusters were named as place types and shown on a county map. An ablation removing minority and limited-English features gave silhouette 0.155 vs 0.156 and Adjusted Rand Index 0.735. A Random Forest regressor (80/20 split) predicted upward mobility from the 16 SVI measures with R^2 0.600, MAE 0.0281, RMSE 0.0394, vs linear regression R^2 0.503; residuals were analyzed by cluster (e.g., 61% of immigrant-gateway counties above prediction).
summary.question: Can grouping counties by data reveal real, distinct types of vulnerability and upward mobility that can be explained in plain language?
summary.problem: The CDC SVI collapses four dimensions of hardship into one rank, hiding what kind of support a county needs.
summary.beneficiary: Local planners and policymakers
summary.inputs: County-level SVI measures, upward mobility and urban-rural code
summary.outputs: One of four county-type labels; predicted upward mobility
summary.results: Four county types; silhouette ~0.155; race/language ablation ARI 0.735; RF upward-mobility R^2 0.600 vs linear regression 0.503.

projects.title: Will Your Video Hit or Flop?
projects.title_slide: Will Your Video Hit or Flop?
projects.student_description: The "Will Your Video Hit or Flop?" project is a machine learning application that predicts a YouTube video's success relative to historically trending content using 37 pre-publish and early-performance metadata features. By leveraging a Random Forest model trained on a dataset of 6,668 Trending videos, it generates a 0-100 hit score to give creators a data-backed reality check on their video's potential.

summary.plain: The team built a website where a YouTube creator enters details about a video and gets a 0-100 'hit score' comparing it to thousands of videos that made YouTube Trending. It also predicts views, likes and comments and explains what is driving the score, while warning that it shows patterns, not guarantees.
summary.technical: 6,668 Trending videos from a Kaggle YouTube Trending dataset were described by 37 metadata features across 8 categories (pre-publish and early-performance, including channel authority). Random Forest models predict log-scale views, likes and comments (R^2 up to 0.691 for views, ~0.57 likes, ~0.55 comments per the chart) and a hit/flop classifier (AUC 0.849, accuracy 80.5%, Brier 0.133); linear regression is the interpretable baseline for engagement rate (R^2 0.263). The time-dependent feature hours_since_publish was reframed as a user-selected 'predict at' horizon (24h/48h/7-day) to avoid misuse. The models are served via a FastAPI backend with a deployed web frontend that includes a 'what's driving this' breakdown.
summary.question: Can AI accurately predict a video's trending potential using only its metadata, before it's published?
summary.problem: Creators lack a data-backed sense of how a video is likely to perform before publishing.
summary.beneficiary: YouTube content creators
summary.inputs: 37 video and channel metadata features plus a prediction horizon
summary.outputs: 0-100 hit score, hit/flop classification, predicted views/likes/comments, engagement-rate explanation
summary.results: Hit classifier AUC 0.849, accuracy 80.5%, Brier 0.133; views RF R^2 up to 0.691; engagement-rate LR R^2 0.263.

projects.title: X-IDS: Explainable Network Intrusion Detection Systems
projects.title_slide: X-IDS: Explainable Network Intrusion Detection Systems
projects.student_description: X-IDS, an Explainable Network Intrusion Detection System designed to reduce alert fatigue in Security Operations Centers. This project combines XGBoost machine learning with SHAP explainability to help cybersecurity analysts work smarter, not harder.

summary.plain: The team built a system that flags malicious network traffic and explains why each alert was raised, so security analysts can check alerts faster. Using a well-known intrusion dataset, their tuned model caught almost all attacks with very few false alarms.
summary.technical: The CICIDS2017 dataset (2.8M network flow records, 15 attack types, 79 features) was cleaned, reduced from 79 to 30 features via correlation analysis and domain knowledge, standardized, and split 80/20 (2.26M/565K) for binary benign-vs-attack classification; class imbalance (80/20) was handled with XGBoost scale_pos_weight. Random Forest (98.34% accuracy, 1.21% FPR, 142 s training) was compared with XGBoost (99.50%, 0.48% FPR, 35 s). Learning-rate tuning (0.01/0.10/0.30 shown) gave a final XGBoost with 99.67% accuracy, 98.61% precision, 99.70% recall, 0.34% FPR, and ROC-AUC reported as 0.9997-0.9999. SHAP global importance and summary plots show packet-length, port and inter-arrival-time features driving predictions, with no single feature dominating.
summary.question: Can an explainable ML intrusion detection system reduce alert fatigue for Security Operations Center analysts?
summary.problem: SOCs receive 10,000+ alerts daily and manual triage leads to alert fatigue and missed threats.
summary.beneficiary: Security Operations Center analysts

summary.outputs: Benign/attack prediction with SHAP feature explanations
summary.results: Final XGBoost: accuracy 99.67%, precision 98.61%, recall 99.70%, FPR 0.34%; ROC-AUC ~0.9997.

projects.title: Youth ESG Financial Assistant
projects.student_description: Our goal in this project was to develop an ethical and accessible machine learning–based financial assistant that provides personalized stock and bond investment recommendations to college-aged investors (ages 18–22). These recommendations integrate both financial performance and the user’s ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance) preferences, empowering young investors to make informed, values-aligned investment decisions early in their financial journeys.

summary.plain: The team built an assistant that asks young investors (ages 18-22) a short quiz about how much risk they can handle and which environmental, social and governance issues they care about, then suggests stocks and bonds. They grouped stocks and bonds by risk and return using clustering so the quiz answers can be matched to a group.
summary.technical: Data were assembled from yfinance (real-time stock data), a Kaggle Public Company ESG Ratings dataset, World Bank country ESG data, Trading Economics country credit ratings and FRED 10-year government bond yields for 23 countries; ESG scores were disaggregated into E, S and G components. A Gaussian Mixture Model clustered 588 stocks on beta and performance, with k = 5 chosen via BIC/AIC; K-Means clustered bonds on credit rating and 6-month performance, with k = 2 chosen via elbow and silhouette. A quiz-style survey of ESG preferences and risk aversion maps users to clusters for recommendations. No recommendation-quality evaluation is reported.
summary.question: How can we develop a machine learning model that provides personalized stock and bond investment recommendations for young investors based on both financial performance and individual ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) preferences?
summary.problem: Young investors lack know-how about financial instruments, creating a barrier to starting investing early.
summary.beneficiary: College-aged investors (ages 18-22)
summary.inputs: User quiz answers on ESG preferences and risk aversion; stock beta/performance, ESG components, bond yields and country credit ratings
summary.outputs: Personalized stock and bond recommendations from matched clusters
summary.results: 5 stock clusters (GMM, 588 companies) and 2 bond clusters (K-Means); no accuracy-style evaluation reported.

Project Description.evidence: p2: Describes barrier to entry for young investors and personalized stock/bond recommendations using risk and ESG survey. | p3: Research question on ML model for personalized recommendations based on financial performance and ESG preferences. | p4: Project Evolution: newer data sources, removed stocks/bonds without sufficient data, disaggregated ESG scores to differentiate identical composites, added GMM for stocks.

Algorithm.rationale: Names GMM and K-Means, both labeled unsupervised, with inputs, outputs, and pros/cons (p7). Relates algorithms to data by choosing k via BIC/AIC for stocks and elbow/silhouette for bonds (p8-9) and explaining soft assignments for nuanced stock clustering (p4). No technical errors observed.
Algorithm.evidence: p7: GMM: unsupervised, input stock beta and performance, output cluster number, pro soft assignments, con can model noise. K-Means: unsupervised, input bond performance and credit rating, output cluster, pros quick/interpretable, con outliers. | p8: k=5 chosen for stocks using BIC/AIC. | p9: k=2 chosen for bonds using elbow and silhouette. | p6: Survey results map users to cluster-based recommendations.

Essential Question.rationale: Answers the essential question (p11) addressing both amplification and mitigation, human-in-the-loop decisions, supported by specific bias sources (p10) and positive/negative impacts including greenwashing (p12). Reflects complexity and project-grounded reflection; going well beyond program content cannot be judged.
Essential Question.evidence: p11: Clustering may amplify bias from data sourcing but mitigate subjectivity; users make final decisions. | p10: Sources of bias: stock selection, ESG rating inconsistency, recency, geographic/economic development bias. | p12: Positive: reduces barriers, personalization, ESG. Negative: limited data, greenwashing risk, future may not reflect history.

Next Steps.rationale: Three well-thought-out next steps (expand stock/bond pool, add CDs or mutual funds, reinforcement learning for adaptive personalization), each with a tentative deadline (p15). Steps are concrete and verifiable, though not quantified, so borderline 4/5.
Next Steps.evidence: p15: Expand stocks and bonds (deadline 10/01/2025); add CDs or mutual funds (10/01/2025); reinforcement learning from user behavior (09/10/2025).

Citations.rationale: Fourteen distinct topic-related citations: five dataset sources (yfinance, Trading Economics, World Bank ESG, FRED, Kaggle ESG ratings) on p16 and nine background sources on ESG, bonds, investing by age and clustering on p17. Data sources clearly included.
Citations.evidence: p16: Datasets: yfinance (PyPI), Trading Economics credit ratings, World Bank ESG DataBank, FRED bond yields, Kaggle public company ESG ratings. | p17: Sources: NerdWallet ESG, GeeksforGeeks clustering, scikit-learn clustering comparison, Sustainalytics country risk, Fidelity bond ratings, U.S. Bank strategies by age, IBM K-means, Schwab allocation by age, Medium K-means high-dimensional.

algorithmic_complexity.rationale: Two clustering methods (GMM and K-Means) applied to different asset classes, with GMM a probabilistic model (p7).

data_processing.rationale: Fusion of five sources (yfinance, Kaggle ESG, World Bank, Trading Economics, FRED) with ESG disaggregation (p4, p5).

methodological_breadth.rationale: Two integrated components: clustering of stocks/bonds and survey-based preference mapping (p6, p7).

validation_rigor.rationale: Only cluster-number selection (BIC/AIC, elbow, silhouette); no evaluation of recommendations (p8, p9).

engineering.rationale: Live API data requests and a live demo slide suggest an interactive assistant, though not shown (p5, p14).

mathematical_depth.rationale: Explains soft vs hard assignments and beta as systematic risk at an intuition level (p7, p8).
